false_positives.candidate:
Buffer docstring still describes Redis sets

The module glossary and the insert steps still say span-buf:s:* keys are sets and that payloads are added to a set. They are sorted sets scored by end_timestamp_precise, trimmed with ZPOPMIN. Operators debugging Redis or a flush incident will run SET commands (SMEMBERS/SCARD) and get WRONGTYPE, and the docstring no longer mentions that spans above 1000 are discarded on insert.

Insert-time ZPOPMIN can drop the root span silently

Once a segment sorted set exceeds 1000 members, the script ZPOPMINs the lowest end_timestamp scores down to 1000. The root/segment span is not protected, and the has-root-span flag is set independently of whether that payload is still in the set. A root that ended before its children, or any span that loses the score tie-break, is deleted and never flushed, while the segment still looks complete downstream and may still use the shorter root timeout. The flush-time guard in _load_segment_data that skipped segments over max_segment_spans (1001) and emitted spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded was removed, and the 1000 cap is hardcoded in Lua rather than passed from SpansBuffer.max_segment_spans. Oversized segments that miss this script (WRONGTYPE, script error, crash between the earlier ZADD and EVALSHA) are now flushed in full with no metric. Drops are silent.

No coverage for eviction, score merges, or the new paginator

Existing buffer tests only insert a handful of spans, all with the same end_timestamp_precise, and still only assert the full segment is flushed. Nothing covers a segment over 1000 spans, ZPOPMIN dropping or preserving the root, ZUNIONSTORE score behavior on redelivery, or WRONGTYPE against a leftover SET key. The audit-log OptimizedCursorPaginator path and negative-offset cursor handling also have no tests, so the datetime crash and bound-bypass path would ship green.

Redirect walk cap cut from 10000 to 1000

The parent-redirect walk that finds the segment key used to run up to 10000 hops, with a comment that a chain past that limit would not be joined correctly. It is now 1000, and the comment is gone. Each span adds a redirect entry. A parent chain longer than 1000 stops early, hsets the new span to an intermediate id, and merges into the wrong set. Those spans are flushed as a separate or truncated segment instead of the real trace segment, with no error.

Set keys switched to sorted sets with no migration

Span buffer keys `span-buf:s:{project:trace}:span_id` were Redis SETs (SADD/SUNIONSTORE/SSCAN) and are now sorted sets (ZADD here, ZCARD/ZUNIONSTORE/ZPOPMIN in add-buffer.lua, ZSCAN in _load_segment_data). The key format is unchanged and nothing deletes or converts existing keys. After deploy, any in-flight segment still stored as a SET makes those commands fail with WRONGTYPE, so process_spans errors and those traces are not buffered until the key expires (redis_ttl defaults to 3600s). A rollback is equally broken: once a new process ZADDs a key, the old SADD/SSCAN code also gets WRONGTYPE. Mixed-version deploys cannot drain the buffer.

ZUNIONSTORE default SUM corrupts end-timestamp scores

Merging segment keys now uses ZUNIONSTORE with the default AGGREGATE SUM (both the span_key merge at this line and the parent_key merge just below). Members are span payloads and scores are end_timestamp_precise, used later by ZPOPMIN to decide which spans to drop. Redis sums scores when the same payload is in both keys. That overlap happens on Kafka redelivery: the span is ZADDed onto the grouped parent key in process_spans and is still present in the previous segment key that this script unions in. The summed score is no longer an end timestamp, so eviction keeps the redelivered span and drops a different span whose real timestamp is older. SUNIONSTORE used to dedupe without changing identity. The union needs AGGREGATE MIN or MAX so the score stays a timestamp.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using Python’s built-in hash() to build cache keys is non-deterministic across processes (hash randomization), so keys won’t match across workers and invalidate_upsampling_cache may fail to delete them. Use a deterministic serialization of project_ids for the cache key.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Allowlist cache key uses process-randomized hash() and can serve the wrong decision

Eligibility is cached for 60s under `error_upsampling_eligible:{org}:{hash(tuple(sorted(project_ids)))}`. CPython `hash()` is salted per process (PYTHONHASHSEED), so the key is not stable across gunicorn workers or between the getter and `invalidate_upsampling_cache`. Shared cache entries never hit across processes, and a delete on one worker cannot evict keys written by another; nothing in this PR calls the invalidator anyway. Within a process, a hash collision between two project-id sets stores one allowlist boolean for both, so a non-allowlisted query can be rewritten to `sum(sample_weight)` (Snuba error or wrong counts) or an allowlisted query can skip upsampling. The key also omits the allowlist contents, so a cached True survives option changes for 60s. The new snuba tests mock `options.get` to different allowlists for the same projects and never clear this cache, so a locmem/Redis hit makes `test_error_upsampling_with_partial_allowlist` and `test_error_upsampling_with_no_allowlisted_projects` assert raw counts while the helper still upsamples. `options.get` is already in-process; this extra `cache.get`/`cache.set` on every events-stats request, including spans and logs, is a hot-path regression and ties the endpoint to cache availability.

true_positives.golden_comment: The upsampling eligibility check passes the outer dataset instead of the actual dataset used by scoped_dataset. In paths where the query ultimately runs against discover (e.g., dashboard split) while the original dataset is metrics, upsampling may be skipped even when all projects are allowlisted.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Upsampling decision ignores the dataset and query actually executed

`_get_event_stats` receives `scoped_dataset` and `query`, but eligibility calls `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects(..., dataset, request)`, using the closed-over request dataset and `request.GET['query']`. `get_event_stats_factory` then calls this helper with a different dataset and a rewritten query: the dashboard split path runs discover with `({query}) AND !event.type:transaction`, and sometimes `event.type:transaction`, while the outer dataset is metrics performance. Those internal queries are therefore classified from the wrong inputs. Error-only split queries on allowlisted projects are not upsampled, and any path where the outer request looks error-focused will also rewrite a later transaction-only execution in the same request. The comment that the cached decision keeps behavior consistent across query execution is the opposite of what this does.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling(), the check `if client_sample_rate:` treats 0.0 as falsy, so a sample_rate of 0.0 is silently skipped and never set on normalized_data.

false_positives.candidate:
Accidental gitlink added without a submodule config

This PR adds a gitlink `sentry-repo` pointing at commit a5d290951def84afdcc4c88d2f1f20023fc36e2a (the PR base) and does not update `.gitmodules` or any other file. That is not part of error upsampling. Merging it records a broken submodule: clones and CI checkouts have no URL for that gitlink, so the tree is dirty or the path fails to populate.

Error-query check is a substring match and false-positives on exclusions

`_is_error_focused_query` lowercases `request.GET['query']` and returns true if it contains the substring `event.type:error`. That matches queries that are not error-focused, including the common discover filters `!event.type:error` and `NOT event.type:error`, as well as `event.type:error OR event.type:transaction`. For an allowlisted project on the discover dataset, those queries rewrite `count()` to `sum(sample_weight)`. Transaction rows often have no error sample weight (or a different transaction sampling weight), so the events-stats request either 500s in Snuba or returns wildly inflated transaction counts. The same check misses real error queries such as `event.type:[error]`. Nothing in the new tests covers a negated or list-form `event.type` filter.

Errors dataset always rewrites count() but upsampled_count is only registered on discover

`_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` returns true for the `sentry.snuba.errors` dataset with no query check, and the events-stats endpoint then asks that dataset to execute `upsampled_count() as count`. The new aggregate is added only inside `discover.py`'s `function_converter`. The errors dataset is a separate snuba module with its own query builder/dataset config; unless that config inherits this exact converter, `dataset=errors` requests on allowlisted projects fail field resolution or Snuba with an unknown function. The new tests never pass `dataset=errors` (they use the default dataset and one discover transaction query), so this path is untested.

Helper tests override setUp without calling super and will not run

`ErrorUpsamplingTest.setUp` does not call `super().setUp()`. Sentry's TestCase setUp is what creates `self.user`, `self.team`, and the rest of the factory state that `self.create_project` uses (`teams=[self.team]` when teams are omitted). This setUp will raise AttributeError before any assertion, so the new unit tests do not actually cover allowlist checks, column rewrite, or the event.type filter.

Top-events ranking still uses raw count() while the series is upsampled

When upsampling is on, only `timeseries_columns` / `y_axes` are rewritten to `upsampled_count()`. `top_events_timeseries` still receives `orderby=self.get_orderby(request)` and `selected_columns=self.get_field_list(...)` unchanged, and the RPC top-events path at the `orderby=` call just above does the same. Top-N selection therefore ranks groups by stored rows, not by `sum(sample_weight)`. With uneven client sample rates that ranking is wrong: a group with 100 real errors at 1% (1 stored row, weight 100) loses to a group with 10 unsampled errors (10 stored rows). The plotted series for the chosen groups is then upsampled, so the chart both picks the wrong groups and does not match the totals used to pick them. `equations` are also left as raw `count()`, so equation widgets diverge from the rewritten count axis.

Transaction upsampling test does not wait for the event to be stored

`test_error_upsampling_with_transaction_events` calls `store_event` for a transaction and immediately queries events-stats, asserting the first bucket `count == 1`. setUp in the same class waits with `wait_for_event_count` after its error inserts, which is required because Snuba ingestion is not synchronous. Without that wait, the transaction is often invisible and the bucket is 0, so the test flakes and does not prove that transaction queries skip upsampling.

Upsampled count sums sample_weight, which this change never writes

`upsampled_count` is `toInt64(sum(sample_weight))` with no null fallback, and the column rewrite assumes every event in an allowlisted project has a meaningful sample_weight. Nothing in this PR sets that column. The only new writer is the test helper `_set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling`, which stores `sample_rate` equal to `contexts.error_sampling.client_sample_rate` (0.1 in the snuba test) and never sets `sample_weight` to `1/rate`. ClickHouse `sum` skips nulls and `toInt64` of an all-null sum is 0, so events without a weight disappear instead of counting as 1. The new stats test expects each single stored event to become `count == 10`; that cannot happen unless an unshown pipeline converts sample_rate 0.1 into sample_weight 10. Allowlisted project charts will undercount or show zeros, including for historical events ingested before weights existed.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using zip(error_ids, events.values()) assumes the get_multi result preserves the input order; dict value order is not guaranteed to match error_ids, so event data can be paired with the wrong ID (missing nodes also shift alignment).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Error payloads are zipped to ids by dict value order

fetch_error_details loads nodestore rows with get_multi(node_ids) and then pairs them with zip(error_ids, events.values()). get_multi returns a dict keyed by node id; .values() is not guaranteed to follow error_ids, and omitted missing keys shorten the sequence. The summary can attach the wrong title, message, and timestamp to an error id, or drop errors. Look up each node id explicitly. timestamp is also passed through uncoerced: if the stored event timestamp is an ISO string, error_events.sort and the < comparison in gen_request_data raise TypeError and the summarize request fails.

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoded empty data passed to TableWidgetVisualization causes it to always render an empty table instead of displaying actual results when the feature flag is enabled.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Table widget flag renders an empty table instead of query results

When organization.features includes use-table-widget-visualization, WidgetCardChart renders TableWidgetVisualization with columns={[]} and tableData hardcoded to data: [] and empty meta. The actual result.data, result.meta, fields, loading state, and custom field renderers are discarded. An empty columns array is also truthy, so the visualization will not fall back to meta.fields. Any org with the flag on sees blank dashboard table widgets.

true_positives.golden_comment: Validation logic incorrectly uses .get('timestamp'), which treats a timestamp of 0 as absent. It should directly check 'timestamp' in self.initial_data to ensure proper field presence detection, preventing both 'age=0' and 'timestamp' from passing mutual-exclusion validation.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Report time-field validation accepts missing and zero values

validate_timestamp and validate_age only run when that field is present, and both use initial_data.get(...) which treats 0 as absent. A report can omit both age and timestamp and still pass, even though the two Reporting API drafts require one of them. A report with timestamp set and age=0 (a valid just-generated report) skips the mutual-exclusion check, so both fields are stored together. The collector then metrics and logs structurally invalid reports instead of returning 422.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The BrowserReportingCollectorEndpoint returns HttpResponse objects but the endpoint inherits from Endpoint which expects rest_framework.response.Response objects.
In BaseDetectorTypeValidator.update(), the validator incorrectly updates instance.type using validated_data.get('detector_type') instead of validated_data.get('type').

Analytics events are recorded before the feature flag check, resulting in analytics being logged for all requests, including those that return 404 due to the feature being disabled. This can lead to misleading analytics data.

false_positives.candidate:
60s deadline cannot finish a 100-identity auth refresh batch

check_auth marks up to chunk_size (default 100) AuthIdentity rows last_synced=now and then enqueues check_auth_identities. That task now has processing_deadline_duration=60 while each identity does a provider refresh over the network. If the worker kills the task at 60s, the remaining ids in the chunk are not refreshed, and because last_synced was already bumped they will not be selected again until the next ~24h cutoff. Auth sessions that should have been invalidated can stay valid for a day.

Hidden span attributes are only removed while searching

HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES (is_segment, project_id, received) is applied only inside the search filter. When searchQuery is empty the function returns the full sorted list, so those fields still render. As soon as the user types a query they disappear, including when the query would otherwise match them. The exclusion needs to run before the empty-search return so the attributes are always hidden.

Issue titles are interpolated into a Markdown link unsanitized

MERGED_PR_SINGLE_ISSUE_TEMPLATE wraps the raw issue title in [**{title}**]({url}). Issue titles are attacker-controlled error messages and routinely contain ] (for example foo[0] or KeyError paths). In CommonMark that closes the link label early, so the Sentry bot comment on GitHub/GitLab gets a broken issue link and can be turned into an arbitrary link or extra Markdown. Truncation to 50 characters does not remove ] or newlines. Escape or strip those characters before formatting.

Merged PR comment helpers are not on the workflow class

get_merged_pr_single_issue_template and _truncate_title were added on the class that owns get_top_5_issues_by_count (the class immediately above OpenPRCommentWorkflow), but the body calls PRCommentWorkflow._truncate_title. GitHubPRCommentWorkflow and GitlabPRCommentWorkflow invoke self.get_merged_pr_single_issue_template / self.get_environment_info. Those workflow classes do not inherit this class, and PRCommentWorkflow does not define _truncate_title, so posting a suspect-issue PR/MR comment raises AttributeError and the comment task fails.

Trace waterfall container no longer fills its parent height

The wrapper that was FlexBox (display:flex, flex-direction:column, flex-grow:1, height:100%) was replaced with Flex direction="column" flex={1}. flex={1} is flex: 1 1 0, not flex-grow: 1, and height: 100% was dropped. The waterfall and its virtualized list size against this container, so the trace view can collapse or stop scrolling to the full viewport height.

true_positives.golden_comment: Backup code validation is case-sensitive due to the use of indexOf(). This causes validation to fail if a user enters uppercase hex characters, as backup codes should be case-insensitive for a better user experience.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Backup codes are compared case-sensitively

Stored codes are lowercase hex (crypto.randomBytes(5).toString("hex")), but the login check uses indexOf on the raw string after only stripping "-". The same comparison is in apps/web/pages/api/auth/two-factor/totp/disable.ts around the backupCode.replaceAll call. The login field placeholder is "XXXXX-XXXXX", so a user who types the code in the casing the UI shows is rejected with incorrect backup code even though the code is valid. Normalize by trimming and lowercasing before compare on both login and disable.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because backupCodes are decrypted and mutated in memory before being written back, two concurrent login requests using the same backupCode could both pass this check and update, so a single backup code may effectively be accepted more than once if used concurrently, weakening the intended one-time-use semantics.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Backup-code consumption is a lost-update race

A matching backup code is marked used by reading the decrypted array, setting that index to null, and writing the whole blob back with a plain user update. Two overlapping logins can both read the same array before either write. If they present the same code, both pass the check and both sessions are created, so a one-time code works twice. If they present different codes, the later write overwrites the earlier one, so one consumed code is restored and can be reused. The update needs to be conditional on the previous ciphertext (or done under a row lock) so a stale write cannot resurrect a used code.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The exported function TwoFactor handles backup codes and is in BackupCode.tsx. Inconsistent naming.
Error message mentions 'backup code login' but this is a disable endpoint, not login

Object URL for backup codes is not revoked on component unmount, leading to a potential memory leak. This can cause increased memory usage over time, especially if the component is mounted and unmounted frequently.

false_positives.candidate:
Backup code plus any TOTP value skips the password

In the credentials authorize() path, the password is verified only when credentials.totpCode is falsy (the existing check around the password branch). The new branch then accepts a backup code whenever credentials.backupCode is non-empty and never checks the TOTP value. A caller who knows only the email and one backup code can therefore sign in by also sending any non-empty totpCode (for example "000000") and omitting or faking the password. That makes a long-lived backup code a single factor and a full account takeover secret, instead of password plus backup code. The login UI happens to send an empty totpCode, but the public credentials endpoint does not. Password verification must run for CAL users on this path, and a dummy totpCode must not select the backup-code branch.

Backup codes are lost if the dialog is dismissed

After TOTP enable succeeds, the only copy of the plaintext backup codes lives in this modal, and onEnable() runs only from the Close button. The Dialog is still wired to the parent's onOpenChange, so Escape, overlay click, or the dialog close control hides it without onEnable() and without any warning that the codes cannot be shown again. There is no later API to reveal or regenerate codes while 2FA stays on, and a refresh on this step drops them too. The settings switch can also stay off because the parent is never told enable finished, so the user is left with 2FA on server-side, no saved codes, and a UI that still looks disabled. This step should block dismiss until the user explicitly finishes, and that path must call onEnable().

Download control submits the enable form

The backup-code footer is inside the Form whose submit handler is handleEnable. Copy and Close call preventDefault because a click otherwise submits that form; the Download control does not, and its Button has no type="button". It is also wrapped in an anchor. Activating Download therefore posts the TOTP enable request again (which can error once 2FA is already on, or replace the page) and can cancel the file download, so the main way to save codes fails. Set type="button" and preventDefault, or render a non-submitting link.

Lost access button submits the disable form

The new Lost access / Go back button sits inside the disable Form and does not set type="button" or preventDefault. The enable modal in this same change had to preventDefault on footer buttons for that reason. Clicking Lost access therefore submits handleDisable with an empty code at the same time as it toggles the backup-code field, so the user gets an incorrect-code or second-factor error instead of a clean switch to the backup-code input. Stop the click from submitting.

Missing-backup-codes copy points at a screen that does not exist

missing_backup_codes says "Please generate them in your settings." Nothing in this PR adds a settings action to generate or rotate backup codes after 2FA is already on; setup refuses when twoFactorEnabled is true, and existing users who enabled 2FA before the migration have a null backupCodes column. Shown at login or when disabling 2FA, the message tells a locked-out user to do something they cannot do. The string should say that codes are only issued during 2FA setup and that an account with none cannot use this fallback.

No test covers backup-code login or single use

The new login and disable-with-backup-code paths are untested. The file's own TODO calls out login and disabling 2FA with a backup code, and the checklist says no test proves the feature. The enable test never clicks backup-codes-close or asserts the codes, and the other test only checks the download filename and that a toast appears, not the file contents, clipboard text, a successful backup-code sign-in, or that a used code is rejected. Those gaps would miss the password bypass, case-sensitive compare, and non-atomic consumption bugs.

true_positives.golden_comment: A null reference occurs in GoogleCalendarService.createEvent() and updateEvent() when mainHostDestinationCalendar is destructured from evt.destinationCalendar but evt.destinationCalendar is null or an empty array, causing mainHostDestinationCalendar to be undefined.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Google Meet bookings crash when destinationCalendar is missing

The Google Meet fallback now reads mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration after destructuring evt.destinationCalendar ?? []. If the array is missing or empty (the new call sites pass null or []), mainHostDestinationCalendar is undefined and this throws before any calendar event is created. The previous code used optional chaining (destinationCalendar?.integration), which fell back to Cal Video. Any Meet booking without a destination calendar now fails inside EventManager.create instead of booking.

true_positives.golden_comment: Logic error: when externalCalendarId is provided, you're searching for a calendar where externalId === externalCalendarId, but this will always fail since you're looking for a calendar that matches itself. Should likely find by credentialId or use different logic.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Google update no longer falls back to a destination calendar id

updateEvent sets calendarId to externalCalendarId, or else find(cal => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId). When externalCalendarId is null or empty that comparison cannot match, so calendarId is undefined and events.update is called with no calendar id. The old code used destinationCalendar.externalId. Bookings whose references have no externalCalendarId (older rows, or creates that did not persist one) can no longer be rescheduled or updated on Google. deleteEvent has the same dead find, but still falls back to "primary"; update does not.

true_positives.golden_comment: Logic inversion in organization creation: The slug property is now conditionally set when IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED is true, instead of when it's false as originally intended. This change, combined with requestedSlug still being set when IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED is true, results in both properties being set when billing is enabled, and neither when disabled
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Organization slug is stored under the opposite billing flag

The spread was changed from !IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED && { slug } to IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED ? { slug } : {}. That inverts org creation: self-hosted (billing disabled) organizations are created with no slug, so org URLs do not resolve, and billing-enabled organizations get slug set immediately instead of only requestedSlug pending approval. The requestedSlug line below was only rewritten from && to a ternary and is unchanged in meaning. This is unrelated to destination calendars and breaks org provisioning.

true_positives.golden_comment: The Calendar interface now requires createEvent(event, credentialId), but some implementations (e.g., Lark/Office365) still declare createEvent(event) only—this breaks the interface contract (also applies to other locations in the PR).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Non-Google adapters still write only the first destination calendar

CalendarManager now passes credential.id into createEvent so each host credential can target its own calendar, but Office 365 createEvent ignores that argument and always posts to destinationCalendar[0].externalId (or /me/calendar/events). Lark createEvent/updateEvent/deleteEvent (larkcalendar CalendarService.ts around line 129) and CalDAV createEvent (packages/lib/CalendarService.ts around line 162) do the same and only read index 0. For a second host, the request is made with that host's token against the first host's calendar id. Office/Lark fail the call; CalDAV filters to no calendars and still returns success, so the host silently gets no event. The collective multi-host fix therefore only works for Google.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `credential` may be undefined when passed to `updateEvent` if `reference.credentialId` is set but the credential is not found. This can lead to a runtime error when `updateEvent` is called with an undefined credential, which should be handled to prevent crashes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
One missing calendar credential aborts every calendar update

updateAllCalendarEvents pushes updateEvent(credential, ...) even when credential is still undefined after the DB lookup (no row, or app.slug missing). getCalendar then throws inside the for-loop, before Promise.all and before later references are handled. The catch maps every calendar reference to success: false and no longer logs the error (console.error was removed), so a single bad host credential silently fails reschedule, location change, and attendee updates for every host.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The optional chaining on mainHostDestinationCalendar?.integration is redundant since you already check mainHostDestinationCalendar in the ternary condition.

false_positives.candidate:
Cancelling remaining recurring events only deletes the first calendar reference

The new multi-reference loop wraps the recurring allRemainingBookings branch, but that branch still does updatedBookings references.find for a single _calendar reference and deletes it with every calendar credential on the booking owner, not with reference.credentialId. It also runs once per outer reference, so the same first event is deleted repeatedly. Other hosts' calendar events on the recurring series are never deleted, and a credential that does not own that event is used. Non-recurring cancel uses the per-reference credential and is fine; recurring collective cancel is not.

Collective host calendars are dropped when the organizer has none

destinationCalendar is set to null when neither the event type nor the organizer has one, and the collective branch then does evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...teamDestinationCalendars). Optional chaining does not assign, so the array of other hosts' destination calendars is discarded. A collective event whose owner has no destination calendar creates no host calendar events at all, which is the case this PR is meant to fix. Initialize the array before pushing (for example evt.destinationCalendar = [...(evt.destinationCalendar ?? []), ...teamDestinationCalendars]).

Confirm and payment flows still pass a single destination calendar

Only handleNewBooking appends every collective host's destinationCalendar before EventManager.create. confirm.handler, the Stripe webhook (packages/features/ee/payments/api/webhook.ts around lines 119 and 229), and the PayPal webhook (paypal-webhook.ts around line 152) still build evt.destinationCalendar from booking.destinationCalendar or the booking owner's calendar only. Collective events that require confirmation or payment create calendar events on that later path, so the other hosts never get a calendar event or a booking reference. Reschedule/cancel then have nothing to update for those hosts.

Google organizer email is always the first destination calendar

createEvent (and updateEvent) always uses destinationCalendar[0].externalId as the organizer attendee email, while the calendar written to is chosen by credentialId. EventManager.createAllCalendarEvents calls createEvent once per host credential with the full array, so host 2's insert is authenticated as host 2 but marked organizer with host 1's calendar id. Google rejects that insert or creates the event under the wrong organizer, so secondary collective hosts do not get a correct event even on Google.

Hangout-link patch uses an undefined calendar id

Insert uses selectedCalendar || "primary", but the follow-up events.patch that writes the Meet link into the description passes calendarId: selectedCalendar with no fallback. selectedCalendar is undefined whenever no destination entry matches credentialId (or externalId is null). The event is created on primary and the patch is sent to an undefined calendar, so the description never gets the hangout link. Previously selectedCalendar was always an external id or "primary".

Video booking references no longer store credentialId

referencesToCreate now sets credentialId only when the result type includes "_calendar", and forces undefined otherwise. Previously non-calendar results kept result.credentialId. Cancel (and any later video cleanup that looks up bookingReference.credentialId) will not find the Zoom/Daily/Meet credential, so the video meeting is left running after the booking is cancelled. New bookings created after this change are affected; updateLocation still copies result.credentialId, so the two paths disagree.

Webhook destinationCalendar changed from object to array

CalendarEvent.destinationCalendar is now DestinationCalendar[] | null, and BOOKING_* webhook payloads spread that field. Subscribers that read destinationCalendar.integration, .externalId, or .credentialId will break. The change is labeled a non-breaking bug fix. Payloads are also inconsistent: handleNewBooking still sends null when unset, while confirm/cancel/payment send []. The e2e fixture was only updated for BOOKING_REJECTED (null to []), so BOOKING_CREATED still expects null and does not lock the new array shape.

true_positives.matched_candidate:

If the parsed payload has no refresh_token, this sets refresh_token to the literal string "refresh_token" and returns that object. true_positives.matched_candidate:

After a Google token refresh, the value written to Credential.key is the object returned by parseRefreshTokenResponse, which is the Zod safeParse wrapper ({success, data}) rather than the credential object. Previously googleCredentialSchema.parse returned the tokens themselves. The next GoogleCalendarService construction calls googleCredentialSchema.parse(credential.key) and throws because access_token is nested under data, so every Google calendar stops working after the first refresh (typically within an hour). This runs even when credential sync is disabled. When sync is enabled it is also wrong in a second way: refreshOAuthTokens returns an unparsed fetch Response, so res.data is undefined and token.access_token throws before a usable token is applied.

true_positives.golden_comment: When APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED and CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT are set, the refreshFunction helper returns the fetch Response, but several callers (for example GoogleCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting res.data, and HubspotCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting a HubspotToken) assume it returns the integration-specific token object. That mismatch will cause runtime errors in the sync-enabled path unless the return type or those call sites are adjusted.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Sync refresh returns a raw Response that callers cannot use

When CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT is set, this returns the fetch Response and never checks response.ok or parses JSON. Callers were not updated to that contract. HubSpot and both Zoho services expect an axios/SDK body with .data or accessToken/expiresIn and will throw or write a non-token value into Credential.key. Google reads res.data. Lark, Webex, and Zoom expect provider-specific JSON (Lark's code/data envelope, Webex's strict scope schema, Zoom's expires_in) and will fail or, in Zoom's case, persist NaN expiry and the stub refresh token. The request also sends only calcomUserId and appSlug, with no documented response schema that those adapters share, so turning the feature on breaks token refresh for the wired apps instead of refreshing them.

true_positives.golden_comment: When the sync endpoint path is used, res is a fetch Response and has no .data; res?.data will be undefined and token.access_token will throw at runtime. This relies on a consistent return shape from refreshOAuthTokens, which isn’t guaranteed currently.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Google refresh persists the Zod result and corrupts the credential

After a Google token refresh, the value written to Credential.key is the object returned by parseRefreshTokenResponse, which is the Zod safeParse wrapper ({success, data}) rather than the credential object. Previously googleCredentialSchema.parse returned the tokens themselves. The next GoogleCalendarService construction calls googleCredentialSchema.parse(credential.key) and throws because access_token is nested under data, so every Google calendar stops working after the first refresh (typically within an hour). This runs even when credential sync is disabled. When sync is enabled it is also wrong in a second way: refreshOAuthTokens returns an unparsed fetch Response, so res.data is undefined and token.access_token throws before a usable token is applied.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `refreshOAuthTokens` function is passed `credentialId` instead of `userId`, which breaks the credential sync functionality by causing incorrect user lookups. This issue can lead to failures in syncing user credentials, impacting user experience.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Zoho Bigin sync sends credential id as the user id

refreshOAuthTokens's third argument is the Cal.com user id, but refreshAccessToken passes credentialId. When credential sync is enabled, the parent app looks up tokens for whatever user has that numeric id, not the owner of this credential. If parsing is later fixed to accept the sync response, those tokens are written onto this credential, so one user can be given another user's Zoho access token. With the current fetch Response return value, tokenInfo.data is undefined and refresh throws instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `jsforce.Connection` is created using stale `credentialKey.access_token` and `credentialKey.instance_url` after a token refresh, which can lead to authentication failures and incorrect data access. Ensure that the connection is established using the refreshed token values instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Salesforce client always refreshes, then crashes on missing prisma

getClient now refreshes the Salesforce token on every CalendarService construction, then calls prisma.credential.update, but prisma is never imported in this file. That throws ReferenceError, the Connection is never returned, and every Salesforce calendar/CRM operation fails after deploy. Even if the import is added, the jsforce Connection is still built with credentialKey.access_token (the pre-refresh token) rather than the access token just fetched, and a failed refresh now takes down calls that previously relied on a still-valid access token. Enabling credential sync makes this worse: parseRefreshTokenResponse switches to the minimum schema, strips instance_url and the other Salesforce fields, and the update overwrites the stored key with that stripped object.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse` function can throw on invalid payloads, resulting in 500 Internal Server Errors instead of the expected 400 Bad Request responses. This can lead to confusion for clients and hinder proper error handling.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Credential sync updates an arbitrary row and can duplicate keys

The handler finds a credential with findFirst({userId, appId}) and no orderBy, then updates only that id. (userId, appId) is not unique: Google's OAuth callback always inserts a new credential row, and two concurrent webhook calls can both observe no row and both create. findFirst may therefore update a credential that is not the one calendar/video code loads, so the webhook returns success while the live tokens stay stale, or it creates duplicates that later refreshes keep splitting. The update path also never sets invalid: false, so a credential already marked invalid stays unusable after the source of truth pushes new keys. Zod parse and symmetricDecrypt/JSON.parse are uncaught, so a bad body or ciphertext becomes an unhandled 500 instead of a 4xx.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The Salesforce integration checks `response.statusText` instead of `response.ok` when handling OAuth token refresh responses. This can lead to unreliable behavior, as a successful response may not be correctly identified, resulting in the use of stale credentials and potential authentication failures.

false_positives.candidate:
No tests for credential write or token-refresh regressions

The new webhook can create or overwrite OAuth credential JSON for any user, and the shared refresh helpers change the success path for Google, Office 365, Zoom, and Salesforce even when sync is off. The PR adds no tests, and the checklist confirms none were run. A test that refreshes a Google or Office 365 credential with sync disabled, and one that posts a valid webhook payload, would have caught the safeParse object being stored and the literal refresh_token overwrite before merge.

Outbound token sync sends no shared secret

The sync POST that is supposed to return a third-party access token authenticates nothing: no CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET, Authorization header, or signed timestamp, only calcomUserId and appSlug. The inbound webhook requires the shared secret, but the call that actually dispenses live OAuth access tokens does not. A self-hoster implementing the contract this client calls (the comment says the response should contain the access token and expiry) exposes user access tokens to anyone who can reach that URL and guess or enumerate a user id.

Zoom sync uses app slug zoomvideo instead of zoom

The refresh call passes appSlug "zoomvideo", but the Zoom credential is stored with appId "zoom" (see the OAuth callback) and the installed-app path uses slug "zoom". The webhook and the parent app store key off the real slug, so a sync refresh asks for an app that does not exist and will not return this user's Zoom tokens. Other adapters in this PR pass the real slug (google-calendar, msteams, office365-calendar).

true_positives.golden_comment: The addGuests.handler.ts blacklist check uses blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest) after lowercasing the blacklist but not the input guest emails, allowing attackers to bypass BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS restrictions by submitting emails with uppercase characters.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Guest emails are not normalized, deduped, or blacklist-safe

Blacklist entries are lowercased, but each guest is compared with includes(guest) and with attendee.email using raw ===. Zod's email() does not lowercase, so Guest@x.com misses a blacklist entry of guest@x.com and is also treated as a new attendee when guest@x.com is already on the booking. The filter also does not dedupe the input array, and ZAddGuestsInputSchema has no .max() or uniqueness check, so one request can insert repeated rows and fan out an unbounded number of meeting invites. The organizer address is not excluded either.

Team admin/owner check requires both roles

isTeamAdminOrOwner is computed with && between isTeamAdmin and isTeamOwner. Those are mutually exclusive membership roles, so the condition is never true for a normal team admin or owner. Team hosts who are not the booking user and not an attendee are always rejected with FORBIDDEN, so the team path this check was meant to allow cannot add guests.

true_positives.golden_comment: The sendAddGuestsEmails function in email-manager.ts passes the full calendarEvent.attendees array when determining which attendees receive AttendeeScheduledEmail vs AttendeeAddGuestsEmail, but checks if newGuests.includes(attendee.email) where newGuests is the input guests array.

true_positives.golden_comment: uniqueGuests filters out existing attendees and blacklisted emails but does not deduplicate duplicates within the input; createMany can insert duplicate attendee rows if the client submits repeated emails.
true_positives.matched_candidate:

Blacklist entries are lowercased, but each guest is compared with includes(guest) and with attendee.email using raw ===. Zod's email() does not lowercase, so Guest@x.com misses a blacklist entry of guest@x.com and is also treated as a new attendee when guest@x.com is already on the booking. true_positives.golden_comment: The `sendAddGuestsEmails` function does not check the `disableStandardEmails` flags in the `EventType` metadata, which may result in sending emails to hosts/attendees even when standard emails are disabled for the event type.
true_positives.matched_candidate:

Every other sender in this file bails out when event type metadata has disableStandardEmails for the host or attendee. sendAddGuestsEmails always emails the organizer, every team member, and every attendee, and the handler never passes eventType.metadata. false_negatives.golden_comment: Starting with an array containing an empty string may cause validation issues. Consider starting with an empty array [] and handling the empty state in the MultiEmail component instead.

false_positives.candidate:
Calendar update uses the caller's credentials after the DB write

Attendees are inserted first, then EventManager is built from ctx.user and getUsersCredentials(ctx.user). The booking host's credentials are loaded on booking.user and never used. When the caller is a team admin or an attendee, the update runs with credentials that do not own the event, so the host calendar/video attendee list is not updated. updateCalendarAttendees is not in a transaction and is not caught; if it throws, the mutation returns an error even though the guests are already stored, and sendAddGuestsEmails never runs, so nobody is notified and a retry is treated as a duplicate.

Guests can be added to cancelled, pending, or past bookings

The handler never checks booking.status or endTime before createMany and before sending mail. Any organizer or attendee can add guests to a CANCELLED, REJECTED, or PENDING booking. The new mail classes always attach an ICS with status CONFIRMED and method REQUEST, so people are invited to a meeting that is not an accepted upcoming event. The bookings list also keeps this action on past confirmed rows (bookedActions is rendered when isBookingInPast && isConfirmed), so the UI offers the same flow after the event has ended.

Host disableGuests setting is not enforced

eventType is loaded but disableGuests is never read. Hosts turn that flag on so bookers cannot invite extra people or forward the meeting link. This mutation still creates attendees and emails them the full invite, including videoCallData (URL and password) when a video reference exists, so the event-type privacy setting is bypassed by anyone who passes the organizer/attendee check.

New guests are stored with an empty name

createMany sets name to "" and copies the organizer timezone and locale. Attendee mail then builds To as `${name} <${email}>`, which is a blank display name, and the scheduled/add-guest templates greet an empty name. Guests also get times in the host timezone because the dialog never collects theirs.

Seated events get extra attendees without seat records

If eventType.seatsPerTimeSlot is set, each attendee is a seat holder backed by a BookingSeat. This handler still createMany's Attendee rows and does not create seats or check remaining capacity. Seat counts, no-show, and per-seat cancel flows that use seatsReferences will disagree with booking.attendees. sendAddGuestsEmails also sends every attendee a normal scheduled/add-guests email and never passes seatsShowAttendees, so hidden seat lists are emailed to the new addresses.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1 reads a possibly stale value and can lose increments under concurrency; consider an atomic increment via Prisma (increment: 1) to avoid race conditions (also applies to the similar update in the catch block).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Overlapping crons lose retry increments and can double-send

Both failure paths write `retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1` from the value loaded at the start of the loop instead of an atomic increment. Two overlapping runs of this cron can both select the same unscheduled reminder, both call Twilio, and both store the same next count. Recipients get duplicate texts, and because the stored count never moves past that shared value the `retryCount > 1` delete may never fire, so the retry cap does not hold under overlap. Claim the row (conditional update of scheduled, or increment in the database) before calling Twilio.

true_positives.golden_comment: The deletion logic in scheduleSMSReminders.ts incorrectly deletes non-SMS workflow reminders (e.g., Email, WhatsApp) that have retryCount > 1. This occurs because the retryCount condition within the OR clause for deletion lacks a method: WorkflowMethods.SMS filter, causing it to apply to all reminder types instead of only SMS reminders, which is the intended scope of this function.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
retryCount cleanup deletes every workflow reminder, not just failed SMS

The new deleteMany ORs the existing past-due SMS clause with `{ retryCount: { gt: 1 } }` and that second clause has no method, scheduled, or date filter. WorkflowReminder is shared by EMAIL, SMS, and WHATSAPP. Every cron run therefore permanently deletes any reminder of any method once retryCount is greater than 1, including a row that was already scheduled and still has a provider referenceId. The comment on line 28 still says this only removes past SMS reminders. Scope the predicate to unscheduled SMS (and filter the later findMany the same way); otherwise any non-SMS writer of this new column, or a scheduled SMS row that ever exceeds the cap, loses the reminder.

false_positives.candidate:
A successful Twilio schedule is counted as a failure if saving the SID throws

twilio.scheduleSMS runs before the update that sets scheduled and referenceId. If Twilio accepts the message and that update throws, the new catch increments retryCount and leaves scheduled false and referenceId unset. The next cron loads the same reminder again and sends another SMS. After retryCount exceeds 1 the row is deleted, so the already accepted Twilio message can no longer be cancelled from a stored SID. Only a failed scheduleSMS call should advance retryCount; if persistence fails after Twilio accepts the message, cancel that message or retry the write without treating it as a failed send.

Missing number or empty body never counts toward the retry cap

retryCount is incremented only when Twilio returns a falsy result or throws, and only inside `if (message?.length > 0 && sendTo)`. If the attendee or step has no phone number, or the step has no reminder body and the template is not REMINDER, the loop skips the row and leaves scheduled false and retryCount at 0. That reminder is loaded again on every cron run until scheduledDate is in the past, which is the unbounded reschedule this PR is meant to stop. Treat a missing destination or empty message as a failed attempt, or delete the reminder immediately.

No test locks the retry cap or the delete scope

The new failure accounting and deleteMany predicate have no tests. A regression should assert that one failed SMS schedule leaves the reminder, that a second failure removes it on the next run, and that email or WhatsApp reminders and already scheduled SMS rows are not deleted by the retryCount clause. Without that, the unscoped OR delete and the off-path skips (no phone number, persistence failure after Twilio accepts) can ship unnoticed.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In getBaseConditions(), the else if (filterConditions) and final else branches are unreachable. This is because getAuthorizationConditions() always returns a non-null Prisma.Sql object, making authConditions always truthy, which means only the first two if/else if conditions are ever evaluated.

Fetching userIdsFromOrg only when teamsFromOrg.length > 0 can exclude org-level members for orgs without child teams; consider deriving from teamIds (which includes orgId) or removing the guard so org-only orgs still include member user bookings.

false_positives.candidate:
OR auth fragment is not fully parenthesized, so extra AND filters skip team bookings

Team and org authorization SQL is built as `(<team predicate>) OR (<user predicate>)` (org reduce at lines 171-174, team reduce at lines 204-207). Those parentheses wrap each branch only, not the whole OR. `getBaseConditions` returns that fragment as-is when there is no event-type or member filter (line 75). AND binds tighter than OR in PostgreSQL, so the intended caller query `WHERE ${await service.getBaseConditions()} AND "startTime" >= ${from} AND "startTime" < ${to}` — the replacement for the removed `findMany`, which ANDed caller filters onto the entire authorization object — is parsed as `team_booking_predicate OR (personal_booking_predicate AND startTime filters)`. Every team booking for that team or org is included no matter what date, status, or other AND predicates the caller adds. Insights over-count and can return bookings outside the window the caller applied. `getBaseConditions` only wraps the auth fragment when a service-level filter is also present (line 73). Wrap the full OR, and the final fragment returned to callers, in parentheses. The new tests expect this unparenthesized text and never run team/org SQL with an additional AND, so they do not catch it.

toEqual(Prisma.sql) does not match nested SQL fragments

Composed conditions are built by nesting `Prisma.sql` values (`(${acc}) OR (${condition})` and the filter AND reduce). Prisma does not flatten nested `strings`/`values` until execution, so the object from `getAuthorizationConditions`/`getFilterConditions` is not deeply equal to a single flat `Prisma.sql` template with the same text. `expect(conditions).toEqual(Prisma.sql`...`)` therefore fails for the team-scope assertion (line 295), the org-scope assertion (line 332), and the combined-filter assertion (line 429) — the cases that use `ANY(...)` and OR. Flat cases (user scope, a single filter, `1=0`) can still pass. The only test that executes SQL is the user-scope `$queryRaw` query, which never hits `ANY` or the OR precedence bug. Compare flattened SQL text and bound values, or run the team/org fragments, instead of `toEqual` on raw `Prisma.Sql` objects.

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: macOS-specific sed syntax with empty string after -i flag will fail on Linux systems
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Webhook helper is macOS-only and writes .env relative to the cwd

The new script updates GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL with sed -i '' (BSD sed). On GNU sed that form treats '' as the script and does not edit the file, so Linux developers never get the tunnel URL written. ENV_FILE is ../.env relative to the current working directory, not the script path: running bash scripts/test-gcal-webhooks.sh from the repo root writes the parent directory's .env, not the app env file. cleanup also always exits 0, so a failed tunnel startup is reported as success.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The updateManyByCredentialId call uses an empty data object, which prevents Prisma's @updatedAt decorator from updating the updatedAt timestamp. This results in inaccurate cache status tracking, as the timestamp isn't updated when the cache is refreshed. To fix this, explicitly set the updatedAt field.

Throwing a generic Error for authentication failures results in a 500 response in tRPC. Instead, it should return a structured TRPCError with an appropriate code, such as FORBIDDEN, to accurately reflect the error type.
Date is formatted with hardcoded 'en-US' locale instead of using the user's locale from useLocale, which can lead to incorrect date representation for users in different locales.

false_positives.candidate:
Backfill stamps every existing cache as updated at migrate time

The new updatedAt column is added as NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW(), so every existing CalendarCache row gets the migration timestamp rather than when it was actually written. CalendarCache has no createdAt; the only freshness signal already stored is expiresAt (writes set it to about now + 30 days). After deploy, every Google credential with any historical cache row shows "Last updated" as the deploy time, including stale and expired caches, which defeats the status feature. Backfill from expiresAt minus the cache TTL (and drop the default only if you still want Prisma @updatedAt to own later writes) before this ships; it cannot be reconstructed later.

Cache delete is undone by active Google watches

deleteCacheHandler only runs calendarCache.deleteMany for the credential. It does not stop google channel subscriptions on SelectedCalendar, and GoogleCalendarService.fetchAvailabilityAndSetCache (called from the webhook path) writes CalendarCache again and then touches those selected calendars. The confirmation copy says the delete cannot be undone, but the next notification recreates the rows. Users clearing a bad cache will see it return with no explanation, and a reload can show a new timestamp as if the delete did not stick.

Cache status treats expired rows as a live cache

getCacheStatusByCredentialIds groups CalendarCache by credentialId and takes max(updatedAt) with no expiresAt filter. getCachedAvailability only treats a row as a hit when expiresAt is still in the future. Any leftover expired row therefore makes connected calendars report cacheUpdatedAt and the dropdown offers "Delete cached data" even though availability lookups are already cache misses. The status does not mean the cache is serving data.

Delegation calendar cache is invisible to status and delete

Cache status is loaded only via getCacheStatusByCredentialIds(connected calendar credential ids). The same repository documents that in-memory delegation credentials use negative ids that are not stored on CalendarCache, and reads for those users are keyed by userId plus the free/busy key so they can reuse a real credential's cache. Those org/delegation Google connections — the users the calendar-cache feature flag is aimed at — always get cacheUpdatedAt null, so the new menu never offers delete. deleteCacheHandler cannot fix that either: it requires a Credential row with id = credentialId and userId = the session user, which does not match a negative in-memory id or a cache row owned by another credential id.

Deleting cache leaves the UI showing the old cache status

deleteCacheMutation only toasts and calls the optional onSuccess prop. Unlike the disconnect mutation in the same component, it never invalidates viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars. That query is what supplies cacheUpdatedAt, and SelectedCalendarsSettingsWebWrapper loads it with refetchOnWindowFocus: false. After a successful delete the menu still shows the previous "Last updated" time and "Delete cached data" until a full remount, so the action looks like it failed.

No tests for deleteCache ownership or status mapping

deleteCache is a new authenticated mutation that deletes every CalendarCache row for a client-supplied credentialId after a userId check, and connectedCalendars now depends on getCacheStatusByCredentialIds. Nothing in the PR covers another user (or a negative delegation id) being rejected, a successful delete actually removing rows, or expired versus live rows being mapped to cacheUpdatedAt. A regression in the ownership where-clause would ship silently.

dev:cron now calls tsx, which this package does not depend on

dev:cron changed from ts-node cron-tester.ts to npx tsx cron-tester.ts. ts-node is a declared devDependency; tsx is not in this package.json, and the app pins Yarn 3.4.1, where npx is not the workspace runner and will try to fetch tsx outside the lockfile. yarn dev:cron fails offline or in CI, or runs an unpinned tsx. This change is unrelated to calendar cache and should stay on the declared runner or add tsx as a dependency and invoke it through Yarn.

true_positives.golden_comment: Asynchronous functions deleteScheduledEmailReminder and deleteScheduledSMSReminder are called without await inside forEach loops. This occurs during booking rescheduling/cancellation, and workflow/workflow step deletion/updates. Consequently, scheduled workflow reminders may not be reliably cancelled, potentially leaving them active.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cancellation of reminders is not awaited and failures are ignored

Booking cancellation starts deleteScheduledEmailReminder / deleteScheduledSMSReminder inside forEach and never awaits them, and those helpers swallow errors. The previous code awaited prisma.workflowReminder deletes in Promise.all; that persistence was removed. On a serverless freeze after the handler returns, or if the update throws, cancelled stays unset and unscheduled reminder rows are not deleted. The scheduleEmailReminders cron will then submit those emails to SendGrid, so cancelled bookings still receive workflow reminders. SMS cancels have the same gap and no retry cron.

true_positives.golden_comment: When immediateDelete is true, the deleteScheduledEmailReminder function cancels the SendGrid email but fails to delete the corresponding WorkflowReminder record from the database. This creates orphaned database entries and is inconsistent with the immediateDelete: false path, which marks the record as cancelled. The SendGrid DELETE API call is also omitted in this path.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
immediateDelete cancels SendGrid but does not record or retry it

If immediateDelete is set, deleteScheduledEmailReminder POSTs a SendGrid batch cancel and returns without setting cancelled or deleting the WorkflowReminder row. Success still leaves a pending cancellation in scheduled_sends until the original send time, which is the 100-cap failure this PR describes. Failure is only console.logged, so the row stays scheduled with cancelled unset and the cron will never retry. Callers cannot tell that cancellation failed. The non-immediate path also only flips cancelled, even when scheduledDate is already inside the 15-minute cron interval, so a reminder due before the next cron tick is still delivered.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The 'cancelled' field is nullable, which can lead to existing records having null values instead of a default of false. This can cause incorrect behavior in the application when checking the cancellation status of reminders.

false_positives.candidate:
Due reminders are deleted before SendGrid is cancelled

The cron first deleteMany's every EMAIL WorkflowReminder with scheduledDate <= now, including rows with cancelled=true, and only then looks up reminders to cancel on SendGrid. A cancelled reminder whose send time has just passed, or that the previous run failed to cancel, is removed from the database with no SendGrid cancel and no retry. If SendGrid has not yet dispatched that sendAt, the email still goes out for a cancelled or rescheduled booking.

No tests for deferred cancel, immediateDelete, or the cron

This change replaces awaited reminder deletes with a cancelled flag, a deferred SendGrid cancel, and an immediateDelete mode, but adds no tests. There is no coverage for paid vs unpaid cancel, reschedule, workflow delete, a SendGrid error mid-batch, or a reminder already inside the cron window. Those paths are what caused reminders to keep sending, and they can regress without a failing test.

One SendGrid cancel failure stalls the whole cancellation queue

All cancelled reminders due within the next hour are cancelled in one try/catch. DB deletes are queued and only committed after every SendGrid POST succeeds. If any request throws (invalid batch id, already cancelled, or SendGrid refusing a send inside its cutoff), the catch logs and skips Promise.all, so earlier successful cancels are not deleted. The next run loads those already-cancelled batches first, they fail again, and reminders later in the list are never cancelled until the blocking row ages out. A single bad row can therefore keep other cancelled-booking emails sending for up to an hour. The same loop also submits every due cancellation at once, so more than 100 in that hour recreates the pending-cancellation cap.

Paid booking cancels return before any reminder cleanup

When bookingToDelete.paid is true the handler refunds, marks the booking REJECTED, and returns at this line. Reminder cancellation only runs later (around the workflowReminders loop). Every paid cancellation therefore leaves WorkflowReminder rows active, including already-submitted SendGrid/Twilio sends, so the bug this PR claims to fix still happens for all paid bookings.

Request-reschedule no longer awaits reminder removal

requestReschedule used to await Promise.all of workflowReminder deletes after best-effort provider cancels. That await was removed. The replacement deleteScheduledEmailReminder / deleteScheduledSMSReminder calls are fired from forEach and not awaited, and email cancellation only sets cancelled when it completes. If the handler returns or the update fails, reminders stay scheduled on SendGrid/Twilio and are not flagged for the cron, so request-reschedule still sends the old workflow reminders.

Reschedule immediately cancels SendGrid and does not wait or roll back

Reschedule passes immediateDelete=true for every email reminder, so each reschedule of an already-submitted reminder adds a pending SendGrid cancellation until the original sendAt (up to 72 hours). Enough reschedules reproduce the 100 pending-cancellation outage the PR is fixing. The forEach is not awaited and the surrounding try/catch cannot see promise rejections. If the SendGrid call fails, the old email still sends and is not marked cancelled for the cron. Cancellation also runs before eventManager.reschedule; a failed reschedule is not rolled back, so the original booking can lose its reminders.

Scheduler still emails reminders for cancelled bookings

The unscheduled-email query only filters method, scheduled=false, and scheduledDate within 72 hours. It does not exclude cancelled=true and does not check booking status (CANCELLED/REJECTED). Far-future reminders are not on SendGrid yet; they are only safe if the cancel path deleted the row. When that delete is skipped, races, or fails (paid cancel, unawaited delete, swallowed error), this cron creates a SendGrid batch and sets scheduled=true, so the reminder is sent anyway.

Workflow delete cancels SendGrid in the background then destroys retry state

Deleting a workflow calls deleteScheduledEmailReminder(..., true) and deleteScheduledSMSReminder from forEach without awaiting, then immediately await workflow.deleteMany, which cascade-deletes the reminder rows, and returns. The SendGrid/Twilio calls are still in flight when the handler finishes, so a serverless runtime can abort them. immediateDelete does not set cancelled, and the rows are gone, so the cron cannot retry. A workflow with many scheduled emails can also submit more than 100 pending cancels at once and fail the same way as the original bug. The same pattern is used when a step is deleted (immediateDelete then workflowStep.delete around line 521). Disabling an event type (around line 376) also dropped the awaited reminder deletes and only fire-and-forgets the new helpers.

true_positives.golden_comment: Consider adding try-catch around the await to handle import failures gracefully
true_positives.matched_candidate:
One app import failure fails every calendar lookup

getCalendar awaits appStore[type] with no try/catch. A rejected dynamic import now rejects the returned promise, whereas the old synchronous registry lookup only returned null for an unimplemented service. getCachedResults does await Promise.all on every calendar credential's getCalendar call, so one bad integration rejects the whole availability fetch and the booking page cannot compute busy times from the other calendars. createEvent and updateEvent likewise await getCalendar outside their create/update catch blocks, so an import failure aborts EventManager instead of recording a failed result for that credential only.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses forEach with async callbacks, which causes asynchronous operations (e.g., calendar/video event deletions, payment refunds) to run concurrently without being awaited. This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Reschedule cleanup uses async forEach and is not awaited

Making getCalendar async was handled by marking the forEach callback async and awaiting inside it. Array.forEach never waits for async callbacks, and the surrounding try/catch only covers the synchronous call, so getCalendar rejections and deleteEvent/deleteMeeting failures become unhandled rejections instead of being logged. The handler then sends the reschedule email and returns true while calendar deletes and video-meeting deletes are still in flight (or not started). On a serverless runtime that freezes after the response, those external events are often left behind after the booking is already marked CANCELLED.

false_positives.candidate:
Recurring cancel never joins calendar deletions

The all-remaining-bookings branch still uses forEach(async) and now awaits getCalendar before deleteEvent. That callback is not collected or awaited, and it pushes the resolved deleteEvent result onto apiDeletes only after the await. The later await Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes)) evaluates concat synchronously, before those callbacks resume, so the snapshot does not include the recurring deletes. The non-recurring branch just below was correctly rewritten to for...of, await getCalendar, and push the delete promise. Recurring cancellations can therefore return after marking bookings CANCELLED without deleting each occurrence from the connected calendars, and getCalendar failures are unhandled rejections.

true_positives.golden_comment: Incorrect end time calculation using slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Working-hours fallback rejects valid split shifts and ignores the slot end

When no date override matches, availability is decided by workingHours.find: any same-day window whose range does not contain the slot makes the callback return true and the slot is rejected. A host with a lunch break (two windows on the same weekday) therefore loses every slot, including ones that sit fully inside the other window. The end minute is copied from slotStartTime rather than the slot end, so a slot that starts inside hours but runs past workingHour.endTime is treated as inside. Days with no working-hour entry never match, so they are treated as free; a fixed host who does not work that weekday is not excluded. For round-robin this filter is what is supposed to keep fixed hosts from being booked outside their own hours, and it does the opposite for split schedules.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Multiple override ranges on one day reject every slot

The date-override filter uses Array.find and treats a true callback as "this slot is not bookable". Each range returns true when the slot merely falls outside that one range. On a day with two ranges (for example 09:00-12:00 and 14:00-17:00), a slot inside the first range is outside the second, so find succeeds and checkIfIsAvailable returns false. Every slot is outside at least one range, so a split date override blocks the entire day instead of opening those windows. The start===end all-day-block branch just above never runs either: it compares two dayjs instances with ===, which is always false, so a zero-length override is not handled as a full-day block.

false_positives.candidate:
In-override slots skip busy checks and can double-book

checkIfIsAvailable now returns true as soon as a date override exists for that calendar day and the slot is not strictly outside it. That return happens before the busy-interval scan, so calendar conflicts and existing Cal bookings are ignored for every fixed host (personal events, collective hosts, and round-robin fixed hosts all go through this path). A host who sets a date override and already has a meeting inside that window will still be offered those slots, and the booking can be confirmed on top of the conflict. Partial overlaps are treated as inside as well: a slot that starts before the override and ends during it is not rejected, so the meeting can begin outside the override hours.

No test for fixed-host overrides on round-robin

The PR's stated fix is that a round-robin event must not offer slots when a fixed host's date override makes them unavailable, including across timezones. The only new assertion re-queries a single-user event in Asia/Dhaka and expects the same UTC instants as Asia/Kolkata. It never builds a ROUND_ROBIN event, never sets hosts[].isFixed, and never places a booking or calendar busy block inside an override. The double-book path, split override ranges, and fixed-host weekly hours can all regress without failing CI.

Override day match compares server-local date to UTC

Whether an override applies is decided by formatting dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset) (local mode, so the server timezone) as YYYY MM DD and comparing it to slotStartTime, which was forced to UTC. isBefore/isAfter later compare absolute instants, but they only run after this date check. On any host whose TZ is not UTC, an override near midnight is attached to the wrong day or skipped entirely, and the fixed host's override is not enforced. Slot generation then falls through to weekly hours.

Override timezone shift wraps at midnight and lands on the wrong day

Date-override start and end are shifted by inviteeUtcOffset - organizerUtcOffset and then reduced to hour and minute only. Those values are minutes within 0-1439, so a shift that crosses midnight is applied to the invitee day already selected from the unadjusted UTC timestamp. An evening override viewed from a timezone ahead shows up as early-morning slots on the previous day; a morning override viewed from a timezone behind can produce endTime < startTime. buildSlots drops ranges with start >= end, and the caller has already removed that user's normal working hours for the day, so the override disappears and the host has no slots. The new test only compares +5:30 and +6:00, a 30-minute gap that never crosses midnight, so it does not catch this. Attendees several hours from the organizer still see the override at the wrong time, which is the bug this change is meant to fix.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code attempts to access integration.metadata[sender][login] without checking for the existence of the sender key. This causes a KeyError for integrations where the sender metadata was not set during creation
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Sender lookup crashes when metadata has no sender

Once no OrganizationIntegration exists, the code compares the OAuth login to integration.metadata["sender"]["login"] with no guard. build_integration only copies sender when pipeline state already has it, and this flow never writes github_authenticated_user into metadata. An ACTIVE Integration without a dict-shaped metadata.sender (older rows, or rows created by this pipeline) raises KeyError or TypeError instead of rendering the installation-failed page. The request 500s, and a missing sender is not treated as a failed authenticity check.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Null reference if github_authenticated_user state is missing
OAuth state uses pipeline.signature (static) instead of a per-request random value

false_positives.candidate:
Installation-not-found test no longer hits the 404 path

test_installation_not_found stubs GET /app/installations/{id} as 404 and previously asserted "The GitHub installation could not be found." It now sends a follow-up setup request with state ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05, while every successful flow in this file uses signature 9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3. OAuthLoginView rejects that state before build_integration, and the test only checks for the generic "Invalid installation request." string, so a regression of the 404 handling still passes. Nothing asserts that a mismatched GitHub user is rejected when no Integration row exists yet, which is the branch that skips the new check.

Installer identity is not checked when creating the integration

The new GitHub-user check only runs after an Integration row already exists and has no OrganizationIntegration. If Integration.objects.get(external_id=installation_id) raises DoesNotExist, GitHubInstallation.dispatch returns pipeline.next_step() immediately, and build_integration never reads github_authenticated_user. installation_id is taken from the query string ahead of pipeline state, and the row is then created with the app JWT via /app/installations/{id}. Anyone who finishes OAuth as themselves can therefore still bind a victim installation_id that is not stored locally yet (webhook not processed or failed, or the Integration row deleted while the GitHub App remains installed). That is the hijack this change is supposed to stop: the attacker's Sentry org gets the victim's installation and repo access. Ownership has to be verified before the integration is created — refuse to continue when the installer cannot be matched, or confirm with GitHub that the OAuth user can access that installation_id — not only in the webhook-already-created branch.

Token exchange omits the authorize redirect_uri

OAuthLoginView puts redirect_uri on the GitHub authorize redirect, but the access-token POST only sends code, client_id, and client_secret. OAuth 2.0 (RFC 6749 §4.1.3) requires that same redirect_uri on the token request when it was included in authorization, and GitHub responds with redirect_uri_mismatch or bad_verification_code otherwise. The comment says this follows OAuth2CallbackView.get_token_params, which does send redirect_uri. Tests stub https://github.com/login/oauth/access_token to always return an access_token, so they stay green while real installs fail into the generic invalid-installation page.

true_positives.golden_comment: The AssignmentSource dataclass uses queued: datetime = timezone.now() as a default field value, which evaluates timezone.now() once at class definition time and shares that single datetime instance across all objects.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
AssignmentSource.queued is a single import-time timestamp and does not survive the task hop

queued is declared as queued: datetime = timezone.now() on a dataclass. That call runs once, when the class body is executed, not when each AssignmentSource is constructed, and it is not a field(default_factory=...). Every source built via from_integration() therefore shares one timestamp from process import, so distinct rapid assignee events cannot be ordered or deduped by queued. to_dict() then puts that raw datetime into the Celery kwargs of sync_assignee_outbound.
