true_positives.golden_comment: Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
join() abandons flusher processes once the deadline has passed

join() gives the entire caller timeout to next_step.join(timeout) before it waits on flusher workers. If that call consumes the timeout, deadline is already in the past and the loop breaks immediately, without waiting for or terminating any remaining flusher process. The previous single-process join always called terminate() even when the deadline had already elapsed. These workers are daemon processes only in the sense that they die if the parent exits; the consumer process stays alive across rebalance. A worker still inside flush_segments or Kafka produce therefore keeps flushing shards the new assignment no longer owns, which duplicates segments onto the buffered-segments topic and conflicts with whichever consumer now owns those Redis shards.

false_positives.candidate:
Restart starts a new flusher before the old one has stopped

_ensure_processes_alive replaces a worker by signalling it (when the isinstance check is fixed) and then immediately calling _create_process_for_shards for the same shard list. kill()/terminate() return as soon as the signal is sent; the old process is not joined, and its handle is overwritten in self.processes so a later join cannot reap or stop it. The old worker can still be inside flush_segments, produce, or done_flush_segments while the new worker starts the same cycle. Both will publish the same segments and both will mutate the same Redis flush keys. The thread path used when produce_to_pipe is set never signals the old thread at all, so tests hit this overlap on every restart.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The magic number 50 for max_wait is used repeatedly throughout the tests. Consider extracting this as a named constant to improve maintainability.
The test test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling has a docstring that doesn't match the test implementation.

false_positives.candidate:
Graceful shutdown does not drain queues or wait for in-flight work

OrderedQueueWorker stops as soon as shutdown is True, before it drains the queue. FixedQueuePool.shutdown sets that flag and only then calls Queue.shutdown(immediate=False), so the graceful drain never happens: after the current item, the worker exits and leaves the rest of the queue unprocessed and incomplete. close() also joins the commit thread (5s) before shutting workers down, so anything completed after that final commit iteration is never committed. join() ignores its timeout and calls close() again. Worker joins are 5s each and sequential, so a stuck handler (the case this mode is meant to isolate) blocks the consumer thread for about num_queues*5 seconds, then the daemon worker keeps running after join returns. Those threads can still apply uptime side effects after partitions were revoked and another owner started, duplicating incidents, while the abandoned queued messages are only redelivered if they were not already acked.

Offsets are committed from a background thread

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy starts a daemon commit thread that calls the Arroyo commit callback every second. That callback is invoked by every other strategy on the consumer thread, which owns the Kafka consumer and the processor's staged-offset map. librdkafka consumers are not thread-safe, and the processor iterates that map while committing. Concurrent commit() from _commit_loop can corrupt staged offsets or raise RuntimeError if the map is mutated during iteration, and close() joins this thread from the consumer thread while it may be inside commit(), which deadlocks if commit needs the processor lock (join then times out after 5s and shutdown continues with a commit still in flight). Commits should be staged in poll()/close() on the consumer thread.

Queue stats test races workers and order is not asserted

test_stats_reporting submits 10 items to a live pool and immediately asserts get_stats()['total_items'] > 0. Workers are already running and the test processor only appends to a list, so the queues can be empty before that assertion; it will flake under load. test_different_groups_distributed similarly asserts that 20 hashed keys hit all 3 queues, which is not guaranteed. test_preserves_order_within_group only checks that 5 results were processed, not that they were processed in offset order, so an ordering regression in the strategy would still pass. None of the tests revoke partitions or call close()/join() and then submit again, so they miss the shared-pool shutdown data loss.

Queues are unbounded and poll() never applies backpressure

Each worker queue is created with queue.Queue() (maxsize 0, unlimited), and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.poll only emits a gauge. submit() never blocks. The strategy docstring claims natural backpressure when queues fill, but nothing stops the consumer thread from pulling the entire partition into memory. One slow subscription blocks only its worker, while every other message on that partition keeps being queued, and the offset watermark cannot advance past the slow item. The process RSS grows with lag until the consumer is OOM-killed; on restart the uncommitted prefix is replayed. poll() or submit() needs a bounded queue and must block when any queue is full so Arroyo stops polling.

Shared queue pool is destroyed on rebalance, then new messages are acked unprocessed

FixedQueuePool is created once on ResultsStrategyFactory and reused by every SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy from create_with_partitions. close() and join() call queue_pool.shutdown(), which shuts the queues down permanently. Arroyo closes the current strategy and builds a new one on every partition revocation/assignment, so after the first rebalance the new strategy submits into already-shut-down queues. queue.Queue.put raises queue.ShutDown, submit() swallows that exception, and the handler marks the offset completed. The commit thread then commits it. Those results are never processed and will not be redelivered, so uptime checks are silently dropped for the rest of the process lifetime. The shared OffsetTracker also keeps last_committed across assignments, so a later strategy can stall or skip commits for replayed offsets. The pool and tracker must be created per strategy instance and only shut down after that instance has finished its own work.

Submit and worker failures are committed as successfully processed

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit catches every exception (grouping_fn errors, BrokerValue assert, queue shutdown, put failures), logs, and calls add_offset plus complete_offset. OrderedQueueWorker.run also completes the offset in a finally block after logging processing exceptions. get_committable_offsets then treats those offsets as safe to commit, and ResultsStrategyFactory commits offset+1 to Kafka. The class docstring says offsets are committed only after successful processing and that no item is lost, but a failed message is acknowledged and never retried. In serial and batched-parallel modes an exception from batching/grouping escapes RunTask and is not committed, so this is a data-loss regression: a bad payload or a transient queue error permanently skips the check result.

true_positives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Warm permission cache is not trusted for denies, so each new resource hits the DB

If cached scopes are present but do not allow the requested resource, Check always falls through to getIdentityPermissions. That path no longer returns the cached set; it singleflight-loads permissions, teams, and the basic role from the DB and overwrites permCache. A just-refreshed cache is therefore ignored for every distinct unauthorized name. The denial cache only dedupes repeats of the same name and folder, and singleflight only coalesces overlapping calls for the same user and action, so sequential Checks (or Checks that do not overlap) each issue a full permission reload. Previously one cached permission set served all checks for that action until TTL.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial-cache test does not actually grant the cached permission

TestService_CacheCheck's "Should deny on explicit cache deny entry" comment says the permission cache allows dash1 so the test proves the denial entry is what short-circuits. The map value stored is false, so scopeMap["dashboards:uid:dash1"] is not a grant. If the denial-cache read were removed, Check would still deny via the empty fake permission store. The test would pass without the new short-circuit, and nothing covers the creator retry: deny, permission appears in the store, next Check within 30s must be allowed.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.

false_positives.candidate:
Denial cache pins false denies for 30s after access is granted

Check returns Allowed=false as soon as permDenialCache contains the user/action/name/folder key, before consulting either the permission cache or the database. On any deny it then stores that key for shortCacheTTL (30s) and never deletes it when a later load would allow the resource. A check that races ahead of the permission insert for a dashboard or folder the user just created (or any grant after a deny) therefore keeps failing until the denial entry expires, which is the failure this PR is meant to fix. The same pin also freezes denies caused by a stale folder tree in checkInheritedPermissions: once recorded, the denial is served even after folderCache has been rebuilt and inherited access would succeed.

true_positives.golden_comment: The rendered GrafanaRuleListItem is missing the required key prop for React list items. This can cause rendering issues when the list order changes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Filtered Grafana rules are rendered without a list key

Replacing GrafanaRuleLoader dropped key={key} on the grafana branch of the filtered-rule list. Datasource and unknown rows still use key, and getRuleKey still builds a frontend id specifically to avoid duplicate keys. Without it, React reconciles Grafana rows by index as infinite scroll appends pages, so row state (open menus, silence drawer, action buttons) can attach to the wrong rule.

true_positives.golden_comment: RuleActionsButtons is invoked with only promRule, but SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer inside RuleActionsButtons still depends on a Grafana Ruler rule being present, so for Grafana rules coming from list views the 'Silence notifications' menu entry (now driven by Grafana Prom abilities) will toggle showSilenceDrawer without ever rendering the drawer. This means clicking 'Silence notifications' for these rules has no visible effect, even when abilities indicate silencing is allowed.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Silence click does nothing in the ruler-less list

List items enable Silence from Grafana Prometheus abilities and AlertRuleMenu calls handleSilence, which only sets showSilenceDrawer. The drawer is still mounted only when rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule) is true, and SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer requires a RulerGrafanaRuleDTO. The new GrafanaRuleListItem passes promRule and no ruler rule, so the menu item appears and clicking it never opens a silence drawer.

false_positives.candidate:
Federated rule groups are no longer treated as immutable

useAllAlertRuleAbilities now delegates to useAllRulerRuleAbilities, which hardcodes isFederated to false (with a TODO) instead of calling isFederatedRuleGroup on the combined rule's group. Federated Mimir/GEM groups were previously immutable, so Update, Delete, Pause, Restore, and Delete permanently were not offered. Those actions are now reported as supported for every existing useAlertRuleAbility/useAllAlertRuleAbilities caller, not only the new list, and the UI can offer edits the previous guard blocked.

Pause and Delete stay hidden without a ruler rule

Alert list rows now pass only a Prometheus rule into AlertRuleMenu, and canPause/canDelete are computed from those prom abilities. The Pause item is still rendered only when rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule) is true (line 123), and Delete only when rulerRule is set (line 165), with onClick forwarding that ruler DTO. In the new list both are therefore never shown, even for users who have pause/delete permission. The rewritten GrafanaGroupLoader test grants AlertingRuleDelete and then expects exactly four menu items (silence, copy link, duplicate, export), so it locks this regression in instead of catching it.

Recording rules lose export, pause, and restore

useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities sets isAlertingRule via prometheusRuleType.grafana.alertingRule and uses that flag for ModifyExport, Pause, Restore, and DeletePermanently. The ruler equivalent used rulerRuleType.grafana.rule, which is true for both Grafana alerting and recording rules (only Silence excluded recording rules). Grafana recording rules in the new list therefore cannot be exported or paused even when the user can edit them, and is_paused exists on those rules.

Rule view links no longer include returnTo

The removed GrafanaRuleListItem built the view href with createReturnTo() so the rule view could navigate back to the current list URL, including filters and search. The new item links to /alerting/grafana/${uid}/view with no returnTo query. Opening a rule from the list or filtered list drops that context, so Back/return no longer restores the list the user came from.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The applyTemplateVariables method is called with request.filters as the third parameter, but this parameter is not used in the corresponding test setup.

false_positives.candidate:
$__auto is not resolved before splitting; the new test only stubs it

The new tests claim a query such as count_over_time({a="b"}[$__auto]) is interpolated to a concrete range before split execution, but they only pass because createLokiDatasource is given a templateSrv.replace stub that string-replaces $__auto. $__auto is a Loki query macro, not a Grafana template variable, and TemplateSrv.replace does not define it. The only interpolation this PR adds is applyTemplateVariables, which leaves $__auto in the expression. It is still resolved later by the Loki backend (the same step path calculateStep says it replicates from pkg/tsdb/loki/step.go) or by runQuery, using each sub-request's split time range. Chunks therefore still get a step derived from the chunk instead of the original range, which is the failure mode early interpolation is supposed to prevent. The unit test cannot catch that because the stub removes $__auto before runQuery is observed. Substitute $__auto from the original request range before partitioning, and do not fake that substitution in templateSrv.replace.

Shard splitting applies template variables and ad-hoc filters twice

runSplitQuery now maps every target through datasource.applyTemplateVariables(..., request.filters) before executing. runShardSplitQuery does the same before grouping, then builds each shard sub-request from those already interpolated targets and calls runSplitQuery. On the shard-splitting path template application therefore runs twice per target (once up front, then once per shard group inside runSplitQuery). applyTemplateVariables is not idempotent: its contract appends ad-hoc filters to the LogQL expression, so the second call inserts the same matchers again, for example {app="foo", env="prod", __stream_shard__=~"1|2", env="prod"}. Loki rejects duplicate label matchers, so dashboards with ad-hoc filters and shard splitting fail or change query meaning. A variable value that itself contains $ or ${...} is expanded again on the second pass and can be corrupted. The updated shard test expects applyTemplateVariables to be called 5 times for a single target (1 initial call plus 1 per shard group), which locks in the double application. Interpolate once for sharding decisions in runShardSplitQuery, and do not call applyTemplateVariables again in runSplitQuery on targets that are already interpolated (or strip filters from the sub-request so they cannot be reapplied).

true_positives.golden_comment: The traceID is no longer logged for plugin requests. During a refactoring, the tracing import and the logic to extract and add traceID from the context to log parameters were removed from the LoggerMiddleware. The newly introduced ContextualLoggerMiddleware does not add this information, resulting in missing traceID in plugin request logs and impacting debugging and request tracing capabilities.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Plugin request completion logs drop traceID

logRequest used to add traceID from tracing.TraceIDFromContext before emitting "Plugin Request Completed". That argument was removed, and ContextualLoggerMiddleware.instrumentContext does not put it back (it only sets endpoint, pluginId, dsName, dsUID, and uname). The plugin tracing middleware does not store traceID as a log contextual attribute either, so Logger.FromContext will not restore it. Completion logs, including alerting and other non-HTTP plugin calls, can no longer be correlated with the span started for the request.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `TestLogger.FromContext` method returns a new `TestLogger` instance via `NewTestLogger()` instead of returning the receiver (f). This causes logs to be recorded on an un-referenced instance, leading to broken test assertions that expect logs to be recorded on the original logger.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TestLogger.FromContext discards the logger under test

FromContext ignores both the receiver and the context and returns NewTestLogger(), a fresh instance whose Logs are not the caller's. LoggerMiddleware now records every completion exclusively via logger.FromContext(ctx).Info, so a test that injects *TestLogger and asserts InfoLogs, ErrorLogs, or contextual fields will see no calls even when a request was logged. The fake should return itself, or a child that writes into the same Logs and exposes contextual attributes.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The ContextualLoggerMiddleware methods (QueryData, CallResource, CheckHealth, CollectMetrics) panic when a nil request is received. This occurs because they directly access req.PluginContext (via the instrumentContext function) without first checking if req is nil. This is a regression, as previous middleware layers gracefully handled nil requests.

false_positives.candidate:
Moved request log fields have no test coverage

pluginId, endpoint, datasource identity, and user were removed from LoggerMiddleware's explicit log parameters and are now supposed to arrive via ContextualLoggerMiddleware plus Logger.FromContext. Nothing in this change tests that path: there is no test for the new middleware, and metrics_middleware_test.go only renames the metrics constructor. A mis-ordered middleware stack or a FromContext implementation that drops those attributes would ship without failing CI, which is how traceID was already dropped.

true_positives.golden_comment: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Device limit check and insert are not atomic

CreateOrUpdateDevice counts rows in one session, then inserts in another, with no transaction, row lock, or advisory lock. Concurrent anonymous requests (including across HA instances, which do not share the in-process cache) can all observe count < device_limit and all insert. Nothing in the schema caps the number of rows, so the overshoot sticks: active devices refresh updated_at about every 29 minutes and never fall out of the 30-day window used by the count. The limit can be permanently exceeded until those extra devices go idle for 30 days.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Device-limit denial is cached, so a retry is allowed

tagDeviceUI writes the device cache key (29-minute TTL) before CreateOrUpdateDevice returns. When the store returns ErrDeviceLimitReached, that error is now propagated and Anonymous.Authenticate denies the request, but the cache entry is left in place. The next TagDevice call for the same X-Grafana-Device-Id hits the cache, returns nil, and anonymous authentication succeeds even though the device was never stored. After one rejection per process, the configured limit is not enforced for the rest of the TTL; the new store test never calls TagDevice twice, so it does not catch this.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Anonymous authentication now fails entirely if anonDeviceService.TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. Previously, device tagging was asynchronous and non-blocking. This change prevents anonymous users from authenticating when the device limit is reached.
The updateDevice function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when rowsAffected == 0, but zero affected rows means the device doesn't exist or falls outside the time window, not that a limit was reached.

Time window calculation inconsistency: Using device.UpdatedAt.UTC().Add(-anonymousDeviceExpiration) as the lower bound but device.UpdatedAt as the current time may not match the intended logic. Consider using time.Now().UTC() consistently.

false_positives.candidate:
Anonymous auth now waits on device tagging even when the limit is off

Tagging used to run in a background goroutine with a detached 2-minute timeout and a panic recover, so it could not stall authentication. It is now a synchronous TagDevice call on the request context for every anonymous login, including the default device_limit of 0 (unlimited), which still does a database upsert on each cache miss. A slow or stuck database delays or ties up all anonymous requests until the DB call returns or the request is cancelled; a panic in tagging is no longer isolated from the request.

Limit test never covers auth, cache, or an existing device

TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit only asserts that a second new device ID is rejected by the store. It does not check that a device already inside the 30-day window can still be updated when count == device_limit, and nothing in impl_test or the auth client tests asserts that a second TagDevice/Authenticate after ErrDeviceLimitReached stays denied. Those are the paths that actually decide whether anonymous users are blocked, and both currently fail open.

Omitting the device ID header skips the limit and still grants anonymous access

The new limit is enforced only inside TagDevice, and TagDevice returns nil immediately when X-Grafana-Device-Id is missing. Authenticate then still returns an anonymous identity with the configured org role. The header is client-supplied, so any caller can keep using anonymous auth after device_limit is exhausted by simply not sending it (or by rotating IDs until the cache bypass above applies). The cap does not actually bound anonymous access.

Provider signature change is not matched by Wire

ProvideAnonymousDeviceService now takes db.DB instead of anonstore.AnonStore, and ProvideAnonDBStore gained a deviceLimit parameter. Grafana constructs these via the committed Wire graph (pkg/server/wire.go / wire_gen.go), which is not updated in this PR. wire_gen.go still calls the old signatures, so the server package will not compile until Wire is regenerated and the generated file is included.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses Error log level for what appears to be debugging information. This will pollute error logs in production. Consider using Debug or Info level instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup success path logs full ID lists at error level

CleanAnnotations and CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags call r.log.Error on every batch, including when the fetch returns no rows and err is nil (lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576, and 579). Each call dumps the entire ID slice and the SQL condition. These run before the empty-batch stop, so every cleanup cycle emits error logs even when nothing is deleted, and a large backlog emits two error lines per batch with tens of thousands of IDs. That floods logs, looks like a failing job to anything alerting on error level, and can stall the cleaner on log serialization. These look like leftover diagnostics and should be removed, or reduced to debug without the ID list.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cleanup job ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which can lead to increased database load and contention due to more frequent execution of cleanup tasks. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with performance expectations.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Global cleanup interval accidentally cut from 10 minutes to 1

Run now uses time.NewTicker(time.Minute * 1) instead of 10 minutes. This is unrelated to the annotation deadlock fix and is not described in the PR. It schedules every cleanup job (snapshots, dashboard versions, images, annotations, invites, short URLs, query history) ten times as often. clean() is synchronous with a 9-minute timeout chosen for the old 10-minute cadence; if a pass takes longer than a minute the ticker's buffered tick starts the next pass immediately, so a busy instance can run cleanup continuously and multiply DB load. Restore the 10-minute interval unless a faster schedule is an intentional, documented change.

false_positives.candidate:
SQLite ID list is built with quadratic string concatenation

When the DB is SQLite and AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize exceeds 999, deleteByIDs inlines every ID with values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v) in a loop. Each step copies the whole string, so a batch of N IDs copies O(N^2) bytes. The new test uses batch size 32767, which is on this path and copies on the order of gigabytes of temporary strings, adding multi-second latency and GC pressure exactly when the batch is large. Build the IN list with strings.Builder (or chunks) instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: The context is being created with d.Log instead of the log variable that was initialized with additional context values (name, kind, method). This means those values won't be propagated to the logging context.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Delete puts the unscoped logger into the context

Delete builds log with name, kind, and method, then calls klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log) instead of klog.NewContext(ctx, log). Storage.Delete and the async Legacy.Delete therefore do not see those fields, unlike Create, Update, and DeleteCollection, which install the enriched logger. Delete failures will be missing the object identity in contextual logs.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Successful Delete uses object name as the metric kind label

The success path of Delete calls recordStorageDuration with name (the object name) as the kind argument (line 106). Every other call, including the error path two lines above, passes options.Kind. Object names are unbounded, so each deleted object creates a new Prometheus series on that label and the process (and any scraper) will grow memory without bound under normal delete traffic.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In DualWriterMode3's DeleteCollection method, when a storage operation fails, recordStorageDuration is incorrectly called with recordLegacyDuration instead.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy Create races on the caller's object

After Storage.Create returns, the handler encodes the returned object while a goroutine calls Legacy.Create on the same obj pointer (line 55) with no deep copy. Storage and legacy implementations mutate metadata in place (resourceVersion, UID, timestamps). That is a data race with response serialization and can tear or overwrite the object returned to the client. Previously the legacy create finished before Create returned, so this race did not exist. Copy the object (and do not share it with the caller) before the goroutine.

Async legacy writes are cancelled with the request

Create, Update, Delete, and DeleteCollection start the legacy write in a goroutine whose context is derived from the incoming request context via context.WithTimeoutCause (Create line 51, Update line 135, Delete line 110, DeleteCollection line 163). When the handler returns, the apiserver cancels that request context, which cancels the child immediately. The 10s timeout never extends past the parent, so the legacy "safety" write is aborted (or races the cancel) instead of running to completion. Mode 3 will report success for unified storage while the legacy copy is systematically dropped, and a later rollback to legacy will be missing creates, updates, and deletes.

Destroy does not wait for in-flight legacy writes

Each successful write spawns an unbounded goroutine that may block on legacy storage for up to 10s, and nothing tracks those goroutines. Destroy (line 172) immediately calls Legacy.Destroy() and Storage.Destroy(). On shutdown or storage teardown, in-flight legacy creates/updates/deletes run against a closed store (panic or error) or are dropped when the process exits, so the safety copy is lost exactly when it is needed for rollback.

Legacy Update reapplies objInfo instead of the stored result

Update now passes the original objInfo into asynchronous Legacy.Update (line 139). The previous implementation snapshotted the object already written to unified storage and passed an updateWrapper so legacy stored that same object. UpdatedObjectInfo is not guaranteed to be reusable or to return an independent object: a second UpdatedObject call can conflict because the request resourceVersion is the unified-storage version, not the legacy one, can apply a patch to a different base and diverge, or can return the same pointer the API response is still encoding while legacy mutates it. Legacy will not reliably receive the write that unified storage just acknowledged.

Legacy write failures are no longer logged

The async legacy Create (line 56), Update (line 140), Delete (line 113), and DeleteCollection (line 165) ignore the error except for a duration metric. The previous synchronous implementation logged these failures. Combined with the mis-labeled metrics, a legacy timeout, conflict, or outage leaves the two stores diverged with no log line an operator can alert on. The request still returns success, which is intended, but the safety write's failure must be logged.

Storage failures and legacy writes recorded on the wrong metric

On Storage.Create failure the code calls recordLegacyDuration (line 45) with the storage start time, and Update does the same at line 129. Those paths never called legacy, so legacy failure rate is inflated and the unified-storage failure is invisible to the storage metric. DeleteCollection's async legacy path does the opposite: line 166 calls recordStorageDuration for the legacy DeleteCollection result, so legacy errors are counted as storage errors and legacy latency is not recorded. Alerts and dashboards for mode 3 will point at the wrong store.

Tests never wait for or assert the async legacy write

Mode 3 unit tests return as soon as the synchronous storage call finishes (Create at line 65, and the same pattern in Update, Delete, and DeleteCollection). They never wait for the goroutine, never AssertExpectations, and would still pass if the legacy write were removed. The success-path mocks are also invoked from a goroutine after the test can return, which races testify's mock. The new playlist integration cases (pkg/tests/apis/playlist/playlist_test.go line 132 and the unified-storage mode 3 case) call doPlaylistTests, which immediately compares the legacy HTTP API (line 529 and getFromBothAPIs) with k8s results. That assumed synchronous dual-write; under mode 3 it will flake or fail when the legacy copy has not landed yet.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Write lock held across manifest load and can clear a filled cache

GetWebAssets copies entryPointAssetsCache under a read lock, drops that lock, then at line 48 takes the exclusive lock and holds it for the whole readWebAssetsFromFile call (line 60). It never re-reads the cache after acquiring the write lock, and line 69 always stores result, including nil. Callers that all observed a nil cache therefore each load the manifest while holding the process-wide mutex, so a startup burst does N sequential disk reads and blocks every other GetWebAssets for that I/O. In Dev the fast path is skipped on purpose, so every call takes this exclusive section and asset loads are globally serialized on disk I/O. A waiter whose load fails after another caller already published a value replaces that cache with nil, so later non-dev requests miss and reload. Load outside the lock; under the lock, return the existing cache when not in Dev and it is already set, and do not store a nil result over a populated cache.

true_positives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Write lock held across manifest load and can clear a filled cache

GetWebAssets copies entryPointAssetsCache under a read lock, drops that lock, then at line 48 takes the exclusive lock and holds it for the whole readWebAssetsFromFile call (line 60). It never re-reads the cache after acquiring the write lock, and line 69 always stores result, including nil. Callers that all observed a nil cache therefore each load the manifest while holding the process-wide mutex, so a startup burst does N sequential disk reads and blocks every other GetWebAssets for that I/O. In Dev the fast path is skipped on purpose, so every call takes this exclusive section and asset loads are globally serialized on disk I/O. A waiter whose load fails after another caller already published a value replaces that cache with nil, so later non-dev requests miss and reload. Load outside the lock; under the lock, return the existing cache when not in Dev and it is already set, and do not store a nil result over a populated cache.

false_positives.candidate:
No concurrent test for the cache race fix

This change only wraps the global entryPointAssetsCache in a mutex inside GetWebAssets and adds no test. Nothing runs concurrent GetWebAssets calls under the race detector, or checks that a successful fill is reused by waiters and is not cleared by a concurrent failed load. The data race this PR is fixing can come back with no regression coverage.

true_positives.golden_comment: The DB methods NewInMemoryDB().RunCommands, DB.QueryFramesInto, and DB.TablesList in pkg/expr/sql/db.go return hardcoded 'not implemented' errors after removing the go-duck dependency.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Live SQL path still builds DuckDB commands and reports invalid SQL

Dashboard and alerting server-side expressions still enter through UnmarshalSQLCommand/NewSQLCommand, not ExpressionQueryReader. NewSQLCommand always calls sql.TablesList, which interpolates the user query into SELECT json_serialize_sql('...') and calls RunCommands. That now fails only because the new DB stub returns an error, and the failure is turned into BadRequest sql-invalid-sql with public text "error reading SQL command". Callers are told the SQL is invalid rather than that SQL expressions were disabled, and TablesList logs the raw query and the constructed command at error level on every attempt. The RCE/LFI closure on this path is entirely the stub; the old injection string is still built for every SQL expression. Reject in NewSQLCommand before TablesList, with an explicit disabled error, and do not assemble or log a DuckDB command.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The enableSqlExpressions function has flawed logic that always returns false, effectively disabling SQL expressions unconditionally:

false_positives.candidate:
Disabled SQL expressions are reported as not implemented

When QueryTypeSQL is read, the new gate always fails and returns "sqlExpressions is not implemented". The feature was implemented and is being turned off because of CVE-2024-9264; the feature flag is still present and documented as the switch for it. Clients and support will treat this as an unfinished feature rather than a security disable, and the message does not match the legacy path's "error reading SQL command" either.

No regression test that SQL expressions cannot run

This change is the in-repo fix for a critical RCE/LFI bug, but it adds no test that UnmarshalSQLCommand/NewSQLCommand reject SQL expressions, that ExpressionQueryReader rejects QueryTypeSQL even when FlagSqlExpressions is on, or that RunCommands/QueryFramesInto do not execute caller SQL. The only verification cited is manual. A later edit that fills in the DB stub or "fixes" enableSqlExpressions can re-open execution with nothing in CI failing.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
BuildIndex no longer excludes concurrent builds of the same key

BuildIndex used to hold cacheMu for the whole build, which serialized bleve.New and cache publication. The lock is now taken only to publish b.cache[key] at the end, and nothing single-flights a key. getOrCreateIndex still does GetIndex then build with no per-key lock, so two searches or watch events for a missing namespace (indexes below InitMinCount, or any key created after startup) both pass the cache miss and call BuildIndex together. For file indexes both call bleve.New on the same directory and race the index files; for memory indexes both succeed. The slower build then overwrites b.cache[key], so the cached index can be the staler one, the other index is leaked and never closed, and callers that already received the losing index keep searching a copy that will not receive later watch updates.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.

false_positives.candidate:
Failed constructor Init leaks watchers and never cancels its context

NewResourceServer calls s.Init and, on error, returns nil without s.cancel() or Stop. Init can already have run lifecycle.Init (opening the DB) and search.init, which starts the background WatchWriteEvents poller and the handleEvent goroutine, before a later step such as initWatcher fails. Callers only receive the error, so they have no server handle to Stop, the cancellable context is abandoned, and those goroutines run until process exit. On the search-watch path a later backend stop then panics, as described above. The error path needs to cancel and stop anything Init already started before returning.

Parallel index init races on shared err and counter

init now actually builds many namespaces at once (errgroup plus the BuildIndex lock removal). Every worker does totalBatchesIndexed++ and err = s.build(...) on the same outer variables with no mutex or atomic. That is a data race: a failed build can return another worker's nil error, so group.Wait can succeed and the process starts with a missing index, or a successful worker can return another worker's error and fail startup. The namespaced_indexed span attribute is also racy and can be wrong. Each worker needs its own err variable, and the counter must be atomic or updated after Wait.

Postgres storage-server integration test is skipped instead of fixed

TestIntegrationWillRunInstrumentationServerWhenTargetHasNoHttpServer is the integration test that constructs and runs the storage-server target. This PR makes NewResourceServer block on full unified-storage Init (DB plus index build) during that construction, then skips the test whenever GRAFANA_TEST_DB=postgres, with a TODO that it fails in Drone and works locally. CI no longer exercises storage-server startup on postgres, so a postgres-specific failure in the new eager Init path — the behavior this PR adds — will not fail the build.

Search watch goroutine panics when the event channel closes

After index build, init starts a goroutine that does v := <-events and always calls handleEvent. watchctx is context.Background(), not the server's cancellable context, so server.Stop cannot stop it. SQL WatchWriteEvents closes the channel when the backend stops, and server.Stop calls lifecycle.Stop (the SQL backend implements LifecycleHooks) before cancelling the server context. A closed channel yields a nil event; handleEvent immediately reads evt.Type and panics, crashing the process. Because Init now always runs from NewResourceServer, every storage-server shutdown hits this. The loop must exit on !ok and must use the server context. The same unbounded read exists in initWatcher.

Server watch now starts only after the full index build

Init used to call initWatcher before search.init. It now builds every search index first and only then starts the server broadcaster's WatchWriteEvents. That poller does not replay history; it starts at whatever the latest RV is when it is called. Writes committed during the startup index build (other HA replicas; WatchWriteEvents is documented to observe remote writes) are therefore never pushed to the broadcaster. A client that reconnects with Since set to the last RV it saw misses those events. Previously the broadcaster poller was already running for the whole index build, so those events were captured. Start the server watcher before the long index build, or replay from the RV observed before the build.

Startup index watch cursor skips writes made during the build

build returns the resource version of the list snapshot and documents that watchers must apply every event after that RV, but init discards both return values and only then calls WatchWriteEvents. That helper records the latest RV at call time and the SQL poller emits only history rows after that cursor. With a long startup build — the path this PR moved onto process start — and with namespaces built in parallel, an index finished early misses every write committed after its list and before the slowest build finishes. Those writes are never replayed, so the search index stays permanently stale. The watch must start from each build's returned RV (or from the RV captured before listing), not from a single cursor taken after all builds.

true_positives.golden_comment: Cleanup reference uses incorrect alias - should be 'idp-alias-' + i instead of 'alias'.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Login-cache test cleanup deletes the wrong IdP alias

testCacheIDPForLogin registers cleanup as identityProviders().get("alias")::remove both in the loop that creates idp-alias-0..19 (line 381) and again for idp-alias-20 (line 425). Nothing removes the aliases that were actually created. On a shared test realm, those brokers remain after the test; the DELETE of the non-existent alias "alias" can also fail cleanup. Later cases in this class, including this test’s own exact cache sizes (5/10/6/11), then see extra login providers and become order-dependent. Register cleanup with the alias just created (and the same mistake at the pre-existing line 303 should be fixed the same way).

false_negatives.golden_comment: InfinispanIdentityProviderStorageProvider.getForLogin() recursively calls session.identityProviders().getById() instead of idpDelegate.getById(), causing the cache lookup to re-enter the same caching layer.

false_positives.candidate:
Login-cache invalidation uses the org-wrapped IdP model

update() loads the pre-update provider with getById(), which, when the organization feature is on, returns a wrapper whose isEnabled() is false whenever the organization is missing, disabled, or the organization provider is disabled — even if the stored IdP is enabled. registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate() then treats that wrapper as “not a login IdP”. getForLogin() fills its cache from the delegate query, which only checks the IdP’s own enabled/linkOnly/hideOnLogin/public flags, so that IdP can already be in the cached id set. If the update also makes the raw model ineligible (disable it, set hideOnLogin or linkOnly, or clear kc.org.broker.public) while the organization id is unchanged, both predicate checks fail and the login caches are left untouched. After the organization is enabled again, getById() returns the updated model (the per-IdP cache was invalidated) but the stale id is still in the login list. OrganizationAwareIdentityProviderBean only re-checks isEnabled(), so a hidden, link-only, or non-public broker is rendered on the login page, and any other getForLogin() caller is handed providers that no longer match the method contract. Decide eligibility from the unwrapped delegate model (idpDelegate.getById), not from the organization-aware wrapper.

true_positives.golden_comment: Returns wrong provider (default keystore instead of BouncyCastle)
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getBouncyCastleProvider returns the JDK keystore provider

getBouncyCastleProvider() is documented to return the BouncyCastle or BCFIPS provider. This implementation returns KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider(), which is the platform keystore provider (typically SUN), not BouncyCastle. WildFlyElytronProvider returns null when BC is absent so callers can take a non-BC path. A non-null SUN provider fails those null checks and is then passed to Signature.getInstance or Cipher.getInstance. SUN does not provide SHA256withECDSA (that is SunEC) or BC algorithms such as AES/CBC/PKCS7Padding, so provider-pinned operations throw NoSuchAlgorithmException or use the wrong implementation. For a standalone authz-client this class is the selected CryptoProvider, so return null or throw instead of handing back the keystore provider.

true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
order() breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations

order() was added as an abstract method with no default on the public CryptoProvider interface in keycloak-common. Implementations compiled against the previous interface will not compile, and at runtime ServiceLoader detection calls order() and throws AbstractMethodError, so CryptoIntegration.init fails and the server does not start. A default such as default int order() { return 0; } would keep older providers loadable and sort them below the in-tree providers (200) and AuthzClientCryptoProvider (100).

false_negatives.golden_comment: Dead code exists where ASN1Encoder instances are created and written to, but their results are immediately discarded. The actual encoding is performed by new ASN1Encoder instances created in the subsequent return statement, rendering the earlier operations useless.
When length starts at -1 from indefinite-length encoding, the arithmetic 'length = length - bytes.length' will behave unexpectedly, potentially leading to incorrect processing of encoded data.

false_positives.candidate:
AuthzClient.create freezes the JVM crypto provider

AuthzClient.create(Configuration) calls CryptoIntegration.init(AuthzClient.class.getClassLoader()), and init() keeps the first provider it detects forever. ServiceLoader on the authz-client classloader does not see CryptoProvider services registered only in a child deployment or server classloader. Those order-200 providers are skipped, AuthzClientCryptoProvider (order 100) is installed, and a later CryptoIntegration.init from the server is a no-op. The rest of the JVM then uses a provider that throws UnsupportedOperationException from getSignature, getPemUtils, cipher, certificate, and truststore methods. Creating a client must not permanently install this stub from the library classloader; a later init that can see a higher-order provider has to be able to replace it.

ECDSA integer conversion silently truncates

integerToBytes, used by asn1derToConcatenatedRS, copies the low-order qLength bytes whenever BigInteger.toByteArray() is longer than the coordinate size. It does not require the discarded prefix to be a single 0x00 sign octet, and it does not reject a negative INTEGER. An oversized or negative DER integer therefore becomes a different R or S instead of failing the conversion with IOException. Signature verification then runs against a value that is not the encoded integer, so malformed ECDSA input is mishandled rather than rejected. Throw unless the encoding is at most qLength+1 bytes and any extra leading byte is 0x00.

ECDSA test only checks a self-roundtrip on P-256

The only new coverage of the ASN.1 ECDSA conversion generates one key with KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair(), which is the provider default curve (P-256 on standard JDKs), then runs ES256, ES384, and ES512 with that key. The sole assertion is that decoding the encoder's output matches the intermediate R||S. Signature.verify is never called, and the result is never compared with Java's original DER. A decoder/encoder pair that ignores the real R and S and inverts each other would pass. ES384 and ES512 also never see 48-byte or 66-byte coordinates, so the sign-octet padding path at those widths is untested. Each algorithm needs a key on secp256r1, secp384r1, or secp521r1, and the DER produced from the concatenated form must verify with Signature.verify.

Tied CryptoProviders are chosen non-deterministically

detectProvider no longer throws when ServiceLoader finds more than one CryptoProvider. It sorts by order() descending and returns the first entry. DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, and FIPS1402Provider all return 200, so any two of them tie, and ServiceLoader order is classpath-dependent. The loser is only mentioned in a debug log. Previously this misconfiguration aborted startup. Now a FIPS deployment that also has the non-FIPS provider can keep running with DefaultCryptoProvider even though FIPS1402Provider's constructor has already inserted BCFIPS at JCA position 1 and rewritten ssl.KeyManagerFactory.algorithm / ssl.TrustManagerFactory.algorithm. The process then mixes a non-FIPS CryptoProvider with FIPS JCA settings, or the reverse. When several providers share the highest order, startup should still fail.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistent feature flag bug causing orphaned permissions. The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. Cleanup should occur regardless of which fine-grained authorization version is enabled.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Client-removal cleanup throws or skips V2 resources

The removal listener now runs only when ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ is enabled, but management() returns MgmtPermissionsV2 whenever ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled. If both features are on, ClientRemovedEvent calls ClientPermissionsV2.setPermissionsEnabled, which throws UnsupportedOperationException and can fail client deletion. If only V2 is on, the listener is skipped entirely. Nothing deletes the FGAP resource that getOrCreateResource stored under the client id on the admin-permissions client, so deleted clients leave orphaned resources and policies.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getClientsWithPermission(String scope), iterating resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and returning resource.getName() will only ever consider the type-level 'Clients' resource (per-client resources have no type) and return its name, while AvailableRoleMappingResource#getRoleIdsWithPermissions expects actual client IDs to pass to realm.getClientById, which can lead to incorrect behavior or a null client and subsequent failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Per-client resources are created without a type

getOrCreateResource creates the client resource by name and scopes but never setType(CLIENTS). The aggregate Clients resource created in init() does set its type. ClientPermissionsV2.getClientsWithPermission then uses resourceStore.findByType(..., CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE), so it will not see per-client grants. It will see the aggregate resource and add its name "Clients" to the granted id set, which is not a client id. Callers that filter the client list or role-mapping targets with this set therefore omit clients the user was granted and never match a real client id.

true_positives.golden_comment: In ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission, the method getResourceTypeResource could return null, leading to a NullPointerException in findByResource. Defensive null checks are needed to prevent this issue.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Per-client evaluation skips all-clients policies and can NPE

hasPermission(ClientModel, scope) loads only the per-client resource when one exists and never evaluates the Clients type resource in that case. FGAP requires both: a positive all-clients grant must still apply when the client already has a resource for another scope, and a negative all-clients policy must still deny a positive per-client grant. As written, all-clients manage/view is ignored whenever any per-client resource exists (incorrect deny), and a negative all-clients policy does not override a positive per-client policy (incorrect allow). If the per-client resource is missing and getResourceTypeResource returns null (schema not migrated, or admin permissions not enabled for this server), findByResource(server, null) on line 219 throws NullPointerException and the admin call 500s instead of returning false.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), the resource lookup uses findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId()), but AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource creates per-client resources with the owner set to resourceServer.getClientId(), so this lookup will never find those resources and will always fall back to the 'all-clients' resource, effectively ignoring client-specific permissions.
Remove unused getEvaluationContext private method in ClientPermissionsV2 - it is defined but never called

false_positives.candidate:
Client resource names are not resolved for display

getResourceName resolves Users resources to a username (or "All users") but has no Clients branch. Per-client resources are stored under the internal client id and display name is never set, so permission listings fall through to resource.getDisplayName() and show null instead of the clientId. After a client is deleted the orphaned resource still will not be reported as missing, unlike the user path which throws ModelIllegalStateException.

Configure test rotates the shared admin client secret

testConfigureOnlyOneClient calls generateNewSecret() on myclient, which is the confidential client used by the injected realmAdminClient (and by other tests that log in with client secret mysecret). onAfter only deletes scope permissions and does not restore the secret, name, or default client scopes mutated by these tests. Later tests in the same realm then fail authentication or see a changed client, depending on method order. The new map-roles-client-scope scope is also never exercised.

Role-mapping checks ignore manage-clients and manage

canMapRoles, canMapCompositeRoles, and canMapClientScopeRoles only call hasPermission for that scope. Unlike canManage in the same class, they do not treat AdminRoles.MANAGE_CLIENTS as allowed, and they do not treat a Clients manage grant as allowed. A realm admin (or any caller who can manage the client) is therefore forbidden from mapping client roles, composite roles, or client-scope roles unless a separate FGAP map-roles policy exists. V1 granted these via the manage-clients short-circuit inside permission checks.

Schema init does not add Clients type to existing realms

init() returns immediately when the realm already has an admin-permissions client. That client was created by the earlier Users-only schema, so upgraded realms never get the Clients resource, or the new configure, map-roles-client-scope, and map-roles-composite scopes. Creating or evaluating a Clients permission then fails with missing-scope or missing-resource errors, and ClientPermissionsV2 falls through to a null type resource. Init needs to add any schema resource types and scopes that are not already present.

V2 client permission methods throw instead of degrading

ClientPermissionsV2 is installed for every realm whenever ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is on (MgmtPermissionsV2.clients()), but isPermissionsEnabled, setPermissionsEnabled, getPermissions, resource, and the Policy accessors all throw UnsupportedOperationException. Those methods are still called by the admin client management-permissions API, so opening or updating a client's permissions tab returns 500 for every realm, not only realms using FGAP. canExchangeTo (line 148) throws the same way, so token-exchange permission checks 500 instead of denying. setPermissionsEnabled must no-op or return a normal error, and the boolean/read methods must return false/empty when V2 does not use per-client authz resources.

requireView javadoc describes the wrong contract

requireView is documented as returning true when canView() is true, and requireViewClientScopes (line 101) as returning true when canViewClientScopes() is true. Both methods are void and are specified elsewhere to throw ForbiddenException. Callers reading only these comments will treat them as predicates.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Incorrect method call for exit codes. The picocli.exit() method calls System.exit() directly, which is problematic:
Need to add changelog/release notes documenting the exit code change and migration guidance

false_positives.candidate:
Changed CLI exit codes are not asserted

testFeatureNotEnabled only checks the stderr text for the metadata subcommand and never asserts exit code 4. The same gate in the check subcommand is not tested. testWrongVersions still only checks log text, so nothing locks the recreate result after this PR changes RECREATE_UPGRADE_EXIT_CODE from 4 to 3 and reuses 4 for feature disabled. Automation is supposed to choose rolling versus shutdown from these codes; swapping them would not fail CI.

Default-strategy upgrade tests never enable rolling-updates

createInitialDeployment returns immediately when the update strategy is null, before spec.features.enabled is set to rolling-updates. The parameterized tests include that null strategy, which is the documented default, and still expect a successful rolling upgrade (cache max-count) or recreate upgrade (image change). The new operator guide says this preview feature must be enabled or the operator fails. Those default-strategy deployments therefore run without the feature this change requires, so reconciliation fails or the tests no longer cover the configuration operators must use. Enable rolling-updates on every deployment this helper returns, including the null strategy.

Exit code 4 is documented as a compatibility result

The check-command exit-code table says exit code 4 means "Rolling Upgrade is not possible" because rolling-updates is disabled. The implementation exits 4 before reading metadata or comparing versions, and prints that the command cannot be used. That is not a compatibility decision: a rolling upgrade may still be possible. The guide tells automation to branch only on these exit codes, and exit code 3 is the code that means shut the deployment down and recreate. Describing 4 the same way ("Rolling Upgrade is not possible") leads scripts to treat a missing feature flag as a required outage, or to treat an inconclusive run as a finished negative check. Document 4 as "command did not run; feature not enabled; result inconclusive", and note that the metadata subcommand uses the same code.

true_positives.golden_comment: In GroupPermissionsV2.canManage(), the permission fallback checks for both VIEW and MANAGE scopes (hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)), but canManage() should only grant access for MANAGE scope, not VIEW. This means users with only VIEW permission on groups can pass the canManage() check, granting them write access they should not have. The canView() method correctly checks both VIEW and MANAGE, but canManage() should only check MANAGE.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
All-groups VIEW is treated as manage

GroupPermissionsV2.canManage() returns true when the caller has either VIEW or MANAGE on the all-groups resource. GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup() gates creating a group and moving an existing group to the top level with requireManage(), which only calls this no-arg canManage(). A principal granted only view-all-groups can therefore create groups and reparent any group to the top of the tree. Per-group canManage(GroupModel) correctly checks MANAGE only, so this is not the same as the view-implies-read checks. The new interface javadoc repeats the VIEW-or-MANAGE wording and should not be treated as the intended contract; the evaluation test states that creating a group requires the manage scope.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, hasPermission is called with groupResource.getId() and the same groupResource.getId() is added to granted, but hasPermission resolves resources by name (treating the argument as a group id) and the GroupPermissionEvaluator contract says this method returns group IDs that are later used as UserModel.GROUPS and in getUsersCount group filters. This mismatch means per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions may not yield the expected group IDs for filtering and counts, and evaluation may effectively only look at the type-level 'all-groups' resource; consider revisiting whether this should operate on the underlying group ids (resource names) instead so it aligns with the JPA queries and the interface contract.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
View-members group id lookup returns the wrong ids

getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() is what UsersResource and BruteForceUsersResource pass to user search and getUsersCount as membership constraints (session attribute UserModel.GROUPS). The V2 implementation does two things that make those ids unusable. It asks resourceStore.findByType for type "Groups", but AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource() never calls setType on the per-group resource it creates (only the synthetic all-groups resource is typed), so individual group resources are not returned. For whatever is returned it calls hasPermission(groupResource.getId(), ...) and granted.add(groupResource.getId()). Authorization resource ids are not group ids; V2 stores the group id as the resource name (resolveGroup returns group.getId(), and hasPermission looks that up with findByName). The permission check therefore misses the group resource and falls back to the all-groups resource, and any ids that are added do not match membership rows. Result: an admin with VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS on specific groups gets an empty set (user counts stay 0 or unrestricted, and search is not limited to those groups), while the same scopes on all groups inject non-group ids and the search pre-filter drops every user before canView() can allow them. The new GroupResourceTypeEvaluationTest only covers per-group user search, which still passes via the post-filter when the set is empty, so this path is untested.

false_positives.candidate:
Existing admin-permissions clients never gain Groups scopes or the type resource

init() returns immediately when realm.getAdminPermissionsClient() is already set, and that is the only place this PR creates the Groups resource-type resource and the new scopes manage-membership, manage-members, and view-members. Realms that already enabled admin permissions V2 (the client was created when the schema only had Users and Clients) are not updated. getOrCreateResource then fails with ModelException("No scopes found.") when a group permission is saved, because those scope names are missing. GroupPermissionsV2.hasPermission falls back to getResourceTypeResource(..., "Groups"), which returns null, and policyStore.findByResource(server, null) / resource.getScopes() throws NullPointerException. Any fine-grained admin who can list groups but does not hold MANAGE_USERS/VIEW_USERS hits that path from canView(GroupModel), so group listing 500s instead of being filtered.

Group deletion hits UnsupportedOperationException or leaks authz resources

GroupPermissionsV2.setPermissionsEnabled (and the other GroupPermissionManagement methods) always throw UnsupportedOperationException. AdminPermissions.registerListener still handles GroupModel.GroupRemovedEvent by calling management(...).groups().setPermissionsEnabled(group, false) whenever ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ is enabled. This PR makes MgmtPermissionsV2.groups() return GroupPermissionsV2 whenever ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled, so a server with both features on will throw from that listener during realm.removeGroup. Provider event listeners are not swallowed, so deleting a group fails with a 500 and the removal is rolled back. If only the V2 feature is on, the listener is not registered at all, and nothing deletes the admin-permissions resource whose name is the group id, so group permissions survive as orphans after the group is gone.

Group permission resources have no display name

getResourceName() only resolves a human-readable name for the Users resource type. Group resources created by getOrCreateResource are named with the group id and never get a display name. For a Groups policy the method therefore returns resource.getDisplayName(), which is null. Permission listings in the admin API/UI cannot show which group a permission applies to, unlike users, where the username is resolved from the same resource name.

requireManageMembers javadoc cites the wrong check

The javadoc on requireManageMembers says it throws when canManageMembership(GroupModel) is false. The implementation throws when canManageMembers is false. Those are different scopes (manage-membership vs manage-members). Callers reading only the interface will enforce or test the wrong permission. The new getGroupIdsWithViewPermission javadoc has the same problem: it says it returns a Stream of groups with view permission, but the method returns a Set and both implementations select groups by view-members/manage-members, not view.

true_positives.golden_comment: The translation is in Italian instead of Lithuanian. This should be translated to Lithuanian to match the file's locale (messages_lt.properties).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Lithuanian account totpStep1 replaced with Italian

totpStep1 in the Lithuanian account bundle was replaced with "Installa una delle seguenti applicazioni sul tuo cellulare:", which is Italian, not Lithuanian. The previous Lithuanian sentence (with the FreeOTP/Google Play links) was removed to satisfy the HTML check, but the replacement is the wrong language, so Lithuanian users are instructed in Italian during OTP setup.

true_positives.golden_comment: The totpStep1 value uses Traditional Chinese terms in the Simplified Chinese file (zh_CN), which is likely incorrect for this locale. Please verify the locale‑appropriate translation.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
zh_CN totpStep1 is Traditional Chinese

totpStep1 in messages_zh_CN.properties was set to "在您的手機上安裝以下應用程式之一：", which is Traditional Chinese (手機, 安裝, 應用程式). This file is Simplified Chinese (zh_CN); the rest of the bundle uses simplified characters. zh_CN users will see a Traditional script string on the account OTP setup step.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The anchor sanitization logic has a potential issue where it consumes English matcher groups without proper validation. If the translated text has more anchor tags than the English text, this could lead to incorrect validation results.
The method name 'santizeAnchors' should be 'sanitizeAnchors' (missing 'i').
Field HTML_TAGS should be declared as 'private static final' following Java naming conventions for constants

false_positives.candidate:
Account UI error message switched to Java MessageFormat

error-invalid-multivalued-size in the account-ui bundle was changed from i18next placeholders ({{0}}, {{1}}, {{2}}) to Java MessageFormat choice syntax ({0} and {2,choice,0#values|1#value|1<values}). Every other interpolated string in this file uses {{name}} / {{0}}. The account UI does not evaluate Java ChoiceFormat, so when a multivalued attribute fails size validation the user sees the raw pattern, including literal {0}/{1}/{2} and the choice clause, instead of the attribute name and limits. The previous value(s) wording had no HTML and did not need this change for the sanitizer.

Admin UI error message switched to Java MessageFormat

error-invalid-multivalued-size in the admin-ui bundle was changed from {{0}}/{{1}}/{{2}} to Java MessageFormat, including {2,choice,0#values|1#value|1<values}. This file is loaded by the React admin console (i18next-style {{ }} interpolation), not by java.text.MessageFormat. The choice pattern will be shown literally and the attribute name, minimum, and maximum will not be substituted. The Java choice string belongs only in the server theme bundles (themes/.../admin and login messages_en.properties), which were updated separately.

Anchor mismatch message omits key and file

When a translation anchor does not exactly match the English tag, the verifier only records "Didn't find anchor tag " plus the tag text. Unlike the illegal-HTML message, this omits the message key and the properties file. The Maven plugin reports that string as the build failure, so a CI failure cannot be traced to a key without re-running the check by hand.

Choice-format strip hides HTML from the sanitizer

For keys starting with linkExpirationFormatter.timePeriodUnit and for error-invalid-multivalued-size, normalizeValue deletes every {n,choice,...} substring with the regex \{[0-9]+,choice,[^}]*} before the HTML policy runs. [^}]* matches arbitrary markup, so a translation can put tags or script inside the choice subformat and the verifier will replace that whole subformat with "..." and then compare a string that no longer contains the HTML. Those keys are formatted with java.text.MessageFormat and the chosen alternative is inserted into login, admin, and email messages — including HTML email bodies — so this bypasses the check this PR adds. Strip or neutralize only the choice operator "<", or run the sanitizer on the choice alternatives before discarding them.

Diff highlighter throws when prefix and suffix overlap

When sanitized text differs from the message, the code walks a common prefix (start) and a common suffix (end) and then calls value.substring(start, value.length() - end) and the same on sanitized. If the prefix and suffix overlap — start > length - end — String.substring throws StringIndexOutOfBoundsException. That happens for ordinary edits, for example value "hello" versus sanitized "helo" (one repeated character removed): start=3 and end=2, and sanitized.substring(3, 2) throws. The exception escapes the forEachRemaining lambda, so verify() aborts without recording the "Illegal HTML" diagnostic and without checking the remaining keys of that file. PropertyResourceBundle key order is undefined, so a later illegal entry in the same file may never be reported.

Lithuanian login totpStep1 replaced with Italian

loginTotpStep1 in the Lithuanian login bundle was replaced with the Italian sentence "Installa una delle seguenti applicazioni sul tuo cellulare:". The English source is "Install one of the following applications on your mobile:"; other locales in this PR were actually translated. Lithuanian login users will see Italian text on the OTP setup step.

true_positives.golden_comment: In AccessTokenContext constructor, the fourth Objects.requireNonNull validates grantType twice instead of validating rawTokenId, allowing null rawTokenId values to pass validation.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Null raw token id is not rejected

The AccessTokenContext constructor is meant to reject a null raw token id, but the fourth requireNonNull checks grantType again (the message says "Null rawTokenId not allowed") and never reads rawTokenId. A null raw id is stored. encodeTokenId concatenates it with ':', and Java string conversion turns that null into the literal characters null, so the jti becomes something like onrtac:null. Those ids are not unique and will not round-trip to a real token id. The check must be Objects.requireNonNull(rawTokenId, ...).

true_positives.golden_comment: In isAccessTokenId, the substring for the grant shortcut and the equality check look inverted: the grant shortcut occupies indices 4–5 (substring(4,6)), and a match should return true (combined with UUID check), not false.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Access-token id matcher is inverted and slices the wrong characters

isAccessTokenId is what expectRefresh, expectCodeToToken, expectDeviceCodeToToken, and expectAuthReqIdToToken use to check the new jti format. matchesSafely returns false when items[0].substring(3, 5) equals the expected grant shortcut, so a correct shortcut is treated as a mismatch. The slice is also wrong: the prefix is session (2) + token type (2) + grant (2), so the grant shortcut is substring(4, 6), not substring(3, 5). A default regular refresh token id is like onrtrt:<uuid>; substring(3, 5) is rt, which equals RefreshTokenGrantTypeFactory.GRANT_SHORTCUT, so expectRefresh fails on a correctly encoded token. For authorization-code (ac), device (dg), and CIBA (ci) the wrong slice does not equal the shortcut, so the inverted check never fires and those assertions pass even if the grant shortcut is wrong, as long as the suffix looks like a UUID. If the prefix is shorter than 5 characters, substring throws StringIndexOutOfBoundsException instead of failing the assertion.

true_positives.golden_comment: Javadoc mentions "usually like 3-letters shortcut" but some implementations use 2-letter shortcuts ("ac", "cc", "rt", "te", "pc", "ci", "ro"). Consider updating documentation to reflect actual usage pattern.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getShortcut() is a new abstract SPI method with no default

OAuth2GrantTypeFactory.getShortcut() was added with no default implementation. DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.postInit calls it on every OAuth2GrantType factory. An existing custom grant-type factory compiled against the previous SPI will throw AbstractMethodError during that call and prevent the server from starting, and will not compile against this interface until it is updated. A default that returns a reserved unknown shortcut (or skipping factories that cannot provide one) would keep old providers from taking down startup. The new javadoc on line 30 also says the shortcut is "usually like 3-letters", but the encoder only accepts exactly two characters and will not successfully decode anything else.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistent feature flag bug causing orphaned permissions. The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. Cleanup should occur regardless of which fine-grained authorization version is enabled.

If both features are on, ClientRemovedEvent calls ClientPermissionsV2.setPermissionsEnabled, which throws UnsupportedOperationException and can fail client deletion. If only V2 is on, the listener is skipped entirely. Nothing deletes the FGAP resource that getOrCreateResource stored under the client id on the admin-permissions client, so deleted clients leave orphaned resources and policies.

It does not require the discarded prefix to be a single 0x00 sign octet, and it does not reject a negative INTEGER. An oversized or negative DER integer therefore becomes a different R or S instead of failing the conversion with IOException. Signature verification then runs against a value that is not the encoded integer, so malformed ECDSA input is mishandled rather than rejected. ES384 and ES512 also never see 48-byte or 66-byte coordinates, so the sign-octet padding path at those widths is untested. Each algorithm needs a key on secp256r1, secp384r1, or secp521r1, and the DER produced from the concatenated form must verify with Signature.verify.
