OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key applies math.floor/math.ceil to the order-by attribute, and value_from_cursor returns the raw cursor number. OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint uses this class with order_by="-datetime" whenever optimized_pagination=true and the caller is a superuser or has global access. Audit log rows are ordered by a datetime, not a number. On a non-empty first page, build_cursor calls get_item_key and raises TypeError because math.floor cannot accept a datetime. On any request that includes a cursor, build_queryset compares the timestamp column to that raw integer (DateTimePaginator converts via fromtimestamp and a multiplier; this class does not), which PostgreSQL rejects. The opt-in path therefore returns HTTP 500 for every organization that has audit log entries instead of a page of results.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
BuildIndex no longer excludes concurrent builds of the same key

BuildIndex used to hold cacheMu for the whole build, which serialized bleve.New and cache publication. The lock is now taken only to publish b.cache[key] at the end, and nothing single-flights a key. getOrCreateIndex still does GetIndex then build with no per-key lock, so two searches or watch events for a missing namespace (indexes below InitMinCount, or any key created after startup) both pass the cache miss and call BuildIndex together. For file indexes both call bleve.New on the same directory and race the index files; for memory indexes both succeed. The slower build then overwrites b.cache[key], so the cached index can be the staler one, the other index is leaked and never closed, and callers that already received the losing index keep searching a copy that will not receive later watch updates.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue describe the exact same race condition in `BuildIndex` where moving the `b.cacheMu` lock from the beginning of the function to only the final cache assignment allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the index for the same key.

false_positives.candidate:
Parallel index init races on shared err and counter

init now actually builds many namespaces at once (errgroup plus the BuildIndex lock removal). Every worker does totalBatchesIndexed++ and err = s.build(...) on the same outer variables with no mutex or atomic. That is a data race: a failed build can return another worker's nil error, so group.Wait can succeed and the process starts with a missing index, or a successful worker can return another worker's error and fail startup. The namespaced_indexed span attribute is also racy and can be wrong. Each worker needs its own err variable, and the counter must be atomic or updated after Wait.

Startup index watch cursor skips writes made during the build

build returns the resource version of the list snapshot and documents that watchers must apply every event after that RV, but init discards both return values and only then calls WatchWriteEvents. That helper records the latest RV at call time and the SQL poller emits only history rows after that cursor. With a long startup build — the path this PR moved onto process start — and with namespaces built in parallel, an index finished early misses every write committed after its list and before the slowest build finishes. Those writes are never replayed, so the search index stays permanently stale. The watch must start from each build's returned RV (or from the RV captured before listing), not from a single cursor taken after all builds.

Search watch goroutine panics when the event channel closes

After index build, init starts a goroutine that does v := <-events and always calls handleEvent. watchctx is context.Background(), not the server's cancellable context, so server.Stop cannot stop it. SQL WatchWriteEvents closes the channel when the backend stops, and server.Stop calls lifecycle.Stop (the SQL backend implements LifecycleHooks) before cancelling the server context. A closed channel yields a nil event; handleEvent immediately reads evt.Type and panics, crashing the process. Because Init now always runs from NewResourceServer, every storage-server shutdown hits this. The loop must exit on !ok and must use the server context. The same unbounded read exists in initWatcher.

Failed constructor Init leaks watchers and never cancels its context

NewResourceServer calls s.Init and, on error, returns nil without s.cancel() or Stop. Init can already have run lifecycle.Init (opening the DB) and search.init, which starts the background WatchWriteEvents poller and the handleEvent goroutine, before a later step such as initWatcher fails. Callers only receive the error, so they have no server handle to Stop, the cancellable context is abandoned, and those goroutines run until process exit. On the search-watch path a later backend stop then panics, as described above. The error path needs to cancel and stop anything Init already started before returning.

Server watch now starts only after the full index build

Init used to call initWatcher before search.init. It now builds every search index first and only then starts the server broadcaster's WatchWriteEvents. That poller does not replay history; it starts at whatever the latest RV is when it is called. Writes committed during the startup index build (other HA replicas; WatchWriteEvents is documented to observe remote writes) are therefore never pushed to the broadcaster. A client that reconnects with Since set to the last RV it saw misses those events. Previously the broadcaster poller was already running for the whole index build, so those events were captured. Start the server watcher before the long index build, or replay from the RV observed before the build.

Postgres storage-server integration test is skipped instead of fixed

TestIntegrationWillRunInstrumentationServerWhenTargetHasNoHttpServer is the integration test that constructs and runs the storage-server target. This PR makes NewResourceServer block on full unified-storage Init (DB plus index build) during that construction, then skips the test whenever GRAFANA_TEST_DB=postgres, with a TODO that it fails in Drone and works locally. CI no longer exercises storage-server startup on postgres, so a postgres-specific failure in the new eager Init path — the behavior this PR adds — will not fail the build.

false_positives.candidate:
Shared queue pool is destroyed on rebalance, then new messages are acked unprocessed

FixedQueuePool is created once on ResultsStrategyFactory and reused by every SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy from create_with_partitions. close() and join() call queue_pool.shutdown(), which shuts the queues down permanently. Arroyo closes the current strategy and builds a new one on every partition revocation/assignment, so after the first rebalance the new strategy submits into already-shut-down queues. queue.Queue.put raises queue.ShutDown, submit() swallows that exception, and the handler marks the offset completed. The commit thread then commits it. Those results are never processed and will not be redelivered, so uptime checks are silently dropped for the rest of the process lifetime. The shared OffsetTracker also keeps last_committed across assignments, so a later strategy can stall or skip commits for replayed offsets. The pool and tracker must be created per strategy instance and only shut down after that instance has finished its own work.

Submit and worker failures are committed as successfully processed

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit catches every exception (grouping_fn errors, BrokerValue assert, queue shutdown, put failures), logs, and calls add_offset plus complete_offset. OrderedQueueWorker.run also completes the offset in a finally block after logging processing exceptions. get_committable_offsets then treats those offsets as safe to commit, and ResultsStrategyFactory commits offset+1 to Kafka. The class docstring says offsets are committed only after successful processing and that no item is lost, but a failed message is acknowledged and never retried. In serial and batched-parallel modes an exception from batching/grouping escapes RunTask and is not committed, so this is a data-loss regression: a bad payload or a transient queue error permanently skips the check result.

Queues are unbounded and poll() never applies backpressure

Each worker queue is created with queue.Queue() (maxsize 0, unlimited), and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.poll only emits a gauge. submit() never blocks. The strategy docstring claims natural backpressure when queues fill, but nothing stops the consumer thread from pulling the entire partition into memory. One slow subscription blocks only its worker, while every other message on that partition keeps being queued, and the offset watermark cannot advance past the slow item. The process RSS grows with lag until the consumer is OOM-killed; on restart the uncommitted prefix is replayed. poll() or submit() needs a bounded queue and must block when any queue is full so Arroyo stops polling.

Graceful shutdown does not drain queues or wait for in-flight work

OrderedQueueWorker stops as soon as shutdown is True, before it drains the queue. FixedQueuePool.shutdown sets that flag and only then calls Queue.shutdown(immediate=False), so the graceful drain never happens: after the current item, the worker exits and leaves the rest of the queue unprocessed and incomplete. close() also joins the commit thread (5s) before shutting workers down, so anything completed after that final commit iteration is never committed. join() ignores its timeout and calls close() again. Worker joins are 5s each and sequential, so a stuck handler (the case this mode is meant to isolate) blocks the consumer thread for about num_queues*5 seconds, then the daemon worker keeps running after join returns. Those threads can still apply uptime side effects after partitions were revoked and another owner started, duplicating incidents, while the abandoned queued messages are only redelivered if they were not already acked.

Offsets are committed from a background thread

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy starts a daemon commit thread that calls the Arroyo commit callback every second. That callback is invoked by every other strategy on the consumer thread, which owns the Kafka consumer and the processor's staged-offset map. librdkafka consumers are not thread-safe, and the processor iterates that map while committing. Concurrent commit() from _commit_loop can corrupt staged offsets or raise RuntimeError if the map is mutated during iteration, and close() joins this thread from the consumer thread while it may be inside commit(), which deadlocks if commit needs the processor lock (join then times out after 5s and shutdown continues with a commit still in flight). Commits should be staged in poll()/close() on the consumer thread.

Queue stats test races workers and order is not asserted

test_stats_reporting submits 10 items to a live pool and immediately asserts get_stats()['total_items'] > 0. Workers are already running and the test processor only appends to a list, so the queues can be empty before that assertion; it will flake under load. test_different_groups_distributed similarly asserts that 20 hashed keys hit all 3 queues, which is not guaranteed. test_preserves_order_within_group only checks that 5 results were processed, not that they were processed in offset order, so an ordering regression in the strategy would still pass. None of the tests revoke partitions or call close()/join() and then submit again, so they miss the shared-pool shutdown data loss.

false_positives.candidate:
Set keys switched to sorted sets with no migration

Span buffer keys `span-buf:s:{project:trace}:span_id` were Redis SETs (SADD/SUNIONSTORE/SSCAN) and are now sorted sets (ZADD here, ZCARD/ZUNIONSTORE/ZPOPMIN in add-buffer.lua, ZSCAN in _load_segment_data). The key format is unchanged and nothing deletes or converts existing keys. After deploy, any in-flight segment still stored as a SET makes those commands fail with WRONGTYPE, so process_spans errors and those traces are not buffered until the key expires (redis_ttl defaults to 3600s). A rollback is equally broken: once a new process ZADDs a key, the old SADD/SSCAN code also gets WRONGTYPE. Mixed-version deploys cannot drain the buffer.

ZUNIONSTORE default SUM corrupts end-timestamp scores

Merging segment keys now uses ZUNIONSTORE with the default AGGREGATE SUM (both the span_key merge at this line and the parent_key merge just below). Members are span payloads and scores are end_timestamp_precise, used later by ZPOPMIN to decide which spans to drop. Redis sums scores when the same payload is in both keys. That overlap happens on Kafka redelivery: the span is ZADDed onto the grouped parent key in process_spans and is still present in the previous segment key that this script unions in. The summed score is no longer an end timestamp, so eviction keeps the redelivered span and drops a different span whose real timestamp is older. SUNIONSTORE used to dedupe without changing identity. The union needs AGGREGATE MIN or MAX so the score stays a timestamp.

Insert-time ZPOPMIN can drop the root span silently

Once a segment sorted set exceeds 1000 members, the script ZPOPMINs the lowest end_timestamp scores down to 1000. The root/segment span is not protected, and the has-root-span flag is set independently of whether that payload is still in the set. A root that ended before its children, or any span that loses the score tie-break, is deleted and never flushed, while the segment still looks complete downstream and may still use the shorter root timeout. The flush-time guard in _load_segment_data that skipped segments over max_segment_spans (1001) and emitted spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded was removed, and the 1000 cap is hardcoded in Lua rather than passed from SpansBuffer.max_segment_spans. Oversized segments that miss this script (WRONGTYPE, script error, crash between the earlier ZADD and EVALSHA) are now flushed in full with no metric. Drops are silent.

Redirect walk cap cut from 10000 to 1000

The parent-redirect walk that finds the segment key used to run up to 10000 hops, with a comment that a chain past that limit would not be joined correctly. It is now 1000, and the comment is gone. Each span adds a redirect entry. A parent chain longer than 1000 stops early, hsets the new span to an intermediate id, and merges into the wrong set. Those spans are flushed as a separate or truncated segment instead of the real trace segment, with no error.

No coverage for eviction, score merges, or the new paginator

Existing buffer tests only insert a handful of spans, all with the same end_timestamp_precise, and still only assert the full segment is flushed. UpdatedObjectInfo is not guaranteed to be reusable or to return an independent object: a second UpdatedObject call can conflict because the request resourceVersion is the unified-storage version, not the legacy one, can apply a patch to a different base and diverge, or can return the same pointer the API response is still encoding while legacy mutates it. Legacy will not reliably receive the write that unified storage just acknowledged.

Legacy write failures are no longer logged

The async legacy Create (line 56), Update (line 140), Delete (line 113), and DeleteCollection (line 165) ignore the error except for a duration metric. The previous synchronous implementation logged these failures. Combined with the mis-labeled metrics, a legacy timeout, conflict, or outage leaves the two stores diverged with no log line an operator can alert on. The request still returns success, which is intended, but the safety write's failure must be logged.

Destroy does not wait for in-flight legacy writes

Each successful write spawns an unbounded goroutine that may block on legacy storage for up to 10s, and nothing tracks those goroutines. Destroy (line 172) immediately calls Legacy.Destroy() and Storage.Destroy(). On shutdown or storage teardown, in-flight legacy creates/updates/deletes run against a closed store (panic or error) or are dropped when the process exits, so the safety copy is lost exactly when it is needed for rollback.

Tests never wait for or assert the async legacy write

Mode 3 unit tests return as soon as the synchronous storage call finishes (Create at line 65, and the same pattern in Update, Delete, and DeleteCollection). They never wait for the goroutine, never AssertExpectations, and would still pass if the legacy write were removed. The success-path mocks are also invoked from a goroutine after the test can return, which races testify's mock. The new playlist integration cases (pkg/tests/apis/playlist/playlist_test.go line 132 and the unified-storage mode 3 case) call doPlaylistTests, which immediately compares the legacy HTTP API (line 529 and getFromBothAPIs) with k8s results. That assumed synchronous dual-write; under mode 3 it will flake or fail when the legacy copy has not landed yet.

runSplitQuery now maps every target through datasource.applyTemplateVariables(..., request.filters) before executing. runShardSplitQuery does the same before grouping, then builds each shard sub-request from those already interpolated targets and calls runSplitQuery. On the shard-splitting path template application therefore runs twice per target (once up front, then once per shard group inside runSplitQuery). applyTemplateVariables is not idempotent: its contract appends ad-hoc filters to the LogQL expression, so the second call inserts the same matchers again, for example {app="foo", env="prod", __stream_shard__=~"1|2", env="prod"}. Chunks therefore still get a step derived from the chunk instead of the original range, which is the failure mode early interpolation is supposed to prevent. The unit test cannot catch that because the stub removes $__auto before runQuery is observed. true_positives.golden_comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Block-hit stats are rolled back on the signup they record

BlockedEmail.should_block? increments match_count and last_match_at and calls record.save while it is invoked from EmailValidator during User validation. User#save runs validations inside the same database transaction, and a blocked address fails validation, so that transaction rolls back and undoes the BlockedEmail update. On a normal install (SiteSetting.call_discourse_hub? false) UsersController#create only calls save, so blocked signup attempts never persist match statistics — last_match_at stays nil and match_count stays 0, which is the signal the model spec says admins use to see whether a rule has ever matched. When call_discourse_hub? is true, create calls user.valid? (line 168) before save, so the first increment commits and the second is rolled back, and the counter moves by 1 instead of 2. The write has to happen outside the user transaction (separate connection, or after the user save/rollback), or the stats feature does not work for the block action.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the problematic design of `BlockedEmail.should_block?` performing database writes (updating statistics) as a side effect of a read/validation check. The candidate issue goes further by explaining the concrete bug this causes in Rails (transaction rollback during validation), as well as the double-counting issue when `valid?` is called before `save`. Because they both point to the exact same flawed mechanism (side effects inside `should_block?`), this is a strong match.

true_positives.golden_comment: The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Exact email match lets blocked addresses sign up

should_block? loads BlockedEmail with a case-sensitive where(email: email) and never strips or downcases. Signup stores whatever was posted (User.new_from_params assigns params[:email] raw), while change_email in UsersController canonicalizes with Email.downcase(...).strip. A row for user@evil.com therefore does not match User@evil.com, user@evil.com with surrounding whitespace, or other case variants, so the new block is bypassed by changing case or padding the address. Uniqueness on blocked_emails.email is also case-sensitive, so both casings can be stored and .first can return either row. Normalize on write (set_defaults) and on lookup the same way change_email does, and compare the normalized value, or the blocklist does not actually block.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the same vulnerability: `BlockedEmail.should_block?` performs a case-sensitive email lookup, which allows users to bypass the blocklist by altering the casing of their email address (e.g., 'User@evil.com' vs 'user@evil.com').

false_positives.candidate:

The hit counter is read-modify-write: match_count += 1 followed by save. Two overlapping signup attempts that match the same blocked row both read the same count and both write count+1, so one hit is dropped. Popular blocked addresses are exactly the rows that get concurrent attempts. Even after the stat update is moved out of the user transaction, this still needs an atomic update (for example update_all("match_count = match_count + 1") on that id) rather than loading the integer into Ruby.

Tests stub the block check and miss signup behavior

EmailValidator examples stub BlockedEmail.should_block?, so they never hit the database, never assert the user.email.blocked message, and never run User#save. BlockedEmail specs only call should_block? directly, which commits the counter outside a user transaction, so they stay green while a real blocked signup rolls the stats back and while a case or whitespace variant is allowed through. There is also no coverage that the domain whitelist/blacklist logic moved out of User still rejects addresses. A User create/save example with a real BlockedEmail row (including a different-case address) is needed or these failures ship untested.

true_positives.golden_comment: -webkit-box-ordinal-group and -moz-box-ordinal-group require values starting from 1, not 0. If $val is 0, this will cause incorrect rendering in older browsers, leading to layout issues.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
order() mixin writes a 0-based value into 1-based ordinal-group

-webkit-box-ordinal-group and -moz-box-ordinal-group are 1-based (initial value 1) and reject 0, while the modern order property and -ms-flex-order are 0-based (initial value 0). The new mixin assigns $val to all of them. Autoprefixer-style output must use $val + 1 for the box-ordinal-group properties. order(2) and order(3) in this PR still sort after default items by accident (old default 1 is less than 2 and 3; modern default 0 is less than 2 and 3), but order(1) will not move an item after default siblings in old WebKit/Firefox, and order(0) or a negative order is invalid or ignored in the 2009 syntax. This is the shared helper the header now depends on, so the off-by-one should be fixed before it is reused.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: `-webkit-box-ordinal-group` and `-moz-box-ordinal-group` are 1-based properties (starting at 1), whereas standard flexbox `order` is 0-based, so passing `$val` (such as 0) directly without incrementing causes invalid/incorrect rendering in older browsers.

Short rows such as closed, pinned, or autoclosed actions therefore show the delete/expand control beside the text rather than pinned to the far side, in every browser that honors the new display. The same change also drops the description's 4em left padding that previously cleared the floated avatar, so non-flex fallbacks will overlap the icon and the text. Put margin-left:auto on the button (and drop the float) to restore the right alignment; .topic-avatar's float:left is likewise ignored and should not be relied on.

Panel right-align does not work in the prefixed flex fallback

.panel used to be float:right (and .title float:left). Those floats were removed and replaced with margin-left:auto plus order, while flexbox() emits display:-webkit-box and display:-moz-box before the modern values. The 2009 box model does not treat auto margins as flexible space, so browsers that only understand those prefixed values (Safari 6.1/7, iOS 7, older Android) keep the notifications, search, and login cluster immediately after the logo instead of on the right edge of the header. The prefixes this PR adds are exactly the browsers that will miss the new alignment, and there is no float fallback left.

Rails serializers expect include_ methods to end with ? for conditional attribute inclusion, a convention followed by other methods in this serializer. Without it, the website_name attribute may not be conditionally included as intended. Additionally, the '.' << website_host string concatenation should be replaced with '.' + website_host or '.#{website_host}' to avoid mutating string literals, which can lead to issues.

include_website_name is never invoked

ActiveModel::Serializer only calls inclusion hooks named include_<attr>?, and every other hook in this file follows that form. include_website_name has no question mark, so it is dead code and website_name is always emitted, including null when the user has no website. Rename it to include_website_name?. As written it only checks website.present?, so renaming alone does not apply the TL0 restriction.

Although the golden comment also mentions a secondary issue regarding string concatenation, the core issue is clearly matched.

website_name bypasses TL0 anonymous field hiding

website_name is derived from website but is not covered by untrusted_attributes, and website_name never calls scope.restrict_user_fields?. For a TL0 user seen anonymously, include_website? is forced false so website is omitted, yet website_name is still serialized. The profile template renders the globe label from model.website_name, so anonymous viewers get the host and, when the heuristic matches, the path of a field this serializer intentionally hides to limit new-user spam. Add website_name to untrusted_attributes (or apply the same guard in include_website_name?) and extend the existing TL0 anonymous serializer example; the new specs only cover a normal user.

Same-domain check misclassifies hosts

The non-equal branches do not test whether the website is actually on the instance domain, so the profile label either appends a path for an unrelated site or drops it for the same site. The elsif treats hosts as the same domain when they have the same label count greater than 2 and share every label except the first, which matches community.co.uk with paypal.co.uk and foo.github.io with bar.github.io and then appends the path. The else branch uses discourse_host.ends_with?("." + website_host), which is true for any suffix, so a website host of com or co.uk matches every forum on that suffix. The common www case fails the other way: a forum on example.com and a website of http://www.example.com/docs has a different label count and example.com does not end with .www.example.com, so only the host is shown. true_positives.golden_comment: The PollFeed job calls open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) without validating the URL, allowing an attacker who controls the feed_polling_url site setting to make the server fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
import_remote uses Kernel#open on attacker-influenced URLs

import_remote calls `open(url).read` without `require 'open-uri'` (unlike PollFeed) and without an http(s)-only client, timeout, or redirect check. Embed URLs are supplied by visitors (TopicRetriever only compares URI#host to embeddable_host, not the scheme, and does not re-check redirects), and PollFeed does the same `open` on feed_polling_url. That is SSRF against internal HTTP services, worker hangs, and, for a non-http setting or feed link, local file read.

That is SSRF against internal HTTP services, worker hangs, and, for a non-http setting or feed link, local file read.' TopicEmbed.import appends the source URL into the post body with raw string interpolation (`<a href='#{url}'>`) and saves the whole document via PostCreator with cook_method raw_html and skip_validations. false_positives.candidate:
Embed controller specs assert the wrong control flow

The success example expects `TopicRetriever.new` and `retrieve` to run inside the request. EmbedController#best does not do that; it calls `Jobs.enqueue(:retrieve_topic, …)` and renders loading. That expectation fails. The other success example renders best.html.erb, which currently cannot compile (`end if`), so the after-hook `response.should be_success` fails as well. The specs will not catch the enqueue/host/throttle behavior that actually shipped.

Cache miss runs a full feed import and drops HTTP fallback

When feed polling is enabled, perform_retrieve synchronously runs `Jobs::PollFeed.new.execute({})` (download and import every feed item) inside the per-URL retrieve job, then only calls fetch_http if that returns normally and the URL is still missing. Any exception from the feed (network error, nil content, bad item) aborts the job before the single-page HTTP fetch, so the embed stays on the loading page forever. A single comment embed also triggers a full import with no timeout isolation.

Unauthenticated embed GETs enqueue unbounded jobs

best only checks that the Referer host equals embeddable_host, then enqueues retrieve_topic for whatever embed_url was passed. Referer is trivial to spoof, embed_url is not checked against embeddable_host or a rate limit in the request, and the Redis throttle lives inside the job and is per URL. An anonymous client can fill the Sidekiq queue with unique URLs; each job still does work (host parse, Redis, sometimes HTTP). Validate the embed URL host before enqueue and throttle enqueues.

embed_url is varchar(255) with a unique index

embed_url is a Rails string column (varchar 255) and is uniquely indexed. Article and tracking URLs routinely exceed 255 characters. Insert then raises on PostgreSQL, TopicEmbed.create! rolls the import back, and that URL can never be embedded. Store embed_url as text (and keep the unique index).

Disqus import now depends on a live remote fetch and drops category

The importer used to create a local topic from the export (permalink stub, optional -c category) and then attach comments. It now calls TopicEmbed.import_remote, which GETs t[:link] and returns nothing usable if the historical URL 404s, redirects oddly, or open() raises. The exception is not rescued inside the thread loop, so one dead link aborts the rest of the file (the ensure only restores the email blacklist and rate limiter). The category option and category_id lookup were removed, and TopicEmbed.import has no category argument, so surviving imports also land in the wrong category.

Post jobs are enqueued inside the outer import transaction

import wraps PostCreator.create in Topic.transaction. PostCreator commits its own nested transaction by joining that outer one, then enqueue_jobs (process_post, feature_topic_users) runs before Topic.transaction commits. If TopicEmbed.create! then fails (unique embed_url race, null id), the outer transaction rolls the post back but the jobs are already queued and run against a missing row. Even on success they can run before commit. Enqueue only after the outer transaction commits, and rescue RecordNotUnique so a raced import reuses the existing embed instead of erroring.

Throttle key can stick forever if expire is skipped

retrieved_recently? uses SETNX and then a separate EXPIRE of 60 seconds. If the process dies between those calls, the key remains with no TTL and that embed URL is never fetched again for non-staff users (they stay on the loading page). Use a single SET key 1 NX EX 60 so the lock cannot outlive the throttle window.

false_negatives.golden_comment: postMessage targetOrigin should be the origin (scheme+host+port), not the full referrer URL; using the full URL will cause the message to be dropped and prevent resizing.

The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.

An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.

true_positives.golden_comment: The downsize method is defined twice. The second definition, which expects a single dimensions string parameter, overrides the first, which expected separate max_width and max_height parameters. This makes the original method unreachable and breaks existing code that calls it with separate width and height arguments.

Second downsize definition replaces the width/height method

Ruby does not overload methods. The new downsize(from, to, dimensions, opts) at this line replaces the downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts) defined just above, so that width/height version never runs. Existing callers that pass numeric max width and height (the previous public signature, which this file still tries to keep) will bind the width to dimensions and the height to opts. optimize then evaluates opts[:allow_animation] and raises NoMethodError, or, if a hash is passed in the height slot, builds a geometry of just the width (for example "1024") instead of "1024x768". Thumbnail generation that still uses the old arity breaks. self.optimize's signature changed the same way (dimensions string instead of width, height), so any external optimize caller is broken too.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: the `downsize` method is defined twice, and since Ruby does not support method overloading, the second definition (taking `dimensions`) overrides the first definition (taking `max_width` and `max_height`), breaking existing callers.

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoding maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024 ignores Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so the client-side limit can diverge from server-side and per-type settings (also applies to the 413 handler below).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Client upload limit is hardcoded and ignores per-type site settings

validateUploadedFile used to enforce Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so images and attachments had independent admin limits. It now always rejects above 10 * 1024 KB and no longer uses type. Attachments larger than max_attachment_size_kb but under 10MB are sent and then fail (or are stored, if the server trusts the client). Images the admin allowed above 10MB are blocked in the composer even though they would not need downsizing. The 413 handler at line 246 has the same hardcode, so a proxy rejection is reported as a 10MB limit even when nginx or max_image_size_kb is different. uploads_controller.rb also downloads API URLs with a fixed 10.megabytes cap, so raising max_image_size_kb above 10MB cannot be honored on that path either.

true_positives.golden_comment: The loop checking `tempfile.size` may never terminate correctly due to stale cached size, leading to potential infinite loops or incorrect file handling after modifications.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
In-place downsize can corrupt the upload and the result is ignored

The new loop calls OptimizedImage.downsize with the same path for input and output (tempfile.path to tempfile.path) and ignores the boolean it returns. ImageMagick convert cannot safely read and write one file: it often truncates the destination before the source is fully read, so a failed or partial convert destroys the upload. The open Tempfile still refers to the original inode, so after convert replaces the path, tempfile.size and whatever Upload.create_for reads from the handle can stay on the old bytes or sit past the new EOF. The loop then either keeps shrinking a stale size or stores a corrupt/empty/original image. If convert or ImageOptim fails, execution still falls through to Upload.create_for. Five 80% passes also only reach about a third of the linear dimensions, so a file can remain over SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb and still be uploaded.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue explicitly identifies the same core problem described in the golden comment: that `tempfile.size` remains stale after external modifications to the file path, causing the loop to keep checking a stale size and leading to incorrect file handling when creating the upload.

false_positives.candidate:
Oversized GIFs lose animation and SVGs are sent through convert

Auto-downsize always goes through OptimizedImage.downsize, whose non-animated instructions run convert with [0] (first frame only). The animated/gifsicle path is selected only when the filesystem path matches /\.GIF$/i. Rack and FileHelper temp paths do not keep the original filename extension, and this call never copies the bytes to a path ending in .gif, so allow_animation: SiteSetting.allow_animated_thumbnails never takes effect. Every oversized GIF is flattened to one frame and that result is what gets stored as the original upload, even when animated thumbnails are allowed. The same branch also runs for any FileHelper.is_image? filename, including SVG, unlike OptimizedImage.create_for which copies SVGs instead of converting them. convert will fail or rasterize the SVG and that output is then saved under the original .svg name.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Passing 80% as the dimensions can fail for animated GIFs when allow_animated_thumbnails is true, since the animated path uses gifsicle --resize-fit which expects WxH geometry, not a percentage; downsizing would then silently fail.

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: Potential nil pointer exception - if no TopicUser record exists, tu will be nil and calling methods on it will crash
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Unsubscribe crashes when the user has no TopicUser row

TopicsController#unsubscribe loads the per-user row with TopicUser.find_by and immediately reads tu.notification_level. If that row does not exist (logged-in user who can see the topic but has never had a topic_users record, or a category/mailing-list recipient whose row was never created), tu is nil and this raises NoMethodError. The email link then returns 500 and the notification level is not changed, so the unsubscribe action fails for exactly the people who need it. Use TopicUser.change (which inserts a row when missing) or create a muted row before updating.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the exact same bug: `tu` can be `nil` when no `TopicUser` record exists, leading to a crash (nil pointer exception / NoMethodError) when attempting to call methods on it.

false_positives.candidate:
One-click unsubscribe does not stop notifications for watching or tracking users

The email copy and the new client string both say the link stops notifications for this topic, but the action only mutes when notification_level is regular or already muted. Watching (3) and tracking (2) are greater than regular, so they are downgraded to regular instead of muted. Regular still generates reply, mention, and quote notifications, so a user who is emailed because they are watching the topic — the main case for a per-topic unsubscribe link — keeps receiving those emails after one click. The confirmation page always claims notifications have stopped, and nothing tells them they must click again to actually mute.

The new action assigns notification_level and calls save! instead of TopicUser.change. change is what sets notifications_changed_at, notifications_reason_id (user_changed), and the MessageBus notification_level_change event. Leaving notifications_reason_id nil means the existing auto-track logic in TopicUser.update_last_read and TopicUser.auto_track will treat the row as never explicitly chosen and set it back to tracking once the user has viewed the topic long enough (or on the next auto_track call). A successful mute is therefore silently reverted the next time they read the topic, and other open tabs are not told the level changed.

Unsubscribe is a cookie-authenticated GET with no recipient token GET /t/:slug/:topic_id/unsubscribe (and /t/:topic_id/unsubscribe, which 301s to the slugged URL) changes notification state with no CSRF token and no per-recipient unsubscribe key. ensure_logged_in only checks the browser session. Any site can trigger it while the victim is logged in (for example an to /t//unsubscribe); the browser sends session cookies, follows the 301, and the second request mutates state. The link also is not bound to the user who was emailed: whoever is logged in is the account that is changed, so a shared browser, staff session, or forwarded mail unsubscribes the wrong person while the recipient keeps getting mail. Email link scanners that do send cookies can apply the change without a click, and because the handler is not idempotent for watching users a second fetch drops them from regular to muted. This needs a POST (or a one-time key like the digest unsubscribe key) that identifies the recipient.

Unsubscribe template will not be resolved by the new route

The route is registered as a top-level topicUnsubscribe at /t/:slug/:id/unsubscribe (app-route-map.js.es6). Ember resolves that to the template, controller, and view names topic-unsubscribe. The controller and view were added under those names, but the template was added at templates/topic/unsubscribe.hbs, which compiles to topic/unsubscribe and is only used by a nested topic.unsubscribe route. Nothing calls renderTemplate to bridge the gap, so after the server has already changed the notification level the confirmation UI throws a missing-template error (or renders an empty outlet). The stop-notifications copy and the notification-level dropdown never appear. No coverage for the unsubscribe action or the new email link

The only spec change passes unsubscribe_url into an existing MessageBuilder example so I18n interpolation does not raise, and still only asserts that the preferences URL is in the body. Nothing asserts the new per-topic sentence or URL, and there is no request/controller spec for TopicsController#unsubscribe. The nil TopicUser crash, the watching-to-regular branch, the missing notifications_reason_id, the slug redirect, and the wrong-session GET mutation would all merge unnoticed.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Typo in property name: 'stopNotificiationsText' should be 'stopNotificationsText' (missing 'n' in 'Notifications')

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: macOS-specific sed syntax with empty string after -i flag will fail on Linux systems
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Webhook helper is macOS-only and writes .env relative to the cwd

The new script updates GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL with sed -i '' (BSD sed). On GNU sed that form treats '' as the script and does not edit the file, so Linux developers never get the tunnel URL written. ENV_FILE is ../.env relative to the current working directory, not the script path: running bash scripts/test-gcal-webhooks.sh from the repo root writes the parent directory's .env, not the app env file. cleanup also always exits 0, so a failed tunnel startup is reported as success.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue explicitly identifies the exact same bug described in the golden comment: the use of macOS-specific BSD sed syntax (`sed -i ''`) which fails on Linux systems using GNU sed.

false_positives.candidate:

deleteCacheMutation only toasts and calls the optional onSuccess prop. Unlike the disconnect mutation in the same component, it never invalidates viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars. That query is what supplies cacheUpdatedAt, and SelectedCalendarsSettingsWebWrapper loads it with refetchOnWindowFocus: false. After a successful delete the menu still shows the previous "Last updated" time and "Delete cached data" until a full remount, so the action looks like it failed.

Cache status treats expired rows as a live cache

getCacheStatusByCredentialIds groups CalendarCache by credentialId and takes max(updatedAt) with no expiresAt filter. getCachedAvailability only treats a row as a hit when expiresAt is still in the future. Any leftover expired row therefore makes connected calendars report cacheUpdatedAt and the dropdown offers "Delete cached data" even though availability lookups are already cache misses. The status does not mean the cache is serving data.

Backfill stamps every existing cache as updated at migrate time

The new updatedAt column is added as NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW(), so every existing CalendarCache row gets the migration timestamp rather than when it was actually written. CalendarCache has no createdAt; the only freshness signal already stored is expiresAt (writes set it to about now + 30 days). After deploy, every Google credential with any historical cache row shows "Last updated" as the deploy time, including stale and expired caches, which defeats the status feature. Backfill from expiresAt minus the cache TTL (and drop the default only if you still want Prisma @updatedAt to own later writes) before this ships; it cannot be reconstructed later.

Cache delete is undone by active Google watches

deleteCacheHandler only runs calendarCache.deleteMany for the credential. It does not stop google channel subscriptions on SelectedCalendar, and GoogleCalendarService.fetchAvailabilityAndSetCache (called from the webhook path) writes CalendarCache again and then touches those selected calendars. The confirmation copy says the delete cannot be undone, but the next notification recreates the rows. Users clearing a bad cache will see it return with no explanation, and a reload can show a new timestamp as if the delete did not stick.

Delegation calendar cache is invisible to status and delete

Cache status is loaded only via getCacheStatusByCredentialIds(connected calendar credential ids). The same repository documents that in-memory delegation credentials use negative ids that are not stored on CalendarCache, and reads for those users are keyed by userId plus the free/busy key so they can reuse a real credential's cache. Those org/delegation Google connections — the users the calendar-cache feature flag is aimed at — always get cacheUpdatedAt null, so the new menu never offers delete. deleteCacheHandler cannot fix that either: it requires a Credential row with id = credentialId and userId = the session user, which does not match a negative in-memory id or a cache row owned by another credential id.

dev:cron now calls tsx, which this package does not depend on

dev:cron changed from ts-node cron-tester.ts to npx tsx cron-tester.ts. ts-node is a declared devDependency; tsx is not in this package.json, and the app pins Yarn 3.4.1, where npx is not the workspace runner and will try to fetch tsx outside the lockfile. yarn dev:cron fails offline or in CI, or runs an unpinned tsx. This change is unrelated to calendar cache and should stay on the declared runner or add tsx as a dependency and invoke it through Yarn.

No tests for deleteCache ownership or status mapping

deleteCache is a new authenticated mutation that deletes every CalendarCache row for a client-supplied credentialId after a userId check, and connectedCalendars now depends on getCacheStatusByCredentialIds. Nothing in the PR covers another user (or a negative delegation id) being rejected, a successful delete actually removing rows, or expired versus live rows being mapped to cacheUpdatedAt. A regression in the ownership where-clause would ship silently.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The updateManyByCredentialId call uses an empty data object, which prevents Prisma's @updatedAt decorator from updating the updatedAt timestamp. This results in inaccurate cache status tracking, as the timestamp isn't updated when the cache is refreshed. To fix this, explicitly set the updatedAt field.

Throwing a generic Error for authentication failures results in a 500 response in tRPC. Instead, it should return a structured TRPCError with an appropriate code, such as FORBIDDEN, to accurately reflect the error type.
Date is formatted with hardcoded 'en-US' locale instead of using the user's locale from useLocale, which can lead to incorrect date representation for users in different locales.

true_positives.golden_comment: Incorrect end time calculation using slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Working-hours fallback rejects valid split shifts and ignores the slot end

When no date override matches, availability is decided by workingHours.find: any same-day window whose range does not contain the slot makes the callback return true and the slot is rejected. A host with a lunch break (two windows on the same weekday) therefore loses every slot, including ones that sit fully inside the other window. The end minute is copied from slotStartTime rather than the slot end, so a slot that starts inside hours but runs past workingHour.endTime is treated as inside. Days with no working-hour entry never match, so they are treated as free; a fixed host who does not work that weekday is not excluded. For round-robin this filter is what is supposed to keep fixed hosts from being booked outside their own hours, and it does the opposite for split schedules.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue explicitly identifies the exact same bug mentioned in the golden comment: 'The end minute is copied from slotStartTime rather than the slot end' (also noted in the title 'ignores the slot end'). Although the candidate bundles this with other related logic issues in the same block, it clearly and accurately points out the golden issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Multiple override ranges on one day reject every slot

The date-override filter uses Array.find and treats a true callback as "this slot is not bookable". Each range returns true when the slot merely falls outside that one range. On a day with two ranges (for example 09:00-12:00 and 14:00-17:00), a slot inside the first range is outside the second, so find succeeds and checkIfIsAvailable returns false. Every slot is outside at least one range, so a split date override blocks the entire day instead of opening those windows. The start===end all-day-block branch just above never runs either: it compares two dayjs instances with ===, which is always false, so a zero-length override is not handled as a full-day block.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue explicitly identifies the exact same bug as the golden comment in its final sentence: 'The start===end all-day-block branch just above never runs either: it compares two dayjs instances with ===, which is always false'. Although the candidate bundles this with another logic bug in the same block, it clearly catches the underlying issue.

false_positives.candidate:
In-override slots skip busy checks and can double-book

checkIfIsAvailable now returns true as soon as a date override exists for that calendar day and the slot is not strictly outside it. That return happens before the busy-interval scan, so calendar conflicts and existing Cal bookings are ignored for every fixed host (personal events, collective hosts, and round-robin fixed hosts all go through this path). A host who sets a date override and already has a meeting inside that window will still be offered those slots, and the booking can be confirmed on top of the conflict. Partial overlaps are treated as inside as well: a slot that starts before the override and ends during it is not rejected, so the meeting can begin outside the override hours.

Override timezone shift wraps at midnight and lands on the wrong day

Date-override start and end are shifted by inviteeUtcOffset - organizerUtcOffset and then reduced to hour and minute only. Those values are minutes within 0-1439, so a shift that crosses midnight is applied to the invitee day already selected from the unadjusted UTC timestamp. An evening override viewed from a timezone ahead shows up as early-morning slots on the previous day; a morning override viewed from a timezone behind can produce endTime < startTime. buildSlots drops ranges with start >= end, and the caller has already removed that user's normal working hours for the day, so the override disappears and the host has no slots. The new test only compares +5:30 and +6:00, a 30-minute gap that never crosses midnight, so it does not catch this. Attendees several hours from the organizer still see the override at the wrong time, which is the bug this change is meant to fix.

Override day match compares server-local date to UTC

Whether an override applies is decided by formatting dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset) (local mode, so the server timezone) as YYYY MM DD and comparing it to slotStartTime, which was forced to UTC. isBefore/isAfter later compare absolute instants, but they only run after this date check. On any host whose TZ is not UTC, an override near midnight is attached to the wrong day or skipped entirely, and the fixed host's override is not enforced. Slot generation then falls through to weekly hours.

No test for fixed-host overrides on round-robin

The PR's stated fix is that a round-robin event must not offer slots when a fixed host's date override makes them unavailable, including across timezones. The only new assertion re-queries a single-user event in Asia/Dhaka and expects the same UTC instants as Asia/Kolkata. It never builds a ROUND_ROBIN event, never sets hosts[].isFixed, and never places a booking or calendar busy block inside an override. The double-book path, split override ranges, and fixed-host weekly hours can all regress without failing CI.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1 reads a possibly stale value and can lose increments under concurrency; consider an atomic increment via Prisma (increment: 1) to avoid race conditions (also applies to the similar update in the catch block).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Overlapping crons lose retry increments and can double-send

Both failure paths write `retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1` from the value loaded at the start of the loop instead of an atomic increment. Two overlapping runs of this cron can both select the same unscheduled reminder, both call Twilio, and both store the same next count. Recipients get duplicate texts, and because the stored count never moves past that shared value the `retryCount > 1` delete may never fire, so the retry cap does not hold under overlap. Claim the row (conditional update of scheduled, or increment in the database) before calling Twilio.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the exact same concurrency/race condition issue where `retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1` reads a stale value and loses increments under concurrent execution, and both note that it applies to both failure paths and recommend atomic updates.

true_positives.golden_comment: The deletion logic in scheduleSMSReminders.ts incorrectly deletes non-SMS workflow reminders (e.g., Email, WhatsApp) that have retryCount > 1. This occurs because the retryCount condition within the OR clause for deletion lacks a method: WorkflowMethods.SMS filter, causing it to apply to all reminder types instead of only SMS reminders, which is the intended scope of this function.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
retryCount cleanup deletes every workflow reminder, not just failed SMS

The new deleteMany ORs the existing past-due SMS clause with `{ retryCount: { gt: 1 } }` and that second clause has no method, scheduled, or date filter. WorkflowReminder is shared by EMAIL, SMS, and WHATSAPP. Every cron run therefore permanently deletes any reminder of any method once retryCount is greater than 1, including a row that was already scheduled and still has a provider referenceId. The comment on line 28 still says this only removes past SMS reminders. Scope the predicate to unscheduled SMS (and filter the later findMany the same way); otherwise any non-SMS writer of this new column, or a scheduled SMS row that ever exceeds the cap, loses the reminder.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue point out the exact same bug: the new `{ retryCount: { gt: 1 } }` condition in the `OR` clause of `deleteMany` lacks the `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` filter, causing it to inadvertently delete non-SMS workflow reminders (like Email and WhatsApp).

false_positives.candidate:
A successful Twilio schedule is counted as a failure if saving the SID throws

twilio.scheduleSMS runs before the update that sets scheduled and referenceId. If Twilio accepts the message and that update throws, the new catch increments retryCount and leaves scheduled false and referenceId unset. The next cron loads the same reminder again and sends another SMS. After retryCount exceeds 1 the row is deleted, so the already accepted Twilio message can no longer be cancelled from a stored SID. Only a failed scheduleSMS call should advance retryCount; if persistence fails after Twilio accepts the message, cancel that message or retry the write without treating it as a failed send.

Missing number or empty body never counts toward the retry cap

retryCount is incremented only when Twilio returns a falsy result or throws, and only inside `if (message?.length > 0 && sendTo)`. If the attendee or step has no phone number, or the step has no reminder body and the template is not REMINDER, the loop skips the row and leaves scheduled false and retryCount at 0. That reminder is loaded again on every cron run until scheduledDate is in the past, which is the unbounded reschedule this PR is meant to stop. Treat a missing destination or empty message as a failed attempt, or delete the reminder immediately.

No test locks the retry cap or the delete scope

The new failure accounting and deleteMany predicate have no tests. A regression should assert that one failed SMS schedule leaves the reminder, that a second failure removes it on the next run, and that email or WhatsApp reminders and already scheduled SMS rows are not deleted by the retryCount clause. Without that, the unscoped OR delete and the off-path skips (no phone number, persistence failure after Twilio accepts) can ship unnoticed.

Team and org authorization SQL is built as `(<team predicate>) OR (<user predicate>)` (org reduce at lines 171-174, team reduce at lines 204-207). Those parentheses wrap each branch only, not the whole OR. `getBaseConditions` returns that fragment as-is when there is no event-type or member filter (line 75). AND binds tighter than OR in PostgreSQL, so the intended caller query `WHERE ${await service.getBaseConditions()} AND "startTime" >= ${from} AND "startTime" < ${to}` — the replacement for the removed `findMany`, which ANDed caller filters onto the entire authorization object — is parsed as `team_booking_predicate OR (personal_booking_predicate AND startTime filters)`. Every team booking for that team or org is included no matter what date, status, or other AND predicates the caller adds. Insights over-count and can return bookings outside the window the caller applied. `getBaseConditions` only wraps the auth fragment when a service-level filter is also present (line 73). Wrap the full OR, and the final fragment returned to callers, in parentheses. The new tests expect this unparenthesized text and never run team/org SQL with an additional AND, so they do not catch it.

toEqual(Prisma.sql) does not match nested SQL fragments

Composed conditions are built by nesting `Prisma.sql` values (`(${acc}) OR (${condition})` and the filter AND reduce). Prisma does not flatten nested `strings`/`values` until execution, so the object from `getAuthorizationConditions`/`getFilterConditions` is not deeply equal to a single flat `Prisma.sql` template with the same text. `expect(conditions).toEqual(Prisma.sql`...`)` therefore fails for the team-scope assertion (line 295), the org-scope assertion (line 332), and the combined-filter assertion (line 429) — the cases that use `ANY(...)` and OR. Flat cases (user scope, a single filter, `1=0`) can still pass. The only test that executes SQL is the user-scope `$queryRaw` query, which never hits `ANY` or the OR precedence bug. Compare flattened SQL text and bound values, or run the team/org fragments, instead of `toEqual` on raw `Prisma.Sql` objects.

This is because getAuthorizationConditions() always returns a non-null Prisma.Sql object, making authConditions always truthy, which means only the first two if/else if conditions are ever evaluated.

Fetching userIdsFromOrg only when teamsFromOrg.length > 0 can exclude org-level members for orgs without child teams; consider deriving from teamIds (which includes orgId) or removing the guard so org-only orgs still include member user bookings.

The removal listener now runs only when ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ is enabled, but management() returns MgmtPermissionsV2 whenever ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled. If both features are on, ClientRemovedEvent calls ClientPermissionsV2.setPermissionsEnabled, which throws UnsupportedOperationException and can fail client deletion. getOrCreateResource creates the client resource by name and scopes but never setType(CLIENTS). The aggregate Clients resource created in init() does set its type. ClientPermissionsV2.getClientsWithPermission then uses resourceStore.findByType(..., CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE), so it will not see per-client grants. It will see the aggregate resource and add its name "Clients" to the granted id set, which is not a client id. Callers that filter the client list or role-mapping targets with this set therefore omit clients the user was granted and never match a real client id.

The candidate describes the same underlying bug, though it emphasizes omitted grants rather than potential null-client failures.

true_positives.golden_comment: In ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission, the method getResourceTypeResource could return null, leading to a NullPointerException in findByResource. Defensive null checks are needed to prevent this issue.
true_positives.matched_candidate:

hasPermission(ClientModel, scope) loads only the per-client resource when one exists and never evaluates the Clients type resource in that case. FGAP requires both: a positive all-clients grant must still apply when the client already has a resource for another scope, and a negative all-clients policy must still deny a positive per-client grant. As written, all-clients manage/view is ignored whenever any per-client resource exists (incorrect deny), and a negative all-clients policy does not override a positive per-client policy (incorrect allow). If the per-client resource is missing and getResourceTypeResource returns null (schema not migrated, or admin permissions not enabled for this server), findByResource(server, null) on line 219 throws NullPointerException and the admin call 500s instead of returning false.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly identifies that getResourceTypeResource can return null and that passing this null to findByResource causes a NullPointerException in hasPermission, matching the golden issue despite also raising policy-evaluation concerns.

That client was created by the earlier Users-only schema, so upgraded realms never get the Clients resource, or the new configure, map-roles-client-scope, and map-roles-composite scopes. Creating or evaluating a Clients permission then fails with missing-scope or missing-resource errors, and ClientPermissionsV2 falls through to a null type resource. Init needs to add any schema resource types and scopes that are not already present.

canMapRoles, canMapCompositeRoles, and canMapClientScopeRoles only call hasPermission for that scope. Unlike canManage in the same class, they do not treat AdminRoles.MANAGE_CLIENTS as allowed, and they do not treat a Clients manage grant as allowed. A realm admin (or any caller who can manage the client) is therefore forbidden from mapping client roles, composite roles, or client-scope roles unless a separate FGAP map-roles policy exists. Per-client resources are stored under the internal client id and display name is never set, so permission listings fall through to resource.getDisplayName() and show null instead of the clientId. After a client is deleted the orphaned resource still will not be reported as missing, unlike the user path which throws ModelIllegalStateException.

Both methods are void and are specified elsewhere to throw ForbiddenException. Callers reading only these comments will treat them as predicates.

The canView() method correctly checks both VIEW and MANAGE, but canManage() should only check MANAGE.

GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup() gates creating a group and moving an existing group to the top level with requireManage(), which only calls this no-arg canManage(). A principal granted only view-all-groups can therefore create groups and reparent any group to the top of the tree. The candidate adds concrete consequences without changing the underlying issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, hasPermission is called with groupResource.getId() and the same groupResource.getId() is added to granted, but hasPermission resolves resources by name (treating the argument as a group id) and the GroupPermissionEvaluator contract says this method returns group IDs that are later used as UserModel.GROUPS and in getUsersCount group filters. This mismatch means per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions may not yield the expected group IDs for filtering and counts, and evaluation may effectively only look at the type-level 'all-groups' resource; consider revisiting whether this should operate on the underlying group ids (resource names) instead so it aligns with the JPA queries and the interface contract.

View-members group id lookup returns the wrong ids

getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() is what UsersResource and BruteForceUsersResource pass to user search and getUsersCount as membership constraints (session attribute UserModel.GROUPS). The V2 implementation does two things that make those ids unusable. It asks resourceStore.findByType for type "Groups", but AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource() never calls setType on the per-group resource it creates (only the synthetic all-groups resource is typed), so individual group resources are not returned. For whatever is returned it calls hasPermission(groupResource.getId(), ...) and granted.add(groupResource.getId()). Authorization resource ids are not group ids; V2 stores the group id as the resource name (resolveGroup returns group.getId(), and hasPermission looks that up with findByName). true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same core mismatch: getGroupIdsWithViewPermission uses authorization resource IDs for permission checks and returned membership constraints, although hasPermission resolves resources by name and consumers require underlying group IDs. It also describes the resulting all-groups fallback and incorrect filtering/counts. Additional observations do not change this semantic match.

GroupPermissionsV2.setPermissionsEnabled (and the other GroupPermissionManagement methods) always throw UnsupportedOperationException. getResourceName() only resolves a human-readable name for the Users resource type. Group resources created by getOrCreateResource are named with the group id and never get a display name. For a Groups policy the method therefore returns resource.getDisplayName(), which is null. Permission listings in the admin API/UI cannot show which group a permission applies to, unlike users, where the username is resolved from the same resource name.

The javadoc on requireManageMembers says it throws when canManageMembership(GroupModel) is false. The implementation throws when canManageMembers is false. The new getGroupIdsWithViewPermission javadoc has the same problem: it says it returns a Stream of groups with view permission, but the method returns a Set and both implementations select groups by view-members/manage-members, not view.

true_positives.golden_comment: Returns wrong provider (default keystore instead of BouncyCastle)
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getBouncyCastleProvider returns the JDK keystore provider

getBouncyCastleProvider() is documented to return the BouncyCastle or BCFIPS provider. This implementation returns KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider(), which is the platform keystore provider (typically SUN), not BouncyCastle. WildFlyElytronProvider returns null when BC is absent so callers can take a non-BC path. A non-null SUN provider fails those null checks and is then passed to Signature.getInstance or Cipher.getInstance. SUN does not provide SHA256withECDSA (that is SunEC) or BC algorithms such as AES/CBC/PKCS7Padding, so provider-pinned operations throw NoSuchAlgorithmException or use the wrong implementation. For a standalone authz-client this class is the selected CryptoProvider, so return null or throw instead of handing back the keystore provider.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: getBouncyCastleProvider returns the default JDK keystore provider rather than the BouncyCastle provider.

true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
order() breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations

order() was added as an abstract method with no default on the public CryptoProvider interface in keycloak-common. Implementations compiled against the previous interface will not compile, and at runtime ServiceLoader detection calls order() and throws AbstractMethodError, so CryptoIntegration.init fails and the server does not start. A default such as default int order() { return 0; } would keep older providers loadable and sort them below the in-tree providers (200) and AuthzClientCryptoProvider (100).
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same backward-compatibility issue: adding abstract order() to CryptoProvider without a default breaks existing implementations. The candidate provides additional compile-time and runtime consequences.

false_positives.candidate:
Tied CryptoProviders are chosen non-deterministically

detectProvider no longer throws when ServiceLoader finds more than one CryptoProvider. It sorts by order() descending and returns the first entry. DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, and FIPS1402Provider all return 200, so any two of them tie, and ServiceLoader order is classpath-dependent. The loser is only mentioned in a debug log. Previously this misconfiguration aborted startup. Now a FIPS deployment that also has the non-FIPS provider can keep running with DefaultCryptoProvider even though FIPS1402Provider's constructor has already inserted BCFIPS at JCA position 1 and rewritten ssl.KeyManagerFactory.algorithm / ssl.TrustManagerFactory.algorithm. The process then mixes a non-FIPS CryptoProvider with FIPS JCA settings, or the reverse. When several providers share the highest order, startup should still fail.

AuthzClient.create freezes the JVM crypto provider

AuthzClient.create(Configuration) calls CryptoIntegration.init(AuthzClient.class.getClassLoader()), and init() keeps the first provider it detects forever. ServiceLoader on the authz-client classloader does not see CryptoProvider services registered only in a child deployment or server classloader. Those order-200 providers are skipped, AuthzClientCryptoProvider (order 100) is installed, and a later CryptoIntegration.init from the server is a no-op. The rest of the JVM then uses a provider that throws UnsupportedOperationException from getSignature, getPemUtils, cipher, certificate, and truststore methods. Creating a client must not permanently install this stub from the library classloader; a later init that can see a higher-order provider has to be able to replace it.

ECDSA integer conversion silently truncates

integerToBytes, used by asn1derToConcatenatedRS, copies the low-order qLength bytes whenever BigInteger.toByteArray() is longer than the coordinate size. It does not require the discarded prefix to be a single 0x00 sign octet, and it does not reject a negative INTEGER. An oversized or negative DER integer therefore becomes a different R or S instead of failing the conversion with IOException. Signature verification then runs against a value that is not the encoded integer, so malformed ECDSA input is mishandled rather than rejected. Throw unless the encoding is at most qLength+1 bytes and any extra leading byte is 0x00.

ECDSA test only checks a self-roundtrip on P-256

The only new coverage of the ASN.1 ECDSA conversion generates one key with KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair(), which is the provider default curve (P-256 on standard JDKs), then runs ES256, ES384, and ES512 with that key. The sole assertion is that decoding the encoder's output matches the intermediate R||S. Signature.verify is never called, and the result is never compared with Java's original DER. A decoder/encoder pair that ignores the real R and S and inverts each other would pass. ES384 and ES512 also never see 48-byte or 66-byte coordinates, so the sign-octet padding path at those widths is untested. Each algorithm needs a key on secp256r1, secp384r1, or secp521r1, and the DER produced from the concatenated form must verify with Signature.verify.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Dead code exists where ASN1Encoder instances are created and written to, but their results are immediately discarded. The actual encoding is performed by new ASN1Encoder instances created in the subsequent return statement, rendering the earlier operations useless.
When length starts at -1 from indefinite-length encoding, the arithmetic 'length = length - bytes.length' will behave unexpectedly, potentially leading to incorrect processing of encoded data.

true_positives.golden_comment: The reader thread isn’t waited for; flipping deletedAll to true and asserting immediately can race and miss exceptions added just after the flag change, making this test flaky.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Concurrency test can pass or hang without observing the race

createMultiDeleteMultiReadMulti starts a non-daemon reader thread and then asserts caughtExceptions is empty without joining that thread (or setting a timeout). deletedAll is set true as soon as the deletes return, so the assertion can run while a groups() call is still in flight and record its exception only after the assert, or the reader may not have overlapped the deletes at all. The test can therefore pass even when the concurrent list still returns 500. If any remove() throws before deletedAll.set(true), the reader stays in while (!deletedAll.get()) forever and, because the thread is not a daemon and is never interrupted, it can hang the suite and keep calling the shared admin client during later tests. The flag needs to be set in a finally, the reader joined with a timeout before the assertion, and the test should fail if the reader never actually ran during the deletes.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same missing synchronization: the reader thread is not joined before asserting, so an in-flight read can add an exception after deletedAll is set and the assertion has already passed. Its additional hang concerns do not change this match.

This prevents correct metric aggregation across flush stages — dashboards and alerts filtering by tag 'shard' will miss data tagged as 'shards' and vice versa.

Flusher timers use mismatched, high-cardinality shard tags

true_positives.golden_comment: The test_basic function in test_consumer.py uses a monkeypatched time.sleep that returns immediately, but then calls time.sleep(0.1) expecting it to actually wait.

The test looks up time.sleep at call time, so it hits the patch and does not wait. join() then sets stopped immediately. The flusher can leave its loop before flush_segments runs with the advanced drift, so the assertion on the produced segment is racy. The new poll/sleep was added to close that race and does not. true_positives.golden_comment: Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Spawn flusher workers are never killed or terminated

Workers are created with multiprocessing.get_context("spawn").Process, so they are SpawnProcess instances. SpawnProcess subclasses multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess, not multiprocessing.Process (the default-context class). Both the hang-restart path (process.kill() around line 254) and join() (process.terminate() around line 346) are guarded by isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process), which is always false for these workers, so the signal is never sent. Crash recovery still works because a dead process is simply replaced, but a hang does not: a second worker is started for the same shards, and once it updates the shared healthy_since value the slot looks healthy, so MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS never fires and the original worker is leaked. That leaked worker can keep calling flush_segments/produce on the same Redis shards as the replacement, duplicating buffered-segments output and racing flush state. On shutdown, a worker blocked in Redis or Kafka produce is also never force-stopped after stopped is set, so it can still produce after those shards have been reassigned.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same underlying bug: spawn-context workers are SpawnProcess instances that fail the isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process) check on POSIX, preventing hung workers from being killed. Its additional shutdown and recovery consequences do not change the core match.
