true_positives.golden_comment: Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
join() abandons flusher processes once the deadline has passed

join() gives the entire caller timeout to next_step.join(timeout) before it waits on flusher workers. If that call consumes the timeout, deadline is already in the past and the loop breaks immediately, without waiting for or terminating any remaining flusher process. The previous single-process join always called terminate() even when the deadline had already elapsed. These workers are daemon processes only in the sense that they die if the parent exits; the consumer process stays alive across rebalance. A worker still inside flush_segments or Kafka produce therefore keeps flushing shards the new assignment no longer owns, which duplicates segments onto the buffered-segments topic and conflicts with whichever consumer now owns those Redis shards.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify that breaking out of the flusher loop after the deadline expires skips termination of remaining processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown. The candidate adds context and consequences but describes the same underlying issue.

false_positives.candidate:
Restart starts a new flusher before the old one has stopped

_ensure_processes_alive replaces a worker by signalling it (when the isinstance check is fixed) and then immediately calling _create_process_for_shards for the same shard list. kill()/terminate() return as soon as the signal is sent; the old process is not joined, and its handle is overwritten in self.processes so a later join cannot reap or stop it. The old worker can still be inside flush_segments, produce, or done_flush_segments while the new worker starts the same cycle. Both will publish the same segments and both will mutate the same Redis flush keys. The thread path used when produce_to_pipe is set never signals the old thread at all, so tests hit this overlap on every restart.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using zip(error_ids, events.values()) assumes the get_multi result preserves the input order; dict value order is not guaranteed to match error_ids, so event data can be paired with the wrong ID (missing nodes also shift alignment).
true_positives.matched_candidate:

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
BuildIndex no longer excludes concurrent builds of the same key

BuildIndex used to hold cacheMu for the whole build, which serialized bleve.New and cache publication. The lock is now taken only to publish b.cache[key] at the end, and nothing single-flights a key. getOrCreateIndex still does GetIndex then build with no per-key lock, so two searches or watch events for a missing namespace (indexes below InitMinCount, or any key created after startup) both pass the cache miss and call BuildIndex together. For file indexes both call bleve.New on the same directory and race the index files; for memory indexes both succeed. The slower build then overwrites b.cache[key], so the cached index can be the staler one, the other index is leaked and never closed, and callers that already received the losing index keep searching a copy that will not receive later watch updates.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same race: moving cacheMu from protecting the entire BuildIndex operation to only the final cache assignment allows multiple goroutines to build an index for the same key concurrently.

false_positives.candidate:
Parallel index init races on shared err and counter

init now actually builds many namespaces at once (errgroup plus the BuildIndex lock removal). Every worker does totalBatchesIndexed++ and err = s.build(...) on the same outer variables with no mutex or atomic. That is a data race: a failed build can return another worker's nil error, so group.Wait can succeed and the process starts with a missing index, or a successful worker can return another worker's error and fail startup. The namespaced_indexed span attribute is also racy and can be wrong. Each worker needs its own err variable, and the counter must be atomic or updated after Wait.

Startup index watch cursor skips writes made during the build

build returns the resource version of the list snapshot and documents that watchers must apply every event after that RV, but init discards both return values and only then calls WatchWriteEvents. That helper records the latest RV at call time and the SQL poller emits only history rows after that cursor. With a long startup build — the path this PR moved onto process start — and with namespaces built in parallel, an index finished early misses every write committed after its list and before the slowest build finishes. Those writes are never replayed, so the search index stays permanently stale. The watch must start from each build's returned RV (or from the RV captured before listing), not from a single cursor taken after all builds.

Search watch goroutine panics when the event channel closes

After index build, init starts a goroutine that does v := <-events and always calls handleEvent. watchctx is context.Background(), not the server's cancellable context, so server.Stop cannot stop it. SQL WatchWriteEvents closes the channel when the backend stops, and server.Stop calls lifecycle.Stop (the SQL backend implements LifecycleHooks) before cancelling the server context. A closed channel yields a nil event; handleEvent immediately reads evt.Type and panics, crashing the process. Because Init now always runs from NewResourceServer, every storage-server shutdown hits this. The loop must exit on !ok and must use the server context. The same unbounded read exists in initWatcher.

Failed constructor Init leaks watchers and never cancels its context

NewResourceServer calls s.Init and, on error, returns nil without s.cancel() or Stop. Init can already have run lifecycle.Init (opening the DB) and search.init, which starts the background WatchWriteEvents poller and the handleEvent goroutine, before a later step such as initWatcher fails. Callers only receive the error, so they have no server handle to Stop, the cancellable context is abandoned, and those goroutines run until process exit. On the search-watch path a later backend stop then panics, as described above. The error path needs to cancel and stop anything Init already started before returning.

Server watch now starts only after the full index build

Init used to call initWatcher before search.init. It now builds every search index first and only then starts the server broadcaster's WatchWriteEvents. That poller does not replay history; it starts at whatever the latest RV is when it is called. Writes committed during the startup index build (other HA replicas; WatchWriteEvents is documented to observe remote writes) are therefore never pushed to the broadcaster. A client that reconnects with Since set to the last RV it saw misses those events. Previously the broadcaster poller was already running for the whole index build, so those events were captured. Start the server watcher before the long index build, or replay from the RV observed before the build.

TestIntegrationWillRunInstrumentationServerWhenTargetHasNoHttpServer is the integration test that constructs and runs the storage-server target. This PR makes NewResourceServer block on full unified-storage Init (DB plus index build) during that construction, then skips the test whenever GRAFANA_TEST_DB=postgres, with a TODO that it fails in Drone and works locally. CI no longer exercises storage-server startup on postgres, so a postgres-specific failure in the new eager Init path — the behavior this PR adds — will not fail the build.

false_positives.candidate:
Shared queue pool is destroyed on rebalance, then new messages are acked unprocessed

FixedQueuePool is created once on ResultsStrategyFactory and reused by every SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy from create_with_partitions. close() and join() call queue_pool.shutdown(), which shuts the queues down permanently. Arroyo closes the current strategy and builds a new one on every partition revocation/assignment, so after the first rebalance the new strategy submits into already-shut-down queues. queue.Queue.put raises queue.ShutDown, submit() swallows that exception, and the handler marks the offset completed. The commit thread then commits it. Those results are never processed and will not be redelivered, so uptime checks are silently dropped for the rest of the process lifetime. The shared OffsetTracker also keeps last_committed across assignments, so a later strategy can stall or skip commits for replayed offsets. The pool and tracker must be created per strategy instance and only shut down after that instance has finished its own work.

Submit and worker failures are committed as successfully processed

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit catches every exception (grouping_fn errors, BrokerValue assert, queue shutdown, put failures), logs, and calls add_offset plus complete_offset. OrderedQueueWorker.run also completes the offset in a finally block after logging processing exceptions. get_committable_offsets then treats those offsets as safe to commit, and ResultsStrategyFactory commits offset+1 to Kafka. The class docstring says offsets are committed only after successful processing and that no item is lost, but a failed message is acknowledged and never retried. In serial and batched-parallel modes an exception from batching/grouping escapes RunTask and is not committed, so this is a data-loss regression: a bad payload or a transient queue error permanently skips the check result.

Queues are unbounded and poll() never applies backpressure

Each worker queue is created with queue.Queue() (maxsize 0, unlimited), and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.poll only emits a gauge. submit() never blocks. The strategy docstring claims natural backpressure when queues fill, but nothing stops the consumer thread from pulling the entire partition into memory. One slow subscription blocks only its worker, while every other message on that partition keeps being queued, and the offset watermark cannot advance past the slow item. The process RSS grows with lag until the consumer is OOM-killed; on restart the uncommitted prefix is replayed. poll() or submit() needs a bounded queue and must block when any queue is full so Arroyo stops polling.

Graceful shutdown does not drain queues or wait for in-flight work

OrderedQueueWorker stops as soon as shutdown is True, before it drains the queue. FixedQueuePool.shutdown sets that flag and only then calls Queue.shutdown(immediate=False), so the graceful drain never happens: after the current item, the worker exits and leaves the rest of the queue unprocessed and incomplete. close() also joins the commit thread (5s) before shutting workers down, so anything completed after that final commit iteration is never committed. join() ignores its timeout and calls close() again. Worker joins are 5s each and sequential, so a stuck handler (the case this mode is meant to isolate) blocks the consumer thread for about num_queues*5 seconds, then the daemon worker keeps running after join returns. Those threads can still apply uptime side effects after partitions were revoked and another owner started, duplicating incidents, while the abandoned queued messages are only redelivered if they were not already acked.

Offsets are committed from a background thread

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy starts a daemon commit thread that calls the Arroyo commit callback every second. That callback is invoked by every other strategy on the consumer thread, which owns the Kafka consumer and the processor's staged-offset map. librdkafka consumers are not thread-safe, and the processor iterates that map while committing. Concurrent commit() from _commit_loop can corrupt staged offsets or raise RuntimeError if the map is mutated during iteration, and close() joins this thread from the consumer thread while it may be inside commit(), which deadlocks if commit needs the processor lock (join then times out after 5s and shutdown continues with a commit still in flight). Commits should be staged in poll()/close() on the consumer thread.

test_stats_reporting submits 10 items to a live pool and immediately asserts get_stats()['total_items'] > 0. Workers are already running and the test processor only appends to a list, so the queues can be empty before that assertion; it will flake under load. test_different_groups_distributed similarly asserts that 20 hashed keys hit all 3 queues, which is not guaranteed. test_preserves_order_within_group only checks that 5 results were processed, not that they were processed in offset order, so an ordering regression in the strategy would still pass. None of the tests revoke partitions or call close()/join() and then submit again, so they miss the shared-pool shutdown data loss.

The key format is unchanged and nothing deletes or converts existing keys. After deploy, any in-flight segment still stored as a SET makes those commands fail with WRONGTYPE, so process_spans errors and those traces are not buffered until the key expires (redis_ttl defaults to 3600s). A rollback is equally broken: once a new process ZADDs a key, the old SADD/SSCAN code also gets WRONGTYPE. Mixed-version deploys cannot drain the buffer.

ZUNIONSTORE default SUM corrupts end-timestamp scores

Merging segment keys now uses ZUNIONSTORE with the default AGGREGATE SUM (both the span_key merge at this line and the parent_key merge just below). Members are span payloads and scores are end_timestamp_precise, used later by ZPOPMIN to decide which spans to drop. Redis sums scores when the same payload is in both keys. That overlap happens on Kafka redelivery: the span is ZADDed onto the grouped parent key in process_spans and is still present in the previous segment key that this script unions in. The summed score is no longer an end timestamp, so eviction keeps the redelivered span and drops a different span whose real timestamp is older. SUNIONSTORE used to dedupe without changing identity. The union needs AGGREGATE MIN or MAX so the score stays a timestamp.

Once a segment sorted set exceeds 1000 members, the script ZPOPMINs the lowest end_timestamp scores down to 1000. A root that ended before its children, or any span that loses the score tie-break, is deleted and never flushed, while the segment still looks complete downstream and may still use the shorter root timeout. The flush-time guard in _load_segment_data that skipped segments over max_segment_spans (1001) and emitted spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded was removed, and the 1000 cap is hardcoded in Lua rather than passed from SpansBuffer.max_segment_spans. Oversized segments that miss this script (WRONGTYPE, script error, crash between the earlier ZADD and EVALSHA) are now flushed in full with no metric. Drops are silent.

The parent-redirect walk that finds the segment key used to run up to 10000 hops, with a comment that a chain past that limit would not be joined correctly. It is now 1000, and the comment is gone. Each span adds a redirect entry. A parent chain longer than 1000 stops early, hsets the new span to an intermediate id, and merges into the wrong set. Those spans are flushed as a separate or truncated segment instead of the real trace segment, with no error.

Existing buffer tests only insert a handful of spans, all with the same end_timestamp_precise, and still only assert the full segment is flushed. The module glossary and the insert steps still say span-buf:s:* keys are sets and that payloads are added to a set. They are sorted sets scored by end_timestamp_precise, trimmed with ZPOPMIN. Operators debugging Redis or a flush incident will run SET commands (SMEMBERS/SCARD) and get WRONGTYPE, and the docstring no longer mentions that spans above 1000 are discarded on insert.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes are cancelled with the request

Create, Update, Delete, and DeleteCollection start the legacy write in a goroutine whose context is derived from the incoming request context via context.WithTimeoutCause (Create line 51, Update line 135, Delete line 110, DeleteCollection line 163). When the handler returns, the apiserver cancels that request context, which cancels the child immediately. The 10s timeout never extends past the parent, so the legacy "safety" write is aborted (or races the cancel) instead of running to completion. Mode 3 will report success for unified storage while the legacy copy is systematically dropped, and a later rollback to legacy will be missing creates, updates, and deletes.

Async legacy Create races on the caller's object

After Storage.Create returns, the handler encodes the returned object while a goroutine calls Legacy.Create on the same obj pointer (line 55) with no deep copy. Storage and legacy implementations mutate metadata in place (resourceVersion, UID, timestamps). That is a data race with response serialization and can tear or overwrite the object returned to the client. Previously the legacy create finished before Create returned, so this race did not exist. Copy the object (and do not share it with the caller) before the goroutine.

Legacy Update reapplies objInfo instead of the stored result

Update now passes the original objInfo into asynchronous Legacy.Update (line 139). The previous implementation snapshotted the object already written to unified storage and passed an updateWrapper so legacy stored that same object. UpdatedObjectInfo is not guaranteed to be reusable or to return an independent object: a second UpdatedObject call can conflict because the request resourceVersion is the unified-storage version, not the legacy one, can apply a patch to a different base and diverge, or can return the same pointer the API response is still encoding while legacy mutates it. Legacy will not reliably receive the write that unified storage just acknowledged.

Storage failures and legacy writes recorded on the wrong metric

On Storage.Create failure the code calls recordLegacyDuration (line 45) with the storage start time, and Update does the same at line 129. Those paths never called legacy, so legacy failure rate is inflated and the unified-storage failure is invisible to the storage metric. DeleteCollection's async legacy path does the opposite: line 166 calls recordStorageDuration for the legacy DeleteCollection result, so legacy errors are counted as storage errors and legacy latency is not recorded. Alerts and dashboards for mode 3 will point at the wrong store.

Legacy write failures are no longer logged

The async legacy Create (line 56), Update (line 140), Delete (line 113), and DeleteCollection (line 165) ignore the error except for a duration metric. The previous synchronous implementation logged these failures. Combined with the mis-labeled metrics, a legacy timeout, conflict, or outage leaves the two stores diverged with no log line an operator can alert on. The request still returns success, which is intended, but the safety write's failure must be logged.

Destroy does not wait for in-flight legacy writes

Each successful write spawns an unbounded goroutine that may block on legacy storage for up to 10s, and nothing tracks those goroutines. Destroy (line 172) immediately calls Legacy.Destroy() and Storage.Destroy(). On shutdown or storage teardown, in-flight legacy creates/updates/deletes run against a closed store (panic or error) or are dropped when the process exits, so the safety copy is lost exactly when it is needed for rollback.

Tests never wait for or assert the async legacy write

Mode 3 unit tests return as soon as the synchronous storage call finishes (Create at line 65, and the same pattern in Update, Delete, and DeleteCollection). They never wait for the goroutine, never AssertExpectations, and would still pass if the legacy write were removed. The success-path mocks are also invoked from a goroutine after the test can return, which races testify's mock. The new playlist integration cases (pkg/tests/apis/playlist/playlist_test.go line 132 and the unified-storage mode 3 case) call doPlaylistTests, which immediately compares the legacy HTTP API (line 529 and getFromBothAPIs) with k8s results. That assumed synchronous dual-write; under mode 3 it will flake or fail when the legacy copy has not landed yet.

On the shard-splitting path template application therefore runs twice per target (once up front, then once per shard group inside runSplitQuery). applyTemplateVariables is not idempotent: its contract appends ad-hoc filters to the LogQL expression, so the second call inserts the same matchers again, for example {app="foo", env="prod", __stream_shard__=~"1|2", env="prod"}. A variable value that itself contains $ or ${...} is expanded again on the second pass and can be corrupted. The updated shard test expects applyTemplateVariables to be called 5 times for a single target (1 initial call plus 1 per shard group), which locks in the double application. The only interpolation this PR adds is applyTemplateVariables, which leaves $__auto in the expression. It is still resolved later by the Loki backend (the same step path calculateStep says it replicates from pkg/tsdb/loki/step.go) or by runQuery, using each sub-request's split time range. Chunks therefore still get a step derived from the chunk instead of the original range, which is the failure mode early interpolation is supposed to prevent. The unit test cannot catch that because the stub removes $__auto before runQuery is observed. false_positives.candidate:

The new limit is enforced only inside TagDevice, and TagDevice returns nil immediately when X-Grafana-Device-Id is missing. Authenticate then still returns an anonymous identity with the configured org role. The header is client-supplied, so any caller can keep using anonymous auth after device_limit is exhausted by simply not sending it (or by rotating IDs until the cache bypass above applies). The cap does not actually bound anonymous access.

Anonymous auth now waits on device tagging even when the limit is off

Tagging used to run in a background goroutine with a detached 2-minute timeout and a panic recover, so it could not stall authentication. It is now a synchronous TagDevice call on the request context for every anonymous login, including the default device_limit of 0 (unlimited), which still does a database upsert on each cache miss. A slow or stuck database delays or ties up all anonymous requests until the DB call returns or the request is cancelled; a panic in tagging is no longer isolated from the request.

ProvideAnonymousDeviceService now takes db.DB instead of anonstore.AnonStore, and ProvideAnonDBStore gained a deviceLimit parameter. Grafana constructs these via the committed Wire graph (pkg/server/wire.go / wire_gen.go), which is not updated in this PR. wire_gen.go still calls the old signatures, so the server package will not compile until Wire is regenerated and the generated file is included.

It does not check that a device already inside the 30-day window can still be updated when count == device_limit, and nothing in impl_test or the auth client tests asserts that a second TagDevice/Authenticate after ErrDeviceLimitReached stays denied. Those are the paths that actually decide whether anonymous users are blocked, and both currently fail open.

The updateDevice function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when rowsAffected == 0, but zero affected rows means the device doesn't exist or falls outside the time window, not that a limit was reached.

Fallback locale files are never loaded from I18n.translate

Because the LRU cache stores that miss under key+locale+backend object id and nothing invalidates it when catalogs are loaded later, a lookup that runs before set_locale (boot, middleware, an earlier before_filter, or another thread) keeps serving the missing string for the life of the cache entry even on later web requests that do call ensure_loaded!.

Resolved strings now depend on SiteSetting.default_locale via FallbackLocaleList#[] and on which fallback catalogs were loaded. default_locale is a runtime admin setting and is not part of the key, and neither ensure_loaded! nor a default-locale change calls I18n.reload! (the only path that nils @cache). After an admin changes the site locale, arg-less I18n.t calls keep returning the previously cached fallback translation until that LRU slot is evicted or the process restarts, so users keep seeing the old language for missing keys.

Nothing asserts that a key missing from the user locale is served from the site locale and then :en, that pluralization still runs on the fallback locale, or that I18n.t falls back when locale is set outside ApplicationController (the mailer/job path). Host regex rejects hosts the old setting allowed

validates_format_of requires a dotted name ending in a letter TLD of 2 to 5 characters. The removed embeddable_hosts setting was a free-form host list. This regex rejects IPv4/IPv6, localhost, and any gTLD longer than 5 letters (.museum, .coffee, .international, and similar). Admins cannot save those hosts, and re-saving a migrated row fails validation, so those sites can no longer be allow-listed even though embedding used to work.

Any category_id is stored with no existence check

save_host assigns category_id from params and only substitutes uncategorized when the value is blank. There is no Category.exists? check, no model validation, and the migration adds no foreign key. A nonexistent id is saved. TopicEmbed.import then passes that id into PostCreator, so new embedded topics are created with a dangling category_id. Deleting a category later leaves the same dangling pointer because nothing cascades.

Hosts are not unique, so category lookup is arbitrary

Nothing validates uniqueness of host, and the new table has no unique index (case-insensitive or otherwise). The admin API and the migration can store duplicate hosts, including Example.com and example.com. record_for_host uses an unordered .first, so two rows for the same host with different categories make the imported topic category nondeterministic. Add a case-insensitive unique index and a matching validation.

New host API and migration have no behavioral tests

Admin::EmbeddableHostsController and Admin::EmbeddingController specs only assert the class inherits AdminController. Nothing exercises create, update, destroy, a missing id, a blank category_id, or an invalid host, and there is no migration spec for missing embed_category / protocol-prefixed hosts. Those are the paths that 500 or drop existing allow-list entries, so the current suite will stay green if they are broken.

true_positives.golden_comment: In .topic-meta-data h5 a, the original code had color: scale-color($primary, $lightness: 30%) but was changed to dark-light-choose(scale-color($primary, $lightness: 70%), scale-color($secondary, $lightness: 30%)). The lightness for the light theme changed from 30% to 70%, which is a dramatic inversion
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Embedded-post author color inverts the lightness conversion

The embedded-post author link was scale-color($primary, $lightness: 30%). This change replaces it with dark-light-choose(scale-color($primary, $lightness: 70%), scale-color($secondary, $lightness: 30%)). Every other conversion in this PR keeps the original lightness on $primary for light themes and uses the complement (100 minus that value) on $secondary for dark themes, which here would be 30% / 70%. The arguments are swapped, so light themes get a much lighter gray (weaker contrast on the light background) and dark themes get the value that was meant for light themes.

true_positives.golden_comment: In the next action, capping the next offset at user_count can produce an empty page (e.g., total equal to limit results in offset == total, showing 2/2 with no members). This can cause confusing UX on the last page.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
totalPages is one too high when the count divides the page size

totalPages uses Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1. When user_count is an exact multiple of limit (50 members, limit 50) that is 2, not 1. showingLast compares currentPage to that value, so the next guard does not fire on the real last page. next then sets offset to min(offset + limit, user_count), which equals user_count and loads an empty page. The same formula also leaves the admin on a blank last page after removing the final member of a page, because findMembers keeps the server's unclamped offset.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same empty-page bug: when the member count equals or is divisible by the page size, next can set offset to user_count and display a blank final page. It also explains how the totalPages calculation allows this navigation.

There is also no spec for the public GroupsController#members contract (limit, offset, and the {members, meta} shape) that this PR changes.

true_positives.golden_comment: The route provides the group's ID in params[:id], but the code attempts to read it from params[:group_id], causing the action to fail. This results in a broken feature when trying to access group memberships.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Add/remove members read group_id but the route only sets id

add_members and remove_member load the group with params.require(:group_id). The new routes are member routes (PUT/DELETE /admin/groups/:id/members), so Rails sets params[:id], not params[:group_id]. The client calls /admin/groups/<id>/members.json and only puts usernames or user_id in the body. require(:group_id) therefore raises ParameterMissing and every add or remove returns 400. destroy and update in this same controller correctly use params[:id]. The controller specs pass group_id straight into the action and never go through the router, so they stay green.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same route parameter mismatch: the routes provide params[:id], while the membership actions require params[:group_id], causing failures when adding or removing group members.

false_positives.candidate:
Public members page only loads 50 users and cannot page

setupController now calls model.findMembers(), which always requests /groups/:name/members.json with the Group model's default limit of 50 and offset 0. The public members template only iterates that one page and has no next/previous or load-more control; paging was added only on the admin group screen. Non-automatic groups previously returned every member, and automatic groups returned up to 200. A group with more than 50 members now hides the rest with no way to reach them.

Creating a group ignores alias_level

create only assigns name and visible. The admin form shows the alias-level combo before the group has an id, and Group#asJSON sends alias_level on POST /admin/groups. update applies params[:alias_level], but create never reads it, so a non-default level (for example everyone/99) is not saved. The client keeps the unsaved value until the group is reloaded, so the admin thinks the setting stuck.

Remove link is shown for automatic groups

The remove control is wrapped in {{#unless automatic}} inside the group-member itemView. With {{each member in members itemView="group-member"}}, Ember sets that view's context to the item view (so {{member}} works) or to the user, not to the admin group. automatic is not the group's automatic flag there; it is missing, so the unless is always true. Automatic groups still show a remove button. The server answers 422, and removeMember has no failure handler, so the admin confirms and the member stays with no error.

Add/remove membership failures are silent and the add field is not cleared

addMembers posts usernames and on success reloads the current offset, but it never clears usernames (the TODO on the line above). The selector still holds the same names, so another click resubmits them. Neither addMembers nor removeMember handles a rejected promise. A 400, 422, or 500 leaves the list unchanged and shows no alert, which looks the same as a successful add of a user who sorts onto a different page because the reload does not reset offset to 0.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The findMembers() call is now asynchronous and unhandled. The controller may not have member data immediately available, creating a race condition.
Expected to return a value at the end of function - code paths without explicit returns will return undefined

true_positives.golden_comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
match_count increment loses updates under concurrency

The hit counter is read-modify-write: match_count += 1 followed by save. Two overlapping signup attempts that match the same blocked row both read the same count and both write count+1, so one hit is dropped. Popular blocked addresses are exactly the rows that get concurrent attempts. Even after the stat update is moved out of the user transaction, this still needs an atomic update (for example update_all("match_count = match_count + 1") on that id) rather than loading the integer into Ruby.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the concurrent-update race caused by the statistics mutation highlighted in the golden comment. Although it focuses on lost counter updates rather than the misleading read-method name, it addresses the same underlying statistics-update concern.

true_positives.golden_comment: The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Exact email match lets blocked addresses sign up

should_block? loads BlockedEmail with a case-sensitive where(email: email) and never strips or downcases. Signup stores whatever was posted (User.new_from_params assigns params[:email] raw), while change_email in UsersController canonicalizes with Email.downcase(...).strip. A row for user@evil.com therefore does not match User@evil.com, user@evil.com with surrounding whitespace, or other case variants, so the new block is bypassed by changing case or padding the address. Uniqueness on blocked_emails.email is also case-sensitive, so both casings can be stored and .first can return either row. Normalize on write (set_defaults) and on lookup the same way change_email does, and compare the normalized value, or the blocklist does not actually block.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same case-sensitive email lookup in BlockedEmail.should_block? that lets blocked users bypass the block by changing email capitalization. Its additional whitespace and normalization concerns do not change the core match.

false_positives.candidate:
Block-hit stats are rolled back on the signup they record

BlockedEmail.should_block? increments match_count and last_match_at and calls record.save while it is invoked from EmailValidator during User validation. User#save runs validations inside the same database transaction, and a blocked address fails validation, so that transaction rolls back and undoes the BlockedEmail update. On a normal install (SiteSetting.call_discourse_hub? false) UsersController#create only calls save, so blocked signup attempts never persist match statistics — last_match_at stays nil and match_count stays 0, which is the signal the model spec says admins use to see whether a rule has ever matched. When call_discourse_hub? is true, create calls user.valid? (line 168) before save, so the first increment commits and the second is rolled back, and the counter moves by 1 instead of 2. The write has to happen outside the user transaction (separate connection, or after the user save/rollback), or the stats feature does not work for the block action.

Tests stub the block check and miss signup behavior

EmailValidator examples stub BlockedEmail.should_block?, so they never hit the database, never assert the user.email.blocked message, and never run User#save. BlockedEmail specs only call should_block? directly, which commits the counter outside a user transaction, so they stay green while a real blocked signup rolls the stats back and while a case or whitespace variant is allowed through. There is also no coverage that the domain whitelist/blacklist logic moved out of User still rejects addresses. A User create/save example with a real BlockedEmail row (including a different-case address) is needed or these failures ship untested.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.

true_positives.golden_comment: -webkit-box-ordinal-group and -moz-box-ordinal-group require values starting from 1, not 0. If $val is 0, this will cause incorrect rendering in older browsers, leading to layout issues.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
order() mixin writes a 0-based value into 1-based ordinal-group

-webkit-box-ordinal-group and -moz-box-ordinal-group are 1-based (initial value 1) and reject 0, while the modern order property and -ms-flex-order are 0-based (initial value 0). The new mixin assigns $val to all of them. Autoprefixer-style output must use $val + 1 for the box-ordinal-group properties. order(2) and order(3) in this PR still sort after default items by accident (old default 1 is less than 2 and 3; modern default 0 is less than 2 and 3), but order(1) will not move an item after default siblings in old WebKit/Firefox, and order(0) or a negative order is invalid or ignored in the 2009 syntax. This is the shared helper the header now depends on, so the off-by-one should be fixed before it is reused.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same off-by-one issue: the legacy box-ordinal-group properties require values starting at 1, but the mixin assigns $val directly, making 0 invalid and causing incorrect layout in older browsers.

false_positives.candidate:
Small-action button float is ignored in the new flex row

.small-action is now a flex container (the new flexbox() mixin sets display:flex), but its action button is still float:right. Float and clear do not apply to flex items, so the button is laid out in source order immediately after .small-action-desc instead of at the right edge. Short rows such as closed, pinned, or autoclosed actions therefore show the delete/expand control beside the text rather than pinned to the far side, in every browser that honors the new display. The same change also drops the description's 4em left padding that previously cleared the floated avatar, so non-flex fallbacks will overlap the icon and the text. Put margin-left:auto on the button (and drop the float) to restore the right alignment; .topic-avatar's float:left is likewise ignored and should not be relied on.

Panel right-align does not work in the prefixed flex fallback

.panel used to be float:right (and .title float:left). Those floats were removed and replaced with margin-left:auto plus order, while flexbox() emits display:-webkit-box and display:-moz-box before the modern values. The 2009 box model does not treat auto margins as flexible space, so browsers that only understand those prefixed values (Safari 6.1/7, iOS 7, older Android) keep the notifications, search, and login cluster immediately after the logo instead of on the right edge of the header. The prefixes this PR adds are exactly the browsers that will miss the new alignment, and there is no float fallback left.

Header category bullet loses its 5px alignment offset

.extra-info-wrapper .badge-wrapper.bullet previously had margin-top:5px so the category bullet lined up with the docked topic title text. That rule was deleted. The badges change only routes the existing display:inline-flex and align-items:baseline through mixins, so it does not add a replacement offset, and the new line-height:1.5 on the wrapper does not shift the bullet relative to the label. Category bullets in the scrolling header extra-info will sit about 5px too high against the category name.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Mixing float: left with flexbox causes layout issues. Further this PR removes the float-based right alignment for .d-header .panel, which may cause the login panel in the non-Ember/noscript header (where .panel is nested inside .row and not a flex item) to stack under the title instead of remaining right-aligned.
-ms-align-items never existed in any version of IE/Edge; the correct legacy property is -ms-flex-align.

true_positives.golden_comment: The include_website_name method is missing the required ? suffix. Rails serializers expect include_ methods to end with ? for conditional attribute inclusion, a convention followed by other methods in this serializer. Without it, the website_name attribute may not be conditionally included as intended. Additionally, the '.' << website_host string concatenation should be replaced with '.' + website_host or '.#{website_host}' to avoid mutating string literals, which can lead to issues.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
include_website_name is never invoked

ActiveModel::Serializer only calls inclusion hooks named include_<attr>?, and every other hook in this file follows that form. include_website_name has no question mark, so it is dead code and website_name is always emitted, including null when the user has no website. Rename it to include_website_name?. As written it only checks website.present?, so renaming alone does not apply the TL0 restriction.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same primary issue: include_website_name lacks the required ? suffix, preventing the serializer from invoking it as a conditional inclusion hook. It does not mention the golden comment's additional string-literal mutation concern, but directly matches the main bug.

false_positives.candidate:
website_name bypasses TL0 anonymous field hiding

website_name is derived from website but is not covered by untrusted_attributes, and website_name never calls scope.restrict_user_fields?. For a TL0 user seen anonymously, include_website? is forced false so website is omitted, yet website_name is still serialized. The profile template renders the globe label from model.website_name, so anonymous viewers get the host and, when the heuristic matches, the path of a field this serializer intentionally hides to limit new-user spam. Add website_name to untrusted_attributes (or apply the same guard in include_website_name?) and extend the existing TL0 anonymous serializer example; the new specs only cover a normal user.

Same-domain check misclassifies hosts

The non-equal branches do not test whether the website is actually on the instance domain, so the profile label either appends a path for an unrelated site or drops it for the same site. The elsif treats hosts as the same domain when they have the same label count greater than 2 and share every label except the first, which matches community.co.uk with paypal.co.uk and foo.github.io with bar.github.io and then appends the path. The else branch uses discourse_host.ends_with?("." + website_host), which is true for any suffix, so a website host of com or co.uk matches every forum on that suffix. The common www case fails the other way: a forum on example.com and a website of http://www.example.com/docs has a different label count and example.com does not end with .www.example.com, so only the host is shown. Comparison is also case-sensitive against Discourse.current_hostname while URI#host is lowercased, so a mixed-case hostname misses the exact-match branch. The new specs only cover example.com vs discourse.org, an exact match, and a parent forums.example.com, so they do not catch this. Compare normalized registrable domains (and an optional www label) instead of stripping one label or using a raw suffix check.

true_positives.golden_comment: The PollFeed job calls open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) without validating the URL, allowing an attacker who controls the feed_polling_url site setting to make the server fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
import_remote uses Kernel#open on attacker-influenced URLs

import_remote calls `open(url).read` without `require 'open-uri'` (unlike PollFeed) and without an http(s)-only client, timeout, or redirect check. If open-uri has not been loaded, Kernel#open treats the URL as a local filename and the fetch fails (Disqus import and embed retrieval blow up). Once open-uri is loaded, it follows redirects to any host with no read timeout, and non-URI strings fall through to file open or pipe execution. Embed URLs are supplied by visitors (TopicRetriever only compares URI#host to embeddable_host, not the scheme, and does not re-check redirects), and PollFeed does the same `open` on feed_polling_url. That is SSRF against internal HTTP services, worker hangs, and, for a non-http setting or feed link, local file read.
true_positives.reasoning: Although the candidate focuses on import_remote and adds other concerns, it explicitly identifies PollFeed opening feed_polling_url without URL restrictions, enabling SSRF against internal services. This matches the golden issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: The current origin validation using indexOf is insufficient and can be bypassed. An attacker could use a malicious domain like evil-discourseUrl.com to pass this check.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
postMessage origin check is a substring match

The resize listener accepts a message when `discourseUrl.indexOf(e.origin) !== -1`. That is the wrong direction and is not an origin equality check. Any origin that is a prefix/substring of the configured forum URL passes, for example origin `http://forum.example.co` against discourseUrl `http://forum.example.com`, or any shorter prefix. A page that can postMessage to the host page (opener or another frame) can then set the embed iframe height. Compare the message origin to the parsed origin of discourseUrl (scheme, host, and port) instead.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify insufficient postMessage origin validation using indexOf: substring matching can allow an attacker-controlled origin to pass instead of requiring exact origin equality. The differing bypass examples do not change the underlying issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: The TopicEmbed.import method is susceptible to a NoMethodError if the contents parameter is nil when attempting to append a string, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Imported HTML is stored and rendered unsanitized

TopicEmbed.import appends the source URL into the post body with raw string interpolation (`<a href='#{url}'>`) and saves the whole document via PostCreator with cook_method raw_html and skip_validations. Post#cook then returns raw unchanged whenever cook_method is raw_html, so the normal PrettyText/Sanitize pipeline never runs. Cooked HTML is rendered with `raw` in the embed view and on the topic page. RSS items (PollFeed also runs CGI.unescapeHTML on the body, turning escaped markup back into tags) and any page fetched for an embed can therefore plant script, event handlers, or a quote-breaking URL such as http://host/?q='><script>… and get stored XSS in the forum origin. The existing sanitize gem is not used, and the topic embed spec locks in cooked == raw.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same XSS issue caused by unescaped URL interpolation in TopicEmbed.import, including a quote-breaking URL example. It does not mention the nil-contents NoMethodError, but directly matches the golden comment's XSS concern.

true_positives.golden_comment: The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Embed template has invalid ERB (`end if`)

The header conditional is closed with `<%- end if %>`, which is not valid Ruby inside ERB. Rendering the success path (a topic id was found and best.html.erb is rendered) raises a SyntaxError/Template::Error, so the embed iframe 500s whenever a discussion already exists. It must be `<% end %>`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the invalid ERB closure `end if`, explain that it causes a render-time error, and recommend replacing it with `end`.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Feed poll crashes on typical RSS items

poll_feed always does `CGI.unescapeHTML(i.content.scrub)` and then TopicEmbed.import. SimpleRSS leaves `content` nil for ordinary RSS 2.0 items that only have `description`/`summary`, so the first such item raises NoMethodError and the hourly job stops, importing nothing after it. String#scrub also does not exist on Ruby 2.0/1.9, which this app still references. There is no per-item rescue, and title/link can be missing the same way. Use a fallback (`content` or `description` or empty string), guard nil, and isolate item failures.

false_positives.candidate:
Embed controller specs assert the wrong control flow

The success example expects `TopicRetriever.new` and `retrieve` to run inside the request. EmbedController#best does not do that; it calls `Jobs.enqueue(:retrieve_topic, …)` and renders loading. That expectation fails. The other success example renders best.html.erb, which currently cannot compile (`end if`), so the after-hook `response.should be_success` fails as well. The specs will not catch the enqueue/host/throttle behavior that actually shipped.

When feed polling is enabled, perform_retrieve synchronously runs `Jobs::PollFeed.new.execute({})` (download and import every feed item) inside the per-URL retrieve job, then only calls fetch_http if that returns normally and the URL is still missing. Any exception from the feed (network error, nil content, bad item) aborts the job before the single-page HTTP fetch, so the embed stays on the loading page forever. A single comment embed also triggers a full import with no timeout isolation.

Unauthenticated embed GETs enqueue unbounded jobs

best only checks that the Referer host equals embeddable_host, then enqueues retrieve_topic for whatever embed_url was passed. Referer is trivial to spoof, embed_url is not checked against embeddable_host or a rate limit in the request, and the Redis throttle lives inside the job and is per URL. An anonymous client can fill the Sidekiq queue with unique URLs; each job still does work (host parse, Redis, sometimes HTTP). Validate the embed URL host before enqueue and throttle enqueues.

embed_url is varchar(255) with a unique index

embed_url is a Rails string column (varchar 255) and is uniquely indexed. Article and tracking URLs routinely exceed 255 characters. Insert then raises on PostgreSQL, TopicEmbed.create! rolls the import back, and that URL can never be embedded. Store embed_url as text (and keep the unique index).

The importer used to create a local topic from the export (permalink stub, optional -c category) and then attach comments. The exception is not rescued inside the thread loop, so one dead link aborts the rest of the file (the ensure only restores the email blacklist and rate limiter). The category option and category_id lookup were removed, and TopicEmbed.import has no category argument, so surviving imports also land in the wrong category.

Post jobs are enqueued inside the outer import transaction

import wraps PostCreator.create in Topic.transaction. PostCreator commits its own nested transaction by joining that outer one, then enqueue_jobs (process_post, feature_topic_users) runs before Topic.transaction commits. If TopicEmbed.create! then fails (unique embed_url race, null id), the outer transaction rolls the post back but the jobs are already queued and run against a missing row. Even on success they can run before commit. Enqueue only after the outer transaction commits, and rescue RecordNotUnique so a raced import reuses the existing embed instead of erroring.

retrieved_recently? uses SETNX and then a separate EXPIRE of 60 seconds. If the process dies between those calls, the key remains with no TTL and that embed URL is never fetched again for non-staff users (they stay on the loading page). Use a single SET key 1 NX EX 60 so the lock cannot outlive the throttle window.

true_positives.golden_comment: The loop checking `tempfile.size` may never terminate correctly due to stale cached size, leading to potential infinite loops or incorrect file handling after modifications.

The open Tempfile still refers to the original inode, so after convert replaces the path, tempfile.size and whatever Upload.create_for reads from the handle can stay on the old bytes or sit past the new EOF. Any leftover expired row therefore makes connected calendars report cacheUpdatedAt and the dropdown offers "Delete cached data" even though availability lookups are already cache misses. Backfill stamps every existing cache as updated at migrate time

The new updatedAt column is added as NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW(), so every existing CalendarCache row gets the migration timestamp rather than when it was actually written. CalendarCache has no createdAt; the only freshness signal already stored is expiresAt (writes set it to about now + 30 days). After deploy, every Google credential with any historical cache row shows "Last updated" as the deploy time, including stale and expired caches, which defeats the status feature. deleteCacheHandler only runs calendarCache.deleteMany for the credential. It does not stop google channel subscriptions on SelectedCalendar, and GoogleCalendarService.fetchAvailabilityAndSetCache (called from the webhook path) writes CalendarCache again and then touches those selected calendars. The confirmation copy says the delete cannot be undone, but the next notification recreates the rows. Users clearing a bad cache will see it return with no explanation, and a reload can show a new timestamp as if the delete did not stick.

Cache status is loaded only via getCacheStatusByCredentialIds(connected calendar credential ids). The same repository documents that in-memory delegation credentials use negative ids that are not stored on CalendarCache, and reads for those users are keyed by userId plus the free/busy key so they can reuse a real credential's cache. Those org/delegation Google connections — the users the calendar-cache feature flag is aimed at — always get cacheUpdatedAt null, so the new menu never offers delete. deleteCacheHandler cannot fix that either: it requires a Credential row with id = credentialId and userId = the session user, which does not match a negative in-memory id or a cache row owned by another credential id.

dev:cron changed from ts-node cron-tester.ts to npx tsx cron-tester.ts. ts-node is a declared devDependency; tsx is not in this package.json, and the app pins Yarn 3.4.1, where npx is not the workspace runner and will try to fetch tsx outside the lockfile. yarn dev:cron fails offline or in CI, or runs an unpinned tsx. This change is unrelated to calendar cache and should stay on the declared runner or add tsx as a dependency and invoke it through Yarn.

deleteCache is a new authenticated mutation that deletes every CalendarCache row for a client-supplied credentialId after a userId check, and connectedCalendars now depends on getCacheStatusByCredentialIds. Nothing in the PR covers another user (or a negative delegation id) being rejected, a successful delete actually removing rows, or expired versus live rows being mapped to cacheUpdatedAt. This results in inaccurate cache status tracking, as the timestamp isn't updated when the cache is refreshed. To fix this, explicitly set the updatedAt field.

Throwing a generic Error for authentication failures results in a 500 response in tRPC. Instead, it should return a structured TRPCError with an appropriate code, such as FORBIDDEN, to accurately reflect the error type.
Date is formatted with hardcoded 'en-US' locale instead of using the user's locale from useLocale, which can lead to incorrect date representation for users in different locales.

true_positives.golden_comment: Incorrect end time calculation using slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime
true_positives.matched_candidate:

When no date override matches, availability is decided by workingHours.find: any same-day window whose range does not contain the slot makes the callback return true and the slot is rejected. A host with a lunch break (two windows on the same weekday) therefore loses every slot, including ones that sit fully inside the other window. The end minute is copied from slotStartTime rather than the slot end, so a slot that starts inside hours but runs past workingHour.endTime is treated as inside. Days with no working-hour entry never match, so they are treated as free; a fixed host who does not work that weekday is not excluded. For round-robin this filter is what is supposed to keep fixed hosts from being booked outside their own hours, and it does the opposite for split schedules.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly identifies that the end minute is copied from slotStartTime rather than slotEndTime, matching the golden issue despite also describing other working-hours bugs.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Multiple override ranges on one day reject every slot

The date-override filter uses Array.find and treats a true callback as "this slot is not bookable". Each range returns true when the slot merely falls outside that one range. On a day with two ranges (for example 09:00-12:00 and 14:00-17:00), a slot inside the first range is outside the second, so find succeeds and checkIfIsAvailable returns false. Every slot is outside at least one range, so a split date override blocks the entire day instead of opening those windows. The start===end all-day-block branch just above never runs either: it compares two dayjs instances with ===, which is always false, so a zero-length override is not handled as a full-day block.
true_positives.reasoning: Although the candidate primarily discusses multiple override ranges, it also explicitly identifies the golden issue: comparing two dayjs instances with === always returns false because they are distinct objects, preventing the start-equals-end branch from running.

false_positives.candidate:
In-override slots skip busy checks and can double-book

checkIfIsAvailable now returns true as soon as a date override exists for that calendar day and the slot is not strictly outside it. That return happens before the busy-interval scan, so calendar conflicts and existing Cal bookings are ignored for every fixed host (personal events, collective hosts, and round-robin fixed hosts all go through this path). A host who sets a date override and already has a meeting inside that window will still be offered those slots, and the booking can be confirmed on top of the conflict. Partial overlaps are treated as inside as well: a slot that starts before the override and ends during it is not rejected, so the meeting can begin outside the override hours.

Override timezone shift wraps at midnight and lands on the wrong day

Date-override start and end are shifted by inviteeUtcOffset - organizerUtcOffset and then reduced to hour and minute only. Those values are minutes within 0-1439, so a shift that crosses midnight is applied to the invitee day already selected from the unadjusted UTC timestamp. An evening override viewed from a timezone ahead shows up as early-morning slots on the previous day; a morning override viewed from a timezone behind can produce endTime < startTime. buildSlots drops ranges with start >= end, and the caller has already removed that user's normal working hours for the day, so the override disappears and the host has no slots. The new test only compares +5:30 and +6:00, a 30-minute gap that never crosses midnight, so it does not catch this. Attendees several hours from the organizer still see the override at the wrong time, which is the bug this change is meant to fix.

Override day match compares server-local date to UTC

Whether an override applies is decided by formatting dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset) (local mode, so the server timezone) as YYYY MM DD and comparing it to slotStartTime, which was forced to UTC. isBefore/isAfter later compare absolute instants, but they only run after this date check. On any host whose TZ is not UTC, an override near midnight is attached to the wrong day or skipped entirely, and the fixed host's override is not enforced. Slot generation then falls through to weekly hours.

The PR's stated fix is that a round-robin event must not offer slots when a fixed host's date override makes them unavailable, including across timezones. The only new assertion re-queries a single-user event in Asia/Dhaka and expects the same UTC instants as Asia/Kolkata. It never builds a ROUND_ROBIN event, never sets hosts[].isFixed, and never places a booking or calendar busy block inside an override. The double-book path, split override ranges, and fixed-host weekly hours can all regress without failing CI.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1 reads a possibly stale value and can lose increments under concurrency; consider an atomic increment via Prisma (increment: 1) to avoid race conditions (also applies to the similar update in the catch block).

Both failure paths write `retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1` from the value loaded at the start of the loop instead of an atomic increment. Two overlapping runs of this cron can both select the same unscheduled reminder, both call Twilio, and both store the same next count. Recipients get duplicate texts, and because the stored count never moves past that shared value the `retryCount > 1` delete may never fire, so the retry cap does not hold under overlap. Claim the row (conditional update of scheduled, or increment in the database) before calling Twilio.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same stale read-modify-write race in retryCount updates, including both failure paths, and notes that an atomic database increment avoids lost increments. Its additional discussion of duplicate sends does not change the underlying match.

true_positives.golden_comment: The deletion logic in scheduleSMSReminders.ts incorrectly deletes non-SMS workflow reminders (e.g., Email, WhatsApp) that have retryCount > 1. This occurs because the retryCount condition within the OR clause for deletion lacks a method: WorkflowMethods.SMS filter, causing it to apply to all reminder types instead of only SMS reminders, which is the intended scope of this function.

WorkflowReminder is shared by EMAIL, SMS, and WHATSAPP. Every cron run therefore permanently deletes any reminder of any method once retryCount is greater than 1, including a row that was already scheduled and still has a provider referenceId. The comment on line 28 still says this only removes past SMS reminders. Scope the predicate to unscheduled SMS (and filter the later findMany the same way); otherwise any non-SMS writer of this new column, or a scheduled SMS row that ever exceeds the cap, loses the reminder.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same missing SMS method filter in the retryCount > 1 deletion clause, which causes non-SMS workflow reminders such as Email and WhatsApp to be deleted. Its additional concerns do not change this core match.

false_positives.candidate:
A successful Twilio schedule is counted as a failure if saving the SID throws

twilio.scheduleSMS runs before the update that sets scheduled and referenceId. If Twilio accepts the message and that update throws, the new catch increments retryCount and leaves scheduled false and referenceId unset. The next cron loads the same reminder again and sends another SMS. After retryCount exceeds 1 the row is deleted, so the already accepted Twilio message can no longer be cancelled from a stored SID. Only a failed scheduleSMS call should advance retryCount; if persistence fails after Twilio accepts the message, cancel that message or retry the write without treating it as a failed send.

Missing number or empty body never counts toward the retry cap

retryCount is incremented only when Twilio returns a falsy result or throws, and only inside `if (message?.length > 0 && sendTo)`. If the attendee or step has no phone number, or the step has no reminder body and the template is not REMINDER, the loop skips the row and leaves scheduled false and retryCount at 0. That reminder is loaded again on every cron run until scheduledDate is in the past, which is the unbounded reschedule this PR is meant to stop. Treat a missing destination or empty message as a failed attempt, or delete the reminder immediately.

The new failure accounting and deleteMany predicate have no tests. A regression should assert that one failed SMS schedule leaves the reminder, that a second failure removes it on the next run, and that email or WhatsApp reminders and already scheduled SMS rows are not deleted by the retryCount clause. Without that, the unscoped OR delete and the off-path skips (no phone number, persistence failure after Twilio accepts) can ship unnoticed.

Team and org authorization SQL is built as `(<team predicate>) OR (<user predicate>)` (org reduce at lines 171-174, team reduce at lines 204-207). Those parentheses wrap each branch only, not the whole OR. `getBaseConditions` returns that fragment as-is when there is no event-type or member filter (line 75). AND binds tighter than OR in PostgreSQL, so the intended caller query `WHERE ${await service.getBaseConditions()} AND "startTime" >= ${from} AND "startTime" < ${to}` — the replacement for the removed `findMany`, which ANDed caller filters onto the entire authorization object — is parsed as `team_booking_predicate OR (personal_booking_predicate AND startTime filters)`. Insights over-count and can return bookings outside the window the caller applied. `getBaseConditions` only wraps the auth fragment when a service-level filter is also present (line 73). Wrap the full OR, and the final fragment returned to callers, in parentheses. The new tests expect this unparenthesized text and never run team/org SQL with an additional AND, so they do not catch it.

Composed conditions are built by nesting `Prisma.sql` values (`(${acc}) OR (${condition})` and the filter AND reduce). Prisma does not flatten nested `strings`/`values` until execution, so the object from `getAuthorizationConditions`/`getFilterConditions` is not deeply equal to a single flat `Prisma.sql` template with the same text. `expect(conditions).toEqual(Prisma.sql`...`)` therefore fails for the team-scope assertion (line 295), the org-scope assertion (line 332), and the combined-filter assertion (line 429) — the cases that use `ANY(...)` and OR. Flat cases (user scope, a single filter, `1=0`) can still pass. The only test that executes SQL is the user-scope `$queryRaw` query, which never hits `ANY` or the OR precedence bug. Compare flattened SQL text and bound values, or run the team/org fragments, instead of `toEqual` on raw `Prisma.Sql` objects.

This is because getAuthorizationConditions() always returns a non-null Prisma.Sql object, making authConditions always truthy, which means only the first two if/else if conditions are ever evaluated.

Fetching userIdsFromOrg only when teamsFromOrg.length > 0 can exclude org-level members for orgs without child teams; consider deriving from teamIds (which includes orgId) or removing the guard so org-only orgs still include member user bookings.

true_positives.golden_comment: The parseRefreshTokenResponse function incorrectly sets refresh_token to the hardcoded string 'refresh_token' when it's missing from the OAuth refresh token response. This invalidates the token, breaking subsequent token refreshes and causing authentication failures.

If the SendGrid call fails, the old email still sends and is not marked cancelled for the cron. Disabling an event type (around line 376) also dropped the awaited reminder deletes and only fire-and-forgets the new helpers.

The same loop also submits every due cancellation at once, so more than 100 in that hour recreates the pending-cancellation cap.

If they present different codes, the later write overwrites the earlier one, so one consumed code is restored and can be reused. An oversized or negative DER integer therefore becomes a different R or S instead of failing the conversion with IOException. Signature verification then runs against a value that is not the encoded integer, so malformed ECDSA input is mishandled rather than rejected. A decoder/encoder pair that ignores the real R and S and inverts each other would pass. Each algorithm needs a key on secp256r1, secp384r1, or secp521r1, and the DER produced from the concatenated form must verify with Signature.verify.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
BuildIndex no longer excludes concurrent builds of the same key

BuildIndex used to hold cacheMu for the whole build, which serialized bleve.New and cache publication. The lock is now taken only to publish b.cache[key] at the end, and nothing single-flights a key. getOrCreateIndex still does GetIndex then build with no per-key lock, so two searches or watch events for a missing namespace (indexes below InitMinCount, or any key created after startup) both pass the cache miss and call BuildIndex together. For file indexes both call bleve.New on the same directory and race the index files; for memory indexes both succeed. The slower build then overwrites b.cache[key], so the cached index can be the staler one, the other index is leaked and never closed, and callers that already received the losing index keep searching a copy that will not receive later watch updates.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate describes the same bug as the golden comment. The cacheMu lock was narrowed to cover only the final cache assignment, so concurrent BuildIndex calls for the same key can each build the index. The candidate also lists further consequences of this.

false_positives.candidate:
Parallel index init races on shared err and counter

init now actually builds many namespaces at once (errgroup plus the BuildIndex lock removal). Every worker does totalBatchesIndexed++ and err = s.build(...) on the same outer variables with no mutex or atomic. That is a data race: a failed build can return another worker's nil error, so group.Wait can succeed and the process starts with a missing index, or a successful worker can return another worker's error and fail startup. The namespaced_indexed span attribute is also racy and can be wrong. Each worker needs its own err variable, and the counter must be atomic or updated after Wait.

Startup index watch cursor skips writes made during the build

build returns the resource version of the list snapshot and documents that watchers must apply every event after that RV, but init discards both return values and only then calls WatchWriteEvents. That helper records the latest RV at call time and the SQL poller emits only history rows after that cursor. With a long startup build — the path this PR moved onto process start — and with namespaces built in parallel, an index finished early misses every write committed after its list and before the slowest build finishes. Those writes are never replayed, so the search index stays permanently stale. The watch must start from each build's returned RV (or from the RV captured before listing), not from a single cursor taken after all builds.

Search watch goroutine panics when the event channel closes

After index build, init starts a goroutine that does v := <-events and always calls handleEvent. watchctx is context.Background(), not the server's cancellable context, so server.Stop cannot stop it. SQL WatchWriteEvents closes the channel when the backend stops, and server.Stop calls lifecycle.Stop (the SQL backend implements LifecycleHooks) before cancelling the server context. A closed channel yields a nil event; handleEvent immediately reads evt.Type and panics, crashing the process. Because Init now always runs from NewResourceServer, every storage-server shutdown hits this. The loop must exit on !ok and must use the server context. The same unbounded read exists in initWatcher.

Failed constructor Init leaks watchers and never cancels its context

NewResourceServer calls s.Init and, on error, returns nil without s.cancel() or Stop. Init can already have run lifecycle.Init (opening the DB) and search.init, which starts the background WatchWriteEvents poller and the handleEvent goroutine, before a later step such as initWatcher fails. Callers only receive the error, so they have no server handle to Stop, the cancellable context is abandoned, and those goroutines run until process exit. On the search-watch path a later backend stop then panics, as described above. The error path needs to cancel and stop anything Init already started before returning.

Server watch now starts only after the full index build

Init used to call initWatcher before search.init. It now builds every search index first and only then starts the server broadcaster's WatchWriteEvents. That poller does not replay history; it starts at whatever the latest RV is when it is called. Writes committed during the startup index build (other HA replicas; WatchWriteEvents is documented to observe remote writes) are therefore never pushed to the broadcaster. A client that reconnects with Since set to the last RV it saw misses those events. Previously the broadcaster poller was already running for the whole index build, so those events were captured. Start the server watcher before the long index build, or replay from the RV observed before the build.

Postgres storage-server integration test is skipped instead of fixed

TestIntegrationWillRunInstrumentationServerWhenTargetHasNoHttpServer is the integration test that constructs and runs the storage-server target. This PR makes NewResourceServer block on full unified-storage Init (DB plus index build) during that construction, then skips the test whenever GRAFANA_TEST_DB=postgres, with a TODO that it fails in Drone and works locally. CI no longer exercises storage-server startup on postgres, so a postgres-specific failure in the new eager Init path — the behavior this PR adds — will not fail the build.
