false_positives.candidate:
Shared queue pool is destroyed on rebalance, then new messages are acked unprocessed

FixedQueuePool is created once on ResultsStrategyFactory and reused by every SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy from create_with_partitions. close() and join() call queue_pool.shutdown(), which shuts the queues down permanently. Arroyo closes the current strategy and builds a new one on every partition revocation/assignment, so after the first rebalance the new strategy submits into already-shut-down queues. queue.Queue.put raises queue.ShutDown, submit() swallows that exception, and the handler marks the offset completed. The commit thread then commits it. Those results are never processed and will not be redelivered, so uptime checks are silently dropped for the rest of the process lifetime. The shared OffsetTracker also keeps last_committed across assignments, so a later strategy can stall or skip commits for replayed offsets. The pool and tracker must be created per strategy instance and only shut down after that instance has finished its own work.

Submit and worker failures are committed as successfully processed

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit catches every exception (grouping_fn errors, BrokerValue assert, queue shutdown, put failures), logs, and calls add_offset plus complete_offset. OrderedQueueWorker.run also completes the offset in a finally block after logging processing exceptions. get_committable_offsets then treats those offsets as safe to commit, and ResultsStrategyFactory commits offset+1 to Kafka. The class docstring says offsets are committed only after successful processing and that no item is lost, but a failed message is acknowledged and never retried. In serial and batched-parallel modes an exception from batching/grouping escapes RunTask and is not committed, so this is a data-loss regression: a bad payload or a transient queue error permanently skips the check result.

Queues are unbounded and poll() never applies backpressure

Each worker queue is created with queue.Queue() (maxsize 0, unlimited), and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.poll only emits a gauge. submit() never blocks. The strategy docstring claims natural backpressure when queues fill, but nothing stops the consumer thread from pulling the entire partition into memory. One slow subscription blocks only its worker, while every other message on that partition keeps being queued, and the offset watermark cannot advance past the slow item. The process RSS grows with lag until the consumer is OOM-killed; on restart the uncommitted prefix is replayed. poll() or submit() needs a bounded queue and must block when any queue is full so Arroyo stops polling.

Graceful shutdown does not drain queues or wait for in-flight work

OrderedQueueWorker stops as soon as shutdown is True, before it drains the queue. FixedQueuePool.shutdown sets that flag and only then calls Queue.shutdown(immediate=False), so the graceful drain never happens: after the current item, the worker exits and leaves the rest of the queue unprocessed and incomplete. close() also joins the commit thread (5s) before shutting workers down, so anything completed after that final commit iteration is never committed. join() ignores its timeout and calls close() again. Worker joins are 5s each and sequential, so a stuck handler (the case this mode is meant to isolate) blocks the consumer thread for about num_queues*5 seconds, then the daemon worker keeps running after join returns. Those threads can still apply uptime side effects after partitions were revoked and another owner started, duplicating incidents, while the abandoned queued messages are only redelivered if they were not already acked.

Offsets are committed from a background thread

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy starts a daemon commit thread that calls the Arroyo commit callback every second. That callback is invoked by every other strategy on the consumer thread, which owns the Kafka consumer and the processor's staged-offset map. librdkafka consumers are not thread-safe, and the processor iterates that map while committing. Concurrent commit() from _commit_loop can corrupt staged offsets or raise RuntimeError if the map is mutated during iteration, and close() joins this thread from the consumer thread while it may be inside commit(), which deadlocks if commit needs the processor lock (join then times out after 5s and shutdown continues with a commit still in flight). Commits should be staged in poll()/close() on the consumer thread.

Queue stats test races workers and order is not asserted

test_stats_reporting submits 10 items to a live pool and immediately asserts get_stats()['total_items'] > 0. Workers are already running and the test processor only appends to a list, so the queues can be empty before that assertion; it will flake under load. test_different_groups_distributed similarly asserts that 20 hashed keys hit all 3 queues, which is not guaranteed. test_preserves_order_within_group only checks that 5 results were processed, not that they were processed in offset order, so an ordering regression in the strategy would still pass. None of the tests revoke partitions or call close()/join() and then submit again, so they miss the shared-pool shutdown data loss.

false_positives.candidate:

Span buffer keys `span-buf:s:{project:trace}:span_id` were Redis SETs (SADD/SUNIONSTORE/SSCAN) and are now sorted sets (ZADD here, ZCARD/ZUNIONSTORE/ZPOPMIN in add-buffer.lua, ZSCAN in _load_segment_data). The key format is unchanged and nothing deletes or converts existing keys. After deploy, any in-flight segment still stored as a SET makes those commands fail with WRONGTYPE, so process_spans errors and those traces are not buffered until the key expires (redis_ttl defaults to 3600s). A rollback is equally broken: once a new process ZADDs a key, the old SADD/SSCAN code also gets WRONGTYPE. Mixed-version deploys cannot drain the buffer.

ZUNIONSTORE default SUM corrupts end-timestamp scores

Merging segment keys now uses ZUNIONSTORE with the default AGGREGATE SUM (both the span_key merge at this line and the parent_key merge just below). Members are span payloads and scores are end_timestamp_precise, used later by ZPOPMIN to decide which spans to drop. Redis sums scores when the same payload is in both keys. That overlap happens on Kafka redelivery: the span is ZADDed onto the grouped parent key in process_spans and is still present in the previous segment key that this script unions in. The summed score is no longer an end timestamp, so eviction keeps the redelivered span and drops a different span whose real timestamp is older. SUNIONSTORE used to dedupe without changing identity. The union needs AGGREGATE MIN or MAX so the score stays a timestamp.

Insert-time ZPOPMIN can drop the root span silently

Once a segment sorted set exceeds 1000 members, the script ZPOPMINs the lowest end_timestamp scores down to 1000. The root/segment span is not protected, and the has-root-span flag is set independently of whether that payload is still in the set. A root that ended before its children, or any span that loses the score tie-break, is deleted and never flushed, while the segment still looks complete downstream and may still use the shorter root timeout. The flush-time guard in _load_segment_data that skipped segments over max_segment_spans (1001) and emitted spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded was removed, and the 1000 cap is hardcoded in Lua rather than passed from SpansBuffer.max_segment_spans. Oversized segments that miss this script (WRONGTYPE, script error, crash between the earlier ZADD and EVALSHA) are now flushed in full with no metric. Drops are silent.

Redirect walk cap cut from 10000 to 1000

The parent-redirect walk that finds the segment key used to run up to 10000 hops, with a comment that a chain past that limit would not be joined correctly. It is now 1000, and the comment is gone. Each span adds a redirect entry. A parent chain longer than 1000 stops early, hsets the new span to an intermediate id, and merges into the wrong set. Those spans are flushed as a separate or truncated segment instead of the real trace segment, with no error.

No coverage for eviction, score merges, or the new paginator

Existing buffer tests only insert a handful of spans, all with the same end_timestamp_precise, and still only assert the full segment is flushed. Nothing covers a segment over 1000 spans, ZPOPMIN dropping or preserving the root, ZUNIONSTORE score behavior on redelivery, or WRONGTYPE against a leftover SET key. The audit-log OptimizedCursorPaginator path and negative-offset cursor handling also have no tests, so the datetime crash and bound-bypass path would ship green.

The module glossary and the insert steps still say span-buf:s:* keys are sets and that payloads are added to a set. They are sorted sets scored by end_timestamp_precise, trimmed with ZPOPMIN. Operators debugging Redis or a flush incident will run SET commands (SMEMBERS/SCARD) and get WRONGTYPE, and the docstring no longer mentions that spans above 1000 are discarded on insert.

true_positives.golden_comment: The upsampling eligibility check passes the outer dataset instead of the actual dataset used by scoped_dataset. Those internal queries are therefore classified from the wrong inputs. The candidate also raises extra points about the query string, but the core issue is the same.

false_positives.candidate:
Error-query check is a substring match and false-positives on exclusions

`_is_error_focused_query` lowercases `request.GET['query']` and returns true if it contains the substring `event.type:error`. That matches queries that are not error-focused, including the common discover filters `!event.type:error` and `NOT event.type:error`, as well as `event.type:error OR event.type:transaction`. For an allowlisted project on the discover dataset, those queries rewrite `count()` to `sum(sample_weight)`. Transaction rows often have no error sample weight (or a different transaction sampling weight), so the events-stats request either 500s in Snuba or returns wildly inflated transaction counts. The same check misses real error queries such as `event.type:[error]`. Nothing in the new tests covers a negated or list-form `event.type` filter.

`upsampled_count` is `toInt64(sum(sample_weight))` with no null fallback, and the column rewrite assumes every event in an allowlisted project has a meaningful sample_weight. Nothing in this PR sets that column. The only new writer is the test helper `_set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling`, which stores `sample_rate` equal to `contexts.error_sampling.client_sample_rate` (0.1 in the snuba test) and never sets `sample_weight` to `1/rate`. Top-N selection therefore ranks groups by stored rows, not by `sum(sample_weight)`. With uneven client sample rates that ranking is wrong: a group with 100 real errors at 1% (1 stored row, weight 100) loses to a group with 10 unsampled errors (10 stored rows). The plotted series for the chosen groups is then upsampled, so the chart both picks the wrong groups and does not match the totals used to pick them. `equations` are also left as raw `count()`, so equation widgets diverge from the rewritten count axis.

This PR adds a gitlink `sentry-repo` pointing at commit a5d290951def84afdcc4c88d2f1f20023fc36e2a (the PR base) and does not update `.gitmodules` or any other file. That is not part of error upsampling. Merging it records a broken submodule: clones and CI checkouts have no URL for that gitlink, so the tree is dirty or the path fails to populate.

`_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` returns true for the `sentry.snuba.errors` dataset with no query check, and the events-stats endpoint then asks that dataset to execute `upsampled_count() as count`. The new tests never pass `dataset=errors` (they use the default dataset and one discover transaction query), so this path is untested.

`ErrorUpsamplingTest.setUp` does not call `super().setUp()`. Sentry's TestCase setUp is what creates `self.user`, `self.team`, and the rest of the factory state that `self.create_project` uses (`teams=[self.team]` when teams are omitted). This setUp will raise AttributeError before any assertion, so the new unit tests do not actually cover allowlist checks, column rewrite, or the event.type filter.

`test_error_upsampling_with_transaction_events` calls `store_event` for a transaction and immediately queries events-stats, asserting the first bucket `count == 1`. setUp in the same class waits with `wait_for_event_count` after its error inserts, which is required because Snuba ingestion is not synchronous. true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup success path logs full ID lists at error level

CleanAnnotations and CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags call r.log.Error on every batch, including when the fetch returns no rows and err is nil (lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576, and 579). Each call dumps the entire ID slice and the SQL condition. These run before the empty-batch stop, so every cleanup cycle emits error logs even when nothing is deleted, and a large backlog emits two error lines per batch with tens of thousands of IDs. That floods logs, looks like a failing job to anything alerting on error level, and can stall the cleaner on log serialization. These look like leftover diagnostics and should be removed, or reduced to debug without the ID list.
true_positives.reasoning: Both point out that debugging info is logged at Error level, which pollutes the error logs, and both suggest moving it to debug level or removing it. The candidate covers the same issue in more detail.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cleanup job ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which can lead to increased database load and contention due to more frequent execution of cleanup tasks. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with performance expectations.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Global cleanup interval accidentally cut from 10 minutes to 1

Run now uses time.NewTicker(time.Minute * 1) instead of 10 minutes. This is unrelated to the annotation deadlock fix and is not described in the PR. It schedules every cleanup job (snapshots, dashboard versions, images, annotations, invites, short URLs, query history) ten times as often. clean() is synchronous with a 9-minute timeout chosen for the old 10-minute cadence; if a pass takes longer than a minute the ticker's buffered tick starts the next pass immediately, so a busy instance can run cleanup continuously and multiply DB load. Restore the 10-minute interval unless a faster schedule is an intentional, documented change.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments flag the same change: the cleanup ticker interval cut from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which increases DB load. The candidate adds more detail but describes the same issue.

false_positives.candidate:
SQLite ID list is built with quadratic string concatenation

When the DB is SQLite and AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize exceeds 999, deleteByIDs inlines every ID with values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v) in a loop. Each step copies the whole string, so a batch of N IDs copies O(N^2) bytes. The new test uses batch size 32767, which is on this path and copies on the order of gigabytes of temporary strings, adding multi-second latency and GC pressure exactly when the batch is large. Build the IN list with strings.Builder (or chunks) instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: The context is being created with d.Log instead of the log variable that was initialized with additional context values (name, kind, method). This means those values won't be propagated to the logging context.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Delete puts the unscoped logger into the context

Delete builds log with name, kind, and method, then calls klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log) instead of klog.NewContext(ctx, log). Storage.Delete and the async Legacy.Delete therefore do not see those fields, unlike Create, Update, and DeleteCollection, which install the enriched logger. Delete failures will be missing the object identity in contextual logs.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug: the context is created with d.Log instead of the enriched log variable, so the name, kind, and method fields are not propagated.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Successful Delete uses object name as the metric kind label

The success path of Delete calls recordStorageDuration with name (the object name) as the kind argument (line 106). Every other call, including the error path two lines above, passes options.Kind. Object names are unbounded, so each deleted object creates a new Prometheus series on that label and the process (and any scraper) will grow memory without bound under normal delete traffic.
true_positives.reasoning: Both point out that the Delete success path passes the object name instead of options.Kind to the metrics recording. This is inconsistent with the other calls. The candidate also notes the cardinality impact, but the underlying issue is the same.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes are cancelled with the request

Create, Update, Delete, and DeleteCollection start the legacy write in a goroutine whose context is derived from the incoming request context via context.WithTimeoutCause (Create line 51, Update line 135, Delete line 110, DeleteCollection line 163). When the handler returns, the apiserver cancels that request context, which cancels the child immediately. The 10s timeout never extends past the parent, so the legacy "safety" write is aborted (or races the cancel) instead of running to completion. Mode 3 will report success for unified storage while the legacy copy is systematically dropped, and a later rollback to legacy will be missing creates, updates, and deletes.

Async legacy Create races on the caller's object

After Storage.Create returns, the handler encodes the returned object while a goroutine calls Legacy.Create on the same obj pointer (line 55) with no deep copy. Storage and legacy implementations mutate metadata in place (resourceVersion, UID, timestamps). That is a data race with response serialization and can tear or overwrite the object returned to the client. Previously the legacy create finished before Create returned, so this race did not exist. Copy the object (and do not share it with the caller) before the goroutine.

Legacy Update reapplies objInfo instead of the stored result

Update now passes the original objInfo into asynchronous Legacy.Update (line 139). The previous implementation snapshotted the object already written to unified storage and passed an updateWrapper so legacy stored that same object. UpdatedObjectInfo is not guaranteed to be reusable or to return an independent object: a second UpdatedObject call can conflict because the request resourceVersion is the unified-storage version, not the legacy one, can apply a patch to a different base and diverge, or can return the same pointer the API response is still encoding while legacy mutates it. Legacy will not reliably receive the write that unified storage just acknowledged.

Storage failures and legacy writes recorded on the wrong metric

On Storage.Create failure the code calls recordLegacyDuration (line 45) with the storage start time, and Update does the same at line 129. Those paths never called legacy, so legacy failure rate is inflated and the unified-storage failure is invisible to the storage metric. DeleteCollection's async legacy path does the opposite: line 166 calls recordStorageDuration for the legacy DeleteCollection result, so legacy errors are counted as storage errors and legacy latency is not recorded. Alerts and dashboards for mode 3 will point at the wrong store.

Legacy write failures are no longer logged

The async legacy Create (line 56), Update (line 140), Delete (line 113), and DeleteCollection (line 165) ignore the error except for a duration metric. The previous synchronous implementation logged these failures. Combined with the mis-labeled metrics, a legacy timeout, conflict, or outage leaves the two stores diverged with no log line an operator can alert on. The request still returns success, which is intended, but the safety write's failure must be logged.

Destroy does not wait for in-flight legacy writes

Each successful write spawns an unbounded goroutine that may block on legacy storage for up to 10s, and nothing tracks those goroutines. Destroy (line 172) immediately calls Legacy.Destroy() and Storage.Destroy(). On shutdown or storage teardown, in-flight legacy creates/updates/deletes run against a closed store (panic or error) or are dropped when the process exits, so the safety copy is lost exactly when it is needed for rollback.

Tests never wait for or assert the async legacy write

Mode 3 unit tests return as soon as the synchronous storage call finishes (Create at line 65, and the same pattern in Update, Delete, and DeleteCollection). They never wait for the goroutine, never AssertExpectations, and would still pass if the legacy write were removed. The success-path mocks are also invoked from a goroutine after the test can return, which races testify's mock. The new playlist integration cases (pkg/tests/apis/playlist/playlist_test.go line 132 and the unified-storage mode 3 case) call doPlaylistTests, which immediately compares the legacy HTTP API (line 529 and getFromBothAPIs) with k8s results. That assumed synchronous dual-write; under mode 3 it will flake or fail when the legacy copy has not landed yet.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In DualWriterMode3's DeleteCollection method, when a storage operation fails, recordStorageDuration is incorrectly called with recordLegacyDuration instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: The rendered GrafanaRuleListItem is missing the required key prop for React list items. This can cause rendering issues when the list order changes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Filtered Grafana rules are rendered without a list key

Replacing GrafanaRuleLoader dropped key={key} on the grafana branch of the filtered-rule list. Datasource and unknown rows still use key, and getRuleKey still builds a frontend id specifically to avoid duplicate keys. Without it, React reconciles Grafana rows by index as infinite scroll appends pages, so row state (open menus, silence drawer, action buttons) can attach to the wrong rule.
true_positives.reasoning: Both point out that the Grafana rule list item is rendered without the React key prop, which can cause reconciliation and rendering problems when the list changes.

true_positives.golden_comment: RuleActionsButtons is invoked with only promRule, but SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer inside RuleActionsButtons still depends on a Grafana Ruler rule being present, so for Grafana rules coming from list views the 'Silence notifications' menu entry (now driven by Grafana Prom abilities) will toggle showSilenceDrawer without ever rendering the drawer. This means clicking 'Silence notifications' for these rules has no visible effect, even when abilities indicate silencing is allowed.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Silence click does nothing in the ruler-less list

List items enable Silence from Grafana Prometheus abilities and AlertRuleMenu calls handleSilence, which only sets showSilenceDrawer. The drawer is still mounted only when rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule) is true, and SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer requires a RulerGrafanaRuleDTO. The new GrafanaRuleListItem passes promRule and no ruler rule, so the menu item appears and clicking it never opens a silence drawer.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug. Silence is enabled from Grafana Prom abilities, but the drawer only renders when a Grafana Ruler rule is present. Since only promRule is passed, clicking Silence toggles state without opening the drawer.

false_positives.candidate:
Pause and Delete stay hidden without a ruler rule

Alert list rows now pass only a Prometheus rule into AlertRuleMenu, and canPause/canDelete are computed from those prom abilities. The Pause item is still rendered only when rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule) is true (line 123), and Delete only when rulerRule is set (line 165), with onClick forwarding that ruler DTO. In the new list both are therefore never shown, even for users who have pause/delete permission. The rewritten GrafanaGroupLoader test grants AlertingRuleDelete and then expects exactly four menu items (silence, copy link, duplicate, export), so it locks this regression in instead of catching it.

Federated rule groups are no longer treated as immutable

useAllAlertRuleAbilities now delegates to useAllRulerRuleAbilities, which hardcodes isFederated to false (with a TODO) instead of calling isFederatedRuleGroup on the combined rule's group. Federated Mimir/GEM groups were previously immutable, so Update, Delete, Pause, Restore, and Delete permanently were not offered. Those actions are now reported as supported for every existing useAlertRuleAbility/useAllAlertRuleAbilities caller, not only the new list, and the UI can offer edits the previous guard blocked.

Recording rules lose export, pause, and restore

useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities sets isAlertingRule via prometheusRuleType.grafana.alertingRule and uses that flag for ModifyExport, Pause, Restore, and DeletePermanently. The ruler equivalent used rulerRuleType.grafana.rule, which is true for both Grafana alerting and recording rules (only Silence excluded recording rules). Grafana recording rules in the new list therefore cannot be exported or paused even when the user can edit them, and is_paused exists on those rules.

Rule view links no longer include returnTo

The removed GrafanaRuleListItem built the view href with createReturnTo() so the rule view could navigate back to the current list URL, including filters and search. The new item links to /alerting/grafana/${uid}/view with no returnTo query. Opening a rule from the list or filtered list drops that context, so Back/return no longer restores the list the user came from.

Shard splitting applies template variables and ad-hoc filters twice

runSplitQuery now maps every target through datasource.applyTemplateVariables(..., request.filters) before executing. runShardSplitQuery does the same before grouping, then builds each shard sub-request from those already interpolated targets and calls runSplitQuery. On the shard-splitting path template application therefore runs twice per target (once up front, then once per shard group inside runSplitQuery). applyTemplateVariables is not idempotent: its contract appends ad-hoc filters to the LogQL expression, so the second call inserts the same matchers again, for example {app="foo", env="prod", __stream_shard__=~"1|2", env="prod"}. Loki rejects duplicate label matchers, so dashboards with ad-hoc filters and shard splitting fail or change query meaning. A variable value that itself contains $ or ${...} is expanded again on the second pass and can be corrupted. The updated shard test expects applyTemplateVariables to be called 5 times for a single target (1 initial call plus 1 per shard group), which locks in the double application. Interpolate once for sharding decisions in runShardSplitQuery, and do not call applyTemplateVariables again in runSplitQuery on targets that are already interpolated (or strip filters from the sub-request so they cannot be reapplied).

$__auto is not resolved before splitting; the new test only stubs it

The new tests claim a query such as count_over_time({a="b"}[$__auto]) is interpolated to a concrete range before split execution, but they only pass because createLokiDatasource is given a templateSrv.replace stub that string-replaces $__auto. $__auto is a Loki query macro, not a Grafana template variable, and TemplateSrv.replace does not define it. The only interpolation this PR adds is applyTemplateVariables, which leaves $__auto in the expression. It is still resolved later by the Loki backend (the same step path calculateStep says it replicates from pkg/tsdb/loki/step.go) or by runQuery, using each sub-request's split time range. Chunks therefore still get a step derived from the chunk instead of the original range, which is the failure mode early interpolation is supposed to prevent. The unit test cannot catch that because the stub removes $__auto before runQuery is observed. Substitute $__auto from the original request range before partitioning, and do not fake that substitution in templateSrv.replace.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The applyTemplateVariables method is called with request.filters as the third parameter, but this parameter is not used in the corresponding test setup.

true_positives.golden_comment: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Device limit check and insert are not atomic

CreateOrUpdateDevice counts rows in one session, then inserts in another, with no transaction, row lock, or advisory lock. Concurrent anonymous requests (including across HA instances, which do not share the in-process cache) can all observe count < device_limit and all insert. Nothing in the schema caps the number of rows, so the overshoot sticks: active devices refresh updated_at about every 29 minutes and never fall out of the 30-day window used by the count. The limit can be permanently exceeded until those extra devices go idle for 30 days.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same race: the device count check and the insert are not atomic, so concurrent requests can exceed the limit. Both suggest a transaction or lock as the fix.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Device-limit denial is cached, so a retry is allowed

tagDeviceUI writes the device cache key (29-minute TTL) before CreateOrUpdateDevice returns. When the store returns ErrDeviceLimitReached, that error is now propagated and Anonymous.Authenticate denies the request, but the cache entry is left in place. The next TagDevice call for the same X-Grafana-Device-Id hits the cache, returns nil, and anonymous authentication succeeds even though the device was never stored. After one rejection per process, the configured limit is not enforced for the rest of the TTL; the new store test never calls TagDevice twice, so it does not catch this.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same bug: the cache is set before CreateOrUpdateDevice runs, and it is not cleared when ErrDeviceLimitReached is returned. Subsequent requests then bypass the device limit for the 29-minute TTL.

false_positives.candidate:
Omitting the device ID header skips the limit and still grants anonymous access

The new limit is enforced only inside TagDevice, and TagDevice returns nil immediately when X-Grafana-Device-Id is missing. Authenticate then still returns an anonymous identity with the configured org role. The header is client-supplied, so any caller can keep using anonymous auth after device_limit is exhausted by simply not sending it (or by rotating IDs until the cache bypass above applies). The cap does not actually bound anonymous access.

Anonymous auth now waits on device tagging even when the limit is off

Tagging used to run in a background goroutine with a detached 2-minute timeout and a panic recover, so it could not stall authentication. It is now a synchronous TagDevice call on the request context for every anonymous login, including the default device_limit of 0 (unlimited), which still does a database upsert on each cache miss. A slow or stuck database delays or ties up all anonymous requests until the DB call returns or the request is cancelled; a panic in tagging is no longer isolated from the request.

Provider signature change is not matched by Wire

ProvideAnonymousDeviceService now takes db.DB instead of anonstore.AnonStore, and ProvideAnonDBStore gained a deviceLimit parameter. Grafana constructs these via the committed Wire graph (pkg/server/wire.go / wire_gen.go), which is not updated in this PR. wire_gen.go still calls the old signatures, so the server package will not compile until Wire is regenerated and the generated file is included.

Limit test never covers auth, cache, or an existing device

TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit only asserts that a second new device ID is rejected by the store. It does not check that a device already inside the 30-day window can still be updated when count == device_limit, and nothing in impl_test or the auth client tests asserts that a second TagDevice/Authenticate after ErrDeviceLimitReached stays denied. Those are the paths that actually decide whether anonymous users are blocked, and both currently fail open.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Anonymous authentication now fails entirely if anonDeviceService.TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. Previously, device tagging was asynchronous and non-blocking. This change prevents anonymous users from authenticating when the device limit is reached.
The updateDevice function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when rowsAffected == 0, but zero affected rows means the device doesn't exist or falls outside the time window, not that a limit was reached.

Time window calculation inconsistency: Using device.UpdatedAt.UTC().Add(-anonymousDeviceExpiration) as the lower bound but device.UpdatedAt as the current time may not match the intended logic. Consider using time.Now().UTC() consistently.

false_positives.candidate:
Fallback locale files are never loaded from I18n.translate

translate in lib/freedom_patches/translate_accelerator.rb only calls load_locale for config.locale (line 68), then either returns translate_no_cache immediately when arguments are present (line 69) or caches that call (line 74). The new FallbackLocaleList#ensure_loaded! is invoked only from ApplicationController#set_locale. Mailers, Sidekiq jobs, rails runner, and any I18n.with_locale / I18n.locale= path never hit that filter, so the lazy loader never reads the site-default or :en YAML. I18n::Backend::Fallbacks then searches empty catalogs and I18n.t becomes "translation missing: ..." for keys that exist only in a fallback locale — the main server-side case this change is for. Because the LRU cache stores that miss under key+locale+backend object id and nothing invalidates it when catalogs are loaded later, a lookup that runs before set_locale (boot, middleware, an earlier before_filter, or another thread) keeps serving the missing string for the life of the cache entry even on later web requests that do call ensure_loaded!.

Translation cache key ignores the fallback chain

The accelerator cache key is only "#{key}#{config.locale}#{config.backend.object_id}" (lib/freedom_patches/translate_accelerator.rb:72). Resolved strings now depend on SiteSetting.default_locale via FallbackLocaleList#[] and on which fallback catalogs were loaded. default_locale is a runtime admin setting and is not part of the key, and neither ensure_loaded! nor a default-locale change calls I18n.reload! (the only path that nils @cache). After an admin changes the site locale, arg-less I18n.t calls keep returning the previously cached fallback translation until that LRU slot is evicted or the process restarts, so users keep seeing the old language for missing keys.

No coverage for fallback order or non-request loading

The new fallback chain in config/initializers/i18n.rb (locale, SiteSetting.default_locale, :en) and the lazy-load hook are untested. Nothing asserts that a key missing from the user locale is served from the site locale and then :en, that pluralization still runs on the fallback locale, or that I18n.t falls back when locale is set outside ApplicationController (the mailer/job path). Without that, the broken load/cache behavior above can ship unnoticed, and a later change to FallbackLocaleList or translate_accelerator can drop fallbacks in production only.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The @loaded_locales instance variable in translate_accelerator.rb is lazily initialized and accessed by multiple concurrent threads without synchronization.

Consider normalizing the input locale (e.g., to a symbol) when checking/loading here to avoid double-loading if the same locale is passed as a String vs Symbol (also applies to other locations in the PR).

true_positives.golden_comment: The traceID is no longer logged for plugin requests. During a refactoring, the tracing import and the logic to extract and add traceID from the context to log parameters were removed from the LoggerMiddleware. The newly introduced ContextualLoggerMiddleware does not add this information, resulting in missing traceID in plugin request logs and impacting debugging and request tracing capabilities.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Plugin request completion logs drop traceID

logRequest used to add traceID from tracing.TraceIDFromContext before emitting "Plugin Request Completed". That argument was removed, and ContextualLoggerMiddleware.instrumentContext does not put it back (it only sets endpoint, pluginId, dsName, dsUID, and uname). The plugin tracing middleware does not store traceID as a log contextual attribute either, so Logger.FromContext will not restore it. Completion logs, including alerting and other non-HTTP plugin calls, can no longer be correlated with the span started for the request.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same problem. The traceID extraction was removed from the plugin request logging, and the new ContextualLoggerMiddleware does not add it back, so plugin request logs no longer contain the traceID.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `TestLogger.FromContext` method returns a new `TestLogger` instance via `NewTestLogger()` instead of returning the receiver (f). This causes logs to be recorded on an un-referenced instance, leading to broken test assertions that expect logs to be recorded on the original logger.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TestLogger.FromContext discards the logger under test

FromContext ignores both the receiver and the context and returns NewTestLogger(), a fresh instance whose Logs are not the caller's. LoggerMiddleware now records every completion exclusively via logger.FromContext(ctx).Info, so a test that injects *TestLogger and asserts InfoLogs, ErrorLogs, or contextual fields will see no calls even when a request was logged. The fake should return itself, or a child that writes into the same Logs and exposes contextual attributes.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug. TestLogger.FromContext returns a new NewTestLogger() instead of the receiver, so logs land on an instance nobody references and test assertions on the original logger fail.

false_positives.candidate:
Moved request log fields have no test coverage

pluginId, endpoint, datasource identity, and user were removed from LoggerMiddleware's explicit log parameters and are now supposed to arrive via ContextualLoggerMiddleware plus Logger.FromContext. Nothing in this change tests that path: there is no test for the new middleware, and metrics_middleware_test.go only renames the metrics constructor. A mis-ordered middleware stack or a FromContext implementation that drops those attributes would ship without failing CI, which is how traceID was already dropped.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The ContextualLoggerMiddleware methods (QueryData, CallResource, CheckHealth, CollectMetrics) panic when a nil request is received. This occurs because they directly access req.PluginContext (via the instrumentContext function) without first checking if req is nil. This is a regression, as previous middleware layers gracefully handled nil requests.

true_positives.golden_comment: The EmbeddableHost model's before_validation callback calls self.host.sub! to strip http://, https://, and path segments, but if self.host is nil, this raises NoMethodError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Nil host crashes before validation

before_validation calls self.host.sub! without checking host. Create/update with a missing or null embeddable_host[host] (the controller assigns params directly) raises NoMethodError instead of a validation error, so the admin API returns 500 rather than 422. Guard nil/blank host and let validates_format_of fail the save.
true_positives.reasoning: Both point to the same bug: the before_validation callback calls self.host.sub! without a nil check, so a nil host raises NoMethodError.

true_positives.golden_comment: The update and destroy methods in Admin::EmbeddableHostsController do not validate the existence of the EmbeddableHost record retrieved by ID. If EmbeddableHost.where(id: params[:id]).first returns nil (i.e., the host does not exist), attempting to call methods on the nil object (e.g., save_host or destroy) will result in a NoMethodError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Update and destroy 500 when the host id is missing

update loads EmbeddableHost.where(id: params[:id]).first and passes it to save_host, which immediately writes host.host. destroy calls host.destroy on the same lookup. A stale or unknown id yields nil, so both actions raise NoMethodError instead of a 404. save_host also assumes params[:embeddable_host] is present; a body without that key raises before any error JSON is rendered.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate raises the same issue: update and destroy in EmbeddableHostsController look up the record with where(id:).first, get nil for an unknown id, and raise NoMethodError. The extra note about missing params does not change the match.

true_positives.golden_comment: record_for_host compares lower(host) = ? but does not normalize the parameter’s case, so mixed‑case referer hosts may fail to match even though comparison intends to be case‑insensitive.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Allow-list lookup drops ports and mishandles case

record_for_host sets host = uri.host and queries lower(host) = ? with that value unchanged. uri.host never includes the port, but the format validator and before_validation keep an optional :port on the stored host, so an entry saved as example.com:8080 never matches a referer of http://example.com:8080/... and host_allowed? stays false. The lower() call is also only applied to the column: a referer whose host has any capital letter (URI preserves case, so Example.com) compares lower(stored) = 'Example.com', which is never true, so the allow-list rejects it. Downcase the lookup value and compare host and port the same way they are stored.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly says lower() is applied only to the column and not to the parameter, so mixed-case referer hosts fail to match. That is the same issue as the golden comment. The candidate also raises a separate port problem, but that does not change the match.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because this migration inserts embeddable_hosts rows with raw SQL, any existing embeddable_hosts values that include http:// or /https:// or path segments won’t go through the EmbeddableHost model’s normalization, so the new host lookup (which compares only the bare host) may fail for migrated data. Consider ensuring that migrated hosts are normalized to the same format as newly created EmbeddableHost records so existing embedding configurations keep working.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Migrated hosts are inserted raw and unquoted

Existing embeddable_hosts values are inserted with execute "INSERT ... VALUES ('#{h}', ...)", bypassing EmbeddableHost's before_validation normalizer. The previous allow-list accepted http:// and https:// prefixes and paths (the old matcher used URI#host), but record_for_host compares only URI#host to the stored string. After upgrade, a saved value such as http://discourse.org or https://example.com/1234 will not match a referer host of discourse.org or example.com, so previously working embeds start returning invalid referer. A host containing a single quote also breaks the SQL or injects statements. Normalize (strip scheme, path, whitespace, and downcase) and insert with bound parameters. Windows newlines left by split("\n") have the same mismatch.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate raises the same concern as the golden comment. Raw SQL inserts bypass EmbeddableHost normalization, so stored hosts that keep a scheme or path will fail the bare-host lookup and break existing embeds. The candidate also mentions SQL injection and CRLF handling, but its core issue is the same.

true_positives.golden_comment: The contents of `category_fabricator.rb` and `embeddable_host_fabricator.rb` have been swapped, resulting in the loss of original category fabricators and potentially causing errors in fabricator usage.

The candidate clearly covers the XSS part, citing the raw `<a href='#{url}'>` interpolation and a quote-breaking URL example. It does not mention the nil case. Since it matches a core part of the golden comment, I count it as a match.

true_positives.golden_comment: The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Embed template has invalid ERB (`end if`)

The header conditional is closed with `<%- end if %>`, which is not valid Ruby inside ERB. Rendering the success path (a topic id was found and best.html.erb is rendered) raises a SyntaxError/Template::Error, so the embed iframe 500s whenever a discussion already exists. It must be `<% end %>`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments point to the same bug: the ERB block is closed with `end if`, which is invalid syntax and raises an error when the template renders. Both also give the same fix, closing it with a plain `end`.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Feed poll crashes on typical RSS items

poll_feed always does `CGI.unescapeHTML(i.content.scrub)` and then TopicEmbed.import. SimpleRSS leaves `content` nil for ordinary RSS 2.0 items that only have `description`/`summary`, so the first such item raises NoMethodError and the hourly job stops, importing nothing after it. String#scrub also does not exist on Ruby 2.0/1.9, which this app still references. There is no per-item rescue, and title/link can be missing the same way. Use a fallback (`content` or `description` or empty string), guard nil, and isolate item failures.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate flags the same bug: i.content is nil for RSS items that only have a description, so calling scrub on it crashes. It also suggests a fallback to description.

false_positives.candidate:
Embed controller specs assert the wrong control flow

The success example expects `TopicRetriever.new` and `retrieve` to run inside the request. EmbedController#best does not do that; it calls `Jobs.enqueue(:retrieve_topic, …)` and renders loading. That expectation fails. The other success example renders best.html.erb, which currently cannot compile (`end if`), so the after-hook `response.should be_success` fails as well. The specs will not catch the enqueue/host/throttle behavior that actually shipped.

Cache miss runs a full feed import and drops HTTP fallback

When feed polling is enabled, perform_retrieve synchronously runs `Jobs::PollFeed.new.execute({})` (download and import every feed item) inside the per-URL retrieve job, then only calls fetch_http if that returns normally and the URL is still missing. Any exception from the feed (network error, nil content, bad item) aborts the job before the single-page HTTP fetch, so the embed stays on the loading page forever. A single comment embed also triggers a full import with no timeout isolation.

Unauthenticated embed GETs enqueue unbounded jobs

best only checks that the Referer host equals embeddable_host, then enqueues retrieve_topic for whatever embed_url was passed. Referer is trivial to spoof, embed_url is not checked against embeddable_host or a rate limit in the request, and the Redis throttle lives inside the job and is per URL. An anonymous client can fill the Sidekiq queue with unique URLs; each job still does work (host parse, Redis, sometimes HTTP). Validate the embed URL host before enqueue and throttle enqueues.

embed_url is varchar(255) with a unique index

embed_url is a Rails string column (varchar 255) and is uniquely indexed. Article and tracking URLs routinely exceed 255 characters. Insert then raises on PostgreSQL, TopicEmbed.create! rolls the import back, and that URL can never be embedded. Store embed_url as text (and keep the unique index).

Disqus import now depends on a live remote fetch and drops category

The importer used to create a local topic from the export (permalink stub, optional -c category) and then attach comments. It now calls TopicEmbed.import_remote, which GETs t[:link] and returns nothing usable if the historical URL 404s, redirects oddly, or open() raises. The exception is not rescued inside the thread loop, so one dead link aborts the rest of the file (the ensure only restores the email blacklist and rate limiter). The category option and category_id lookup were removed, and TopicEmbed.import has no category argument, so surviving imports also land in the wrong category.

Post jobs are enqueued inside the outer import transaction

import wraps PostCreator.create in Topic.transaction. PostCreator commits its own nested transaction by joining that outer one, then enqueue_jobs (process_post, feature_topic_users) runs before Topic.transaction commits. If TopicEmbed.create! then fails (unique embed_url race, null id), the outer transaction rolls the post back but the jobs are already queued and run against a missing row. Even on success they can run before commit. Enqueue only after the outer transaction commits, and rescue RecordNotUnique so a raced import reuses the existing embed instead of erroring.

Throttle key can stick forever if expire is skipped

retrieved_recently? uses SETNX and then a separate EXPIRE of 60 seconds. If the process dies between those calls, the key remains with no TTL and that embed URL is never fetched again for non-staff users (they stay on the loading page). Use a single SET key 1 NX EX 60 so the lock cannot outlive the throttle window.

false_negatives.golden_comment: postMessage targetOrigin should be the origin (scheme+host+port), not the full referrer URL; using the full URL will cause the message to be dropped and prevent resizing.

The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.

An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.

true_positives.golden_comment: The downsize method is defined twice. The second definition, which expects a single dimensions string parameter, overrides the first, which expected separate max_width and max_height parameters. This makes the original method unreachable and breaks existing code that calls it with separate width and height arguments.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Second downsize definition replaces the width/height method

Ruby does not overload methods. The new downsize(from, to, dimensions, opts) at this line replaces the downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts) defined just above, so that width/height version never runs. Existing callers that pass numeric max width and height (the previous public signature, which this file still tries to keep) will bind the width to dimensions and the height to opts. optimize then evaluates opts[:allow_animation] and raises NoMethodError, or, if a hash is passed in the height slot, builds a geometry of just the width (for example "1024") instead of "1024x768". Thumbnail generation that still uses the old arity breaks. self.optimize's signature changed the same way (dimensions string instead of width, height), so any external optimize caller is broken too.
true_positives.reasoning: Both say the second downsize definition overrides the first width/height version, so that version is unreachable and existing callers break.

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoding maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024 ignores Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so the client-side limit can diverge from server-side and per-type settings (also applies to the 413 handler below).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Client upload limit is hardcoded and ignores per-type site settings

validateUploadedFile used to enforce Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so images and attachments had independent admin limits. It now always rejects above 10 * 1024 KB and no longer uses type. Attachments larger than max_attachment_size_kb but under 10MB are sent and then fail (or are stored, if the server trusts the client). Images the admin allowed above 10MB are blocked in the composer even though they would not need downsizing. The 413 handler at line 246 has the same hardcode, so a proxy rejection is reported as a 10MB limit even when nginx or max_image_size_kb is different. uploads_controller.rb also downloads API URLs with a fixed 10.megabytes cap, so raising max_image_size_kb above 10MB cannot be honored on that path either.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate raises the same issue as the golden comment: maxSizeKB is hardcoded to 10*1024 and ignores the per-type site settings. It also notes that the 413 handler has the same hardcode, which the golden comment mentions too.

true_positives.golden_comment: The loop checking `tempfile.size` may never terminate correctly due to stale cached size, leading to potential infinite loops or incorrect file handling after modifications.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
In-place downsize can corrupt the upload and the result is ignored

The new loop calls OptimizedImage.downsize with the same path for input and output (tempfile.path to tempfile.path) and ignores the boolean it returns. ImageMagick convert cannot safely read and write one file: it often truncates the destination before the source is fully read, so a failed or partial convert destroys the upload. The open Tempfile still refers to the original inode, so after convert replaces the path, tempfile.size and whatever Upload.create_for reads from the handle can stay on the old bytes or sit past the new EOF. The loop then either keeps shrinking a stale size or stores a corrupt/empty/original image. If convert or ImageOptim fails, execution still falls through to Upload.create_for. Five 80% passes also only reach about a third of the linear dimensions, so a file can remain over SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb and still be uploaded.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly says tempfile.size can stay stale after the in-place convert, which causes the loop to keep shrinking against an outdated size or to handle the file incorrectly. That is the same issue the golden comment describes.

false_positives.candidate:
Oversized GIFs lose animation and SVGs are sent through convert

Auto-downsize always goes through OptimizedImage.downsize, whose non-animated instructions run convert with [0] (first frame only). The animated/gifsicle path is selected only when the filesystem path matches /\.GIF$/i. Rack and FileHelper temp paths do not keep the original filename extension, and this call never copies the bytes to a path ending in .gif, so allow_animation: SiteSetting.allow_animated_thumbnails never takes effect. Every oversized GIF is flattened to one frame and that result is what gets stored as the original upload, even when animated thumbnails are allowed. The same branch also runs for any FileHelper.is_image? filename, including SVG, unlike OptimizedImage.create_for which copies SVGs instead of converting them. convert will fail or rasterize the SVG and that output is then saved under the original .svg name.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Passing 80% as the dimensions can fail for animated GIFs when allow_animated_thumbnails is true, since the animated path uses gifsicle --resize-fit which expects WxH geometry, not a percentage; downsizing would then silently fail.

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: Potential nil pointer exception - if no TopicUser record exists, tu will be nil and calling methods on it will crash
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Unsubscribe crashes when the user has no TopicUser row

TopicsController#unsubscribe loads the per-user row with TopicUser.find_by and immediately reads tu.notification_level. If that row does not exist (logged-in user who can see the topic but has never had a topic_users record, or a category/mailing-list recipient whose row was never created), tu is nil and this raises NoMethodError. The email link then returns 500 and the notification level is not changed, so the unsubscribe action fails for exactly the people who need it. Use TopicUser.change (which inserts a row when missing) or create a muted row before updating.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug: TopicUser.find_by returns nil when no record exists, so calling methods on tu raises an error.

false_positives.candidate:
One-click unsubscribe does not stop notifications for watching or tracking users

The email copy and the new client string both say the link stops notifications for this topic, but the action only mutes when notification_level is regular or already muted. Watching (3) and tracking (2) are greater than regular, so they are downgraded to regular instead of muted. Regular still generates reply, mention, and quote notifications, so a user who is emailed because they are watching the topic — the main case for a per-topic unsubscribe link — keeps receiving those emails after one click. The confirmation page always claims notifications have stopped, and nothing tells them they must click again to actually mute.

Direct TopicUser save leaves notifications_reason_id nil so auto-track undoes the change

The new action assigns notification_level and calls save! instead of TopicUser.change. change is what sets notifications_changed_at, notifications_reason_id (user_changed), and the MessageBus notification_level_change event. Leaving notifications_reason_id nil means the existing auto-track logic in TopicUser.update_last_read and TopicUser.auto_track will treat the row as never explicitly chosen and set it back to tracking once the user has viewed the topic long enough (or on the next auto_track call). A successful mute is therefore silently reverted the next time they read the topic, and other open tabs are not told the level changed.

Unsubscribe is a cookie-authenticated GET with no recipient token GET /t/:slug/:topic_id/unsubscribe (and /t/:topic_id/unsubscribe, which 301s to the slugged URL) changes notification state with no CSRF token and no per-recipient unsubscribe key. ensure_logged_in only checks the browser session. Any site can trigger it while the victim is logged in (for example an to /t//unsubscribe); the browser sends session cookies, follows the 301, and the second request mutates state. The link also is not bound to the user who was emailed: whoever is logged in is the account that is changed, so a shared browser, staff session, or forwarded mail unsubscribes the wrong person while the recipient keeps getting mail. Email link scanners that do send cookies can apply the change without a click, and because the handler is not idempotent for watching users a second fetch drops them from regular to muted. This needs a POST (or a one-time key like the digest unsubscribe key) that identifies the recipient.

Unsubscribe template will not be resolved by the new route

The route is registered as a top-level topicUnsubscribe at /t/:slug/:id/unsubscribe (app-route-map.js.es6). Ember resolves that to the template, controller, and view names topic-unsubscribe. The controller and view were added under those names, but the template was added at templates/topic/unsubscribe.hbs, which compiles to topic/unsubscribe and is only used by a nested topic.unsubscribe route. Nothing calls renderTemplate to bridge the gap, so after the server has already changed the notification level the confirmation UI throws a missing-template error (or renders an empty outlet). The stop-notifications copy and the notification-level dropdown never appear. Move the template to templates/topic-unsubscribe.hbs, or nest the route as topic.unsubscribe and move the controller/view to match.

No coverage for the unsubscribe action or the new email link

The only spec change passes unsubscribe_url into an existing MessageBuilder example so I18n interpolation does not raise, and still only asserts that the preferences URL is in the body. Nothing asserts the new per-topic sentence or URL, and there is no request/controller spec for TopicsController#unsubscribe. The nil TopicUser crash, the watching-to-regular branch, the missing notifications_reason_id, the slug redirect, and the wrong-session GET mutation would all merge unnoticed.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Typo in property name: 'stopNotificiationsText' should be 'stopNotificationsText' (missing 'n' in 'Notifications')

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: macOS-specific sed syntax with empty string after -i flag will fail on Linux systems
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Webhook helper is macOS-only and writes .env relative to the cwd

The new script updates GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL with sed -i '' (BSD sed). On GNU sed that form treats '' as the script and does not edit the file, so Linux developers never get the tunnel URL written. ENV_FILE is ../.env relative to the current working directory, not the script path: running bash scripts/test-gcal-webhooks.sh from the repo root writes the parent directory's .env, not the app env file. cleanup also always exits 0, so a failed tunnel startup is reported as success.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly says sed -i '' is BSD/macOS-only syntax that fails on GNU sed (Linux). That is the same issue as the golden comment. The candidate also raises extra points, but they don't change the match.

false_positives.candidate:
Deleting cache leaves the UI showing the old cache status

deleteCacheMutation only toasts and calls the optional onSuccess prop. Unlike the disconnect mutation in the same component, it never invalidates viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars. That query is what supplies cacheUpdatedAt, and SelectedCalendarsSettingsWebWrapper loads it with refetchOnWindowFocus: false. After a successful delete the menu still shows the previous "Last updated" time and "Delete cached data" until a full remount, so the action looks like it failed.

Cache status treats expired rows as a live cache

getCacheStatusByCredentialIds groups CalendarCache by credentialId and takes max(updatedAt) with no expiresAt filter. getCachedAvailability only treats a row as a hit when expiresAt is still in the future. Any leftover expired row therefore makes connected calendars report cacheUpdatedAt and the dropdown offers "Delete cached data" even though availability lookups are already cache misses. The status does not mean the cache is serving data.

Backfill stamps every existing cache as updated at migrate time

The new updatedAt column is added as NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW(), so every existing CalendarCache row gets the migration timestamp rather than when it was actually written. CalendarCache has no createdAt; the only freshness signal already stored is expiresAt (writes set it to about now + 30 days). After deploy, every Google credential with any historical cache row shows "Last updated" as the deploy time, including stale and expired caches, which defeats the status feature. Backfill from expiresAt minus the cache TTL (and drop the default only if you still want Prisma @updatedAt to own later writes) before this ships; it cannot be reconstructed later.

Cache delete is undone by active Google watches

deleteCacheHandler only runs calendarCache.deleteMany for the credential. It does not stop google channel subscriptions on SelectedCalendar, and GoogleCalendarService.fetchAvailabilityAndSetCache (called from the webhook path) writes CalendarCache again and then touches those selected calendars. The confirmation copy says the delete cannot be undone, but the next notification recreates the rows. Users clearing a bad cache will see it return with no explanation, and a reload can show a new timestamp as if the delete did not stick.

Delegation calendar cache is invisible to status and delete

Cache status is loaded only via getCacheStatusByCredentialIds(connected calendar credential ids). The same repository documents that in-memory delegation credentials use negative ids that are not stored on CalendarCache, and reads for those users are keyed by userId plus the free/busy key so they can reuse a real credential's cache. Those org/delegation Google connections — the users the calendar-cache feature flag is aimed at — always get cacheUpdatedAt null, so the new menu never offers delete. deleteCacheHandler cannot fix that either: it requires a Credential row with id = credentialId and userId = the session user, which does not match a negative in-memory id or a cache row owned by another credential id.

dev:cron now calls tsx, which this package does not depend on

dev:cron changed from ts-node cron-tester.ts to npx tsx cron-tester.ts. ts-node is a declared devDependency; tsx is not in this package.json, and the app pins Yarn 3.4.1, where npx is not the workspace runner and will try to fetch tsx outside the lockfile. yarn dev:cron fails offline or in CI, or runs an unpinned tsx. This change is unrelated to calendar cache and should stay on the declared runner or add tsx as a dependency and invoke it through Yarn.

No tests for deleteCache ownership or status mapping

deleteCache is a new authenticated mutation that deletes every CalendarCache row for a client-supplied credentialId after a userId check, and connectedCalendars now depends on getCacheStatusByCredentialIds. Nothing in the PR covers another user (or a negative delegation id) being rejected, a successful delete actually removing rows, or expired versus live rows being mapped to cacheUpdatedAt. A regression in the ownership where-clause would ship silently.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The updateManyByCredentialId call uses an empty data object, which prevents Prisma's @updatedAt decorator from updating the updatedAt timestamp. This results in inaccurate cache status tracking, as the timestamp isn't updated when the cache is refreshed. To fix this, explicitly set the updatedAt field.

Throwing a generic Error for authentication failures results in a 500 response in tRPC. Instead, it should return a structured TRPCError with an appropriate code, such as FORBIDDEN, to accurately reflect the error type.
Date is formatted with hardcoded 'en-US' locale instead of using the user's locale from useLocale, which can lead to incorrect date representation for users in different locales.

true_positives.golden_comment: Incorrect end time calculation using slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Working-hours fallback rejects valid split shifts and ignores the slot end

When no date override matches, availability is decided by workingHours.find: any same-day window whose range does not contain the slot makes the callback return true and the slot is rejected. A host with a lunch break (two windows on the same weekday) therefore loses every slot, including ones that sit fully inside the other window. The end minute is copied from slotStartTime rather than the slot end, so a slot that starts inside hours but runs past workingHour.endTime is treated as inside. Days with no working-hour entry never match, so they are treated as free; a fixed host who does not work that weekday is not excluded. For round-robin this filter is what is supposed to keep fixed hosts from being booked outside their own hours, and it does the opposite for split schedules.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly says the end minute is copied from slotStartTime instead of the slot end, which is the golden issue. It also raises other problems, but it still covers this one.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Multiple override ranges on one day reject every slot

The date-override filter uses Array.find and treats a true callback as "this slot is not bookable". Each range returns true when the slot merely falls outside that one range. On a day with two ranges (for example 09:00-12:00 and 14:00-17:00), a slot inside the first range is outside the second, so find succeeds and checkIfIsAvailable returns false. Every slot is outside at least one range, so a split date override blocks the entire day instead of opening those windows. The start===end all-day-block branch just above never runs either: it compares two dayjs instances with ===, which is always false, so a zero-length override is not handled as a full-day block.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate's main point is a different bug, the find logic with multiple ranges. However, it also says explicitly that the start===end branch compares two dayjs instances with ===, which is always false. That is the same issue the golden comment raises.

false_positives.candidate:
In-override slots skip busy checks and can double-book

checkIfIsAvailable now returns true as soon as a date override exists for that calendar day and the slot is not strictly outside it. That return happens before the busy-interval scan, so calendar conflicts and existing Cal bookings are ignored for every fixed host (personal events, collective hosts, and round-robin fixed hosts all go through this path). A host who sets a date override and already has a meeting inside that window will still be offered those slots, and the booking can be confirmed on top of the conflict. Partial overlaps are treated as inside as well: a slot that starts before the override and ends during it is not rejected, so the meeting can begin outside the override hours.

Override timezone shift wraps at midnight and lands on the wrong day

Date-override start and end are shifted by inviteeUtcOffset - organizerUtcOffset and then reduced to hour and minute only. Those values are minutes within 0-1439, so a shift that crosses midnight is applied to the invitee day already selected from the unadjusted UTC timestamp. An evening override viewed from a timezone ahead shows up as early-morning slots on the previous day; a morning override viewed from a timezone behind can produce endTime < startTime. buildSlots drops ranges with start >= end, and the caller has already removed that user's normal working hours for the day, so the override disappears and the host has no slots. The new test only compares +5:30 and +6:00, a 30-minute gap that never crosses midnight, so it does not catch this. Attendees several hours from the organizer still see the override at the wrong time, which is the bug this change is meant to fix.

Override day match compares server-local date to UTC

Whether an override applies is decided by formatting dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset) (local mode, so the server timezone) as YYYY MM DD and comparing it to slotStartTime, which was forced to UTC. isBefore/isAfter later compare absolute instants, but they only run after this date check. On any host whose TZ is not UTC, an override near midnight is attached to the wrong day or skipped entirely, and the fixed host's override is not enforced. Slot generation then falls through to weekly hours.

No test for fixed-host overrides on round-robin

The PR's stated fix is that a round-robin event must not offer slots when a fixed host's date override makes them unavailable, including across timezones. The only new assertion re-queries a single-user event in Asia/Dhaka and expects the same UTC instants as Asia/Kolkata. It never builds a ROUND_ROBIN event, never sets hosts[].isFixed, and never places a booking or calendar busy block inside an override. The double-book path, split override ranges, and fixed-host weekly hours can all regress without failing CI.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1 reads a possibly stale value and can lose increments under concurrency; consider an atomic increment via Prisma (increment: 1) to avoid race conditions (also applies to the similar update in the catch block).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Overlapping crons lose retry increments and can double-send

Both failure paths write `retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1` from the value loaded at the start of the loop instead of an atomic increment. Two overlapping runs of this cron can both select the same unscheduled reminder, both call Twilio, and both store the same next count. Recipients get duplicate texts, and because the stored count never moves past that shared value the `retryCount > 1` delete may never fire, so the retry cap does not hold under overlap. Claim the row (conditional update of scheduled, or increment in the database) before calling Twilio.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate points to the same problem as the golden comment. It flags that `retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1` uses a stale value and loses increments under concurrent runs, notes this applies to both failure paths, and suggests an atomic increment. The extra detail about duplicate sends adds to the point without changing the core issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: The deletion logic in scheduleSMSReminders.ts incorrectly deletes non-SMS workflow reminders (e.g., Email, WhatsApp) that have retryCount > 1. This occurs because the retryCount condition within the OR clause for deletion lacks a method: WorkflowMethods.SMS filter, causing it to apply to all reminder types instead of only SMS reminders, which is the intended scope of this function.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
retryCount cleanup deletes every workflow reminder, not just failed SMS

The new deleteMany ORs the existing past-due SMS clause with `{ retryCount: { gt: 1 } }` and that second clause has no method, scheduled, or date filter. WorkflowReminder is shared by EMAIL, SMS, and WHATSAPP. Every cron run therefore permanently deletes any reminder of any method once retryCount is greater than 1, including a row that was already scheduled and still has a provider referenceId. The comment on line 28 still says this only removes past SMS reminders. Scope the predicate to unscheduled SMS (and filter the later findMany the same way); otherwise any non-SMS writer of this new column, or a scheduled SMS row that ever exceeds the cap, loses the reminder.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same bug: the retryCount clause in the deleteMany OR has no SMS method filter, so it deletes non-SMS reminders (Email, WhatsApp).

false_positives.candidate:
A successful Twilio schedule is counted as a failure if saving the SID throws

twilio.scheduleSMS runs before the update that sets scheduled and referenceId. If Twilio accepts the message and that update throws, the new catch increments retryCount and leaves scheduled false and referenceId unset. The next cron loads the same reminder again and sends another SMS. After retryCount exceeds 1 the row is deleted, so the already accepted Twilio message can no longer be cancelled from a stored SID. Only a failed scheduleSMS call should advance retryCount; if persistence fails after Twilio accepts the message, cancel that message or retry the write without treating it as a failed send.

Missing number or empty body never counts toward the retry cap

retryCount is incremented only when Twilio returns a falsy result or throws, and only inside `if (message?.length > 0 && sendTo)`. If the attendee or step has no phone number, or the step has no reminder body and the template is not REMINDER, the loop skips the row and leaves scheduled false and retryCount at 0. That reminder is loaded again on every cron run until scheduledDate is in the past, which is the unbounded reschedule this PR is meant to stop. Treat a missing destination or empty message as a failed attempt, or delete the reminder immediately.

No test locks the retry cap or the delete scope

The new failure accounting and deleteMany predicate have no tests. A regression should assert that one failed SMS schedule leaves the reminder, that a second failure removes it on the next run, and that email or WhatsApp reminders and already scheduled SMS rows are not deleted by the retryCount clause. Without that, the unscoped OR delete and the off-path skips (no phone number, persistence failure after Twilio accepts) can ship unnoticed.

OR auth fragment is not fully parenthesized, so extra AND filters skip team bookings

Team and org authorization SQL is built as `(<team predicate>) OR (<user predicate>)` (org reduce at lines 171-174, team reduce at lines 204-207). Those parentheses wrap each branch only, not the whole OR. `getBaseConditions` returns that fragment as-is when there is no event-type or member filter (line 75). AND binds tighter than OR in PostgreSQL, so the intended caller query `WHERE ${await service.getBaseConditions()} AND "startTime" >= ${from} AND "startTime" < ${to}` — the replacement for the removed `findMany`, which ANDed caller filters onto the entire authorization object — is parsed as `team_booking_predicate OR (personal_booking_predicate AND startTime filters)`. Every team booking for that team or org is included no matter what date, status, or other AND predicates the caller adds. Insights over-count and can return bookings outside the window the caller applied. `getBaseConditions` only wraps the auth fragment when a service-level filter is also present (line 73).
